L44: ## I. Executive Summary
L45: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L46: These new drug applications (NDAs) for oral (NDA 215974) and injectable (NDA 215973) formulations of lenacapavir (LEN) were submitted by Gilead Sciences. LEN is a first-in-class human immunodeficiency type 1 (HIV-1) capsid inhibitor with Breakthrough Therapy Designation. These NDAs were initially submitted on June 28, 2021 and reviewed by the interdisciplinary review team.
L47: The intended indication for LEN is to be used in combination with other antiretroviral(s) for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment-experienced adult patients with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current antiretroviral regimen due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations.
L48: The product quality deficiencies identified in the first cycle review were: (1) product quality information to support the proposed container presentation in borosilicate glass vials was not acceptable for commercial use due to delamination of the vial containers and concern for glass particulate contamination, and (2) the data supporting aluminosilicate glass vials as an alternative were insufficient for full review. The Product Quality assessment team recommended a complete response based on these deficiencies. On February 28, 2022, Complete Response (CR) letters were issued to NDAs 215973 and 215974 due to product quality deficiencies.
L49: On June 27, 2022, the Applicant resubmitted both NDAs with additional product quality, nonclinical and additional long-term data from clinical Study GS-US-200-4625 (Study 4625). The Clinical, Clinical Virology, Clinical Pharmacology, Pharmacology/Toxicology, Statistics, Product Quality, and Regulatory disciplines did not identify issues that preclude approval.
L50: I, the signatory authority for these applications, agree that the benefit-risk assessment favors approval as described in the Benefit-Risk Framework below. The proposed proprietary name, Sunlenca, was found acceptable.
L51: The Applicant submitted one adequately designed phase 2/3 study, Study 4625, that provided substantial evidence of efficacy for the proposed indication. Supportive evidence of efficacy was provided by Study GS-US-200-4334 (Study 4334).
L52: The available safety data from the clinical trials demonstrate that LEN is safe for its intended use in the heavily treatment-experienced population. Based on the additional nonclinical and clinical data submitted for this second cycle review, I concur that the risks identified in the review of the clinical studies' data can be mitigated through labeling and further evaluated via routine pharmacovigilance and issuance of postmarketing commitments and postmarketing requirements. The risk of persistent injection site nodules and indurations was added to the Warnings and Precautions section of the proposed label, and a subsection for injection site reactions (ISRs) was included in the Adverse Reactions section in labeling. Additionally, the prolonged residual exposure of LEN is an important consideration for potential drug-drug interactions and development of resistance, and these risks have been clearly conveyed in product labeling.
L53: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L54: Additional information is needed to understand the contributing factors of ISRs with LEN, particularly the mechanism driving the persistence of injection site nodules and indurations in some subjects. The Clinical team has recommended a postmarketing requirement for further long-term assessment of ISRs.
L55: Based on our assessment of the relevant nonclinical and clinical data, we determined that particulates are unlikely to be responsible for the development or persistence of ISRs and do not pose an unacceptable safety risk for the indicated population. However, the Product Quality team has recommended three postmarketing commitments to further assess vial and compatibility, and to evaluate an alternative device and/or procedure for withdrawing the LEN injection from the vial to consistently reduce the presence of particulates in the drug product solution.
L56: For detailed information supporting the basis for the benefit-risk assessment, please refer to the details in this Integrated Assessment document and the Review Cycle 1 Integrated Review.
L57: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L58: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L59: Table 3. Benefit-Risk Framework
L60: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of Condition	Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is a transmissible virus that attacks and weakens the immune system. Without effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV-1 infection leads to progressive destruction of the immune system, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illnesses, and premature death in almost all cases.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that approximately 1.2 million people in the United States are living with HIV. In 2019, there were 15,815 deaths among people diagnosed with HIV (CDC 2022).
Maximal and durable suppression of HIV-1 RNA restores and/or preserves the immune system and reduces HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. Most treatment-adherent patients with limited previous HIV treatment experience can maximally and durably suppress HIV-1 RNA using a combination of two or more commercially available drugs from different drug classes.
Treatment failure occurs as a result of drug resistance, drug intolerance, and suboptimal adherence. Resistance-associated substitution(s) selected by one drug often confer(s) resistance to other drugs within that drug class, which further limits treatment options.
Heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) patients have limited remaining options for constructing a fully suppressive antiretroviral (ARV) regimen due to multidrug resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations.
HTE patients with limited treatment options and evidence of ongoing HIV replication despite ART are at high risk of AIDS-related morbidity and mortality.

Current Treatment Options	For patients with multidrug-resistant (MDR) HIV-1 infection, providers must individually tailor combination treatment regimens based on previous ARV exposure, cumulative viral resistance testing, drug safety and tolerability, and comorbid conditions.
The resulting ARV regimens are often burdensome, less well-tolerated, and associated with inadequate HIV-1 RNA suppression.
HTE patients with limited treatment options need new and effective therapies that lack cross-resistance with commercially available products, have a favorable tolerability profile, and allow for convenient dosing.
L61: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Benefit	Efficacy of lenacapavir (LEN) in HTE patients with multidrug resistance (MDR) who were failing treatment due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations was established in Study GS-US-200-4625 (Study 4625), a phase 2/3 study conducted in two cohorts.
The Study 4625 design was consistent with FDA's Guidance for Industry (FDA 2015).
Cohort 1 of Study 4625 was divided into two periods. During the first period, the Functional Monotherapy Period (FMP), 36 subjects in Study 4625 were randomized 2:1 to receive 14 days of oral LEN or placebo, respectively, in addition to their failing regimen. During the second period, the Maintenance Period, all subjects were unblinded and dosed with LEN (via subcutaneous injection following the 14-day oral lead-in) plus an optimized background regimen (OBR) through at least 52 weeks of follow-up. A second cohort enrolled 36 subjects, all of whom received open-label LEN plus an OBR, in parallel with Cohort 1.
The primary efficacy endpoint for Study 4625 was the proportion of subjects in Cohort 1 achieving a reduction in HIV-1 RNA of \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL from baseline at the end of the 14-day FMP. The difference in proportions in HIV-1 RNA \log_{10} copies/mL from Day 1 to Day 14 (LEN minus placebo) was -70.8 (95% confidence interval, -34.9, -90.0), demonstrating statistical superiority of LEN compared to placebo.
Early HIV-1 RNA decreases of >0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL in prior trials have been associated with reduction in clinical disease progression according to the FDA's Guidance for Industry (FDA 2015).
The key secondary efficacy endpoints assessed durability of virologic response following the FMP. After 26 and 52 weeks, 81% and 83% of participants continued to have HIV-1 RNA suppression (<50 copies/mL), respectively.
Supplemental efficacy data were provided by a phase 2 trial, Study GS-US-200-4334 (Study 4334). A total of 183 treatment-naïve people living with HIV (PLWH) was randomized to receive one of three regimens containing LEN or an active comparator (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide coformulated [B/F/TAF]). At the Week 54 analysis, 87% (136/157) of the subjects who received a regimen containing LEN and 92% (23/25) of the
LEN has demonstrated virologic activity in HTE patients with MDR HIV-1 infection who have limited treatment options.
The clinical study design and endpoints were appropriate for the HTE population with limited treatment options.
Reductions in HIV-1 RNA levels are highly predictive of meaningful clinical benefit, and LEN functional monotherapy was superior to placebo for reducing HIV-1 RNA over 14 days.
Study 4625 was uncontrolled during the maintenance period, so there are limitations in performing comparative analyses. However, the Week 52 analysis suggests that LEN contributes to the durability of virologic response when added to an OBR.
Availability of LEN would provide a new and effective first-in-class treatment option for HTE patients with multidrug resistant HIV-1 infection and limited alternative options due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations. Patients who achieve virologic suppression with LEN plus an OBR would have a reduced risk of HIV/AIDS-related morbidity and mortality.
L62: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Risk and Risk Management	
subjects who received B/F/TAF maintained HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL.
Study 4625 enrolled 72 subjects from the HTE patient population, and the safety database included 195 PLWH exposed to at least one 927 mg subcutaneous dose of LEN with the same proposed formulation for marketing. This safety database is smaller than the minimum recommended sample size of 300 to 500, as outlined by FDA's Guidance for Industry (FDA 2015); however, the overall clinical experience with any LEN formulation in PLWH and healthy volunteers was over 1200.
The most common adverse drug reactions during treatment with LEN were injection site reactions (ISRs). Most ISRs were mild to moderate in severity. There was one discontinuation due to an ISR (injection site nodule) in Study 4625. Injection site pain, swelling, and erythema were the most common specific ISRs reported, and typically lasted no more than a few days; however, indurations and nodules were reported to have longer durations, including several nodules that have persisted over 1 year of follow-up.
[REDACTED] (b) (4)
Emergence of resistance to LEN occurred frequently in virologic failures (9/22; 41%). The M66I capsid substitution emerged most frequently, alone or in combination with other LEN resistance-associated capsid substitutions including substitutions at Q67, K70, N74, A105, and T107. Virologic failure isolates with emergent LEN resistance-associated substitutions showed 6- to 1428-fold decreased susceptibility to LEN.
Based on the available data, LEN has an acceptable safety profile. Additional information, however, is needed to understand the contributing factors of ISRs with LEN, particularly the mechanism driving the persistence of injection site nodules and indurations in some subjects. The risk of persistent injection site nodules and indurations was added to the Warnings and Precautions section of the proposed label, and a subsection for ISRs was included in the Adverse Reactions section. This issue will be further addressed via routine pharmacovigilance and the issuance of a PMR.
Based on an assessment of the relevant nonclinical and clinical data, FDA determined that [REDACTED] (b) (4) particulates are unlikely to be responsible for the development or persistence of ISRs and do not pose an unacceptable safety risk for the indicated population. This issue will be further addressed via the issuance of PMCs.
LEN resistance emerges readily in virologic failures, thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen.
LEN resistance substitutions do not confer cross-resistance to other currently FDA-approved ARVs.
L63: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L64: Infection with HIV-1 continues to be a significant public health concern both domestically and internationally. Although the HIV treatment armamentarium is robust, additional effective antiretroviral (ARV) treatment options that provide greater flexibility in meeting patients' individual needs and facilitating their tolerance for and adherence to lifelong HIV-1 treatment are needed. Heavily treatment-experienced patients infected with MDR HIV-1 represent a rare but important subset of patients living with HIV. Patients
L65: with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 who cannot achieve complete virologic suppression with antiretroviral therapy (ART) are at high risk for AIDS-related morbidity and mortality. This population needs new and effective ARV products that lack cross-resistance with commercially available products, have a favorable tolerability profile, and allow for convenient dosing. LEN, a first-in-class HIV-1 capsid inhibitor with Breakthrough Therapy Drug designation, is one such product. The injectable formulation of LEN provides an option with the advantage of providing a new mechanism of action and maintenance dosing every 6 months following a lead-in with oral tablets. However, the prolonged residual exposure is an important consideration for potential drug-drug interactions and risk of development of resistance.
L66: The submitted evidence demonstrates LEN is effective in patients with multidrug resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current antiretroviral regimen due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations. The pivotal study, Study 4625 (CAPELLA), demonstrated superiority of LEN compared to placebo, when added to a failing regimen, for the proportion of subjects achieving a reduction in HIV-1 RNA of \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL after 14 days of treatment. The lack of a control group after Day 14 in Study 4625 limits the ability to precisely quantify the contribution of LEN to long-term virologic suppression. However, the contribution of LEN is reflected by the relatively high rate of virologic suppression achieved with LEN plus an optimized background regimen (OBR) through the Week 52 analysis in a population previously unable to achieve virologic suppression. Additional supportive data from the phase 2 study in treatment-naïve people living with HIV, Study 4334, demonstrated that regimens containing LEN achieved and maintained comparable virologic suppression through the Week 54 analysis to a standard-of-care control arm based on the results of the primary endpoint.
L67: The safety evaluation for LEN was adequate and the demonstrated clinical safety profile of LEN is acceptable for the proposed indication. With the exception of local injection site reactions and the risk of treatment-emergent resistance to LEN, the safety profile of LEN was generally favorable. While generally reported as mild to moderate in severity, injection site indurations and nodules remained persistent in several cases and were a cause of study drug discontinuations in Studies 4625 and 4334. Additional information, however, is needed to understand the contributing factors of ISRs with LEN, particularly the mechanism driving the persistence of injection site nodules and indurations in some subjects. These issues will be further addressed via routine pharmacovigilance and the issuance of a clinical PMR. Resistance to LEN emerges readily in virologic failures, thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen.
L68: Based upon review of all available efficacy and safety data, the benefits of LEN, in combination with other ARVs, clearly outweigh the risks for treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current ARV regimen due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations. The availability of LEN will provide a new and effective treatment option for this patient population.
L69: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L70: ## 3. Introduction
L71: Refer to Section 3 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle, and to Section 12 for additional regulatory history.
L72: The Applicant resubmitted two new drug applications (NDAs) in parallel for the two dosage forms of lenacapavir (LEN) (injection [NDA 215973] and tablet [NDA 215974]) and is seeking the indication of [REDACTED] (b) (4)
L73: LEN is a first-in-class HIV-1 capsid (CA) inhibitor and has been formulated for subcutaneous (SC) injection and as a tablet for oral use. The Applicant previously submitted an original investigational new drug application in 2017 to investigate LEN for injection and in 2018 to investigate LEN for oral use for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. (Refer to Section 12 for additional regulatory history.) This interdisciplinary assessment combines the review of NDA 215973 for LEN SC injection and NDA 215974 for LEN oral tablets.
L74: The Applicant conducted two clinical studies in support of the findings of safety and efficacy for LEN, Study GS-US-200-4625 (Study 4625, also referred to as CAPELLA) and Study GS-US-200-4334 (Study 4334, also referred to as CALIBRATE). Study 4625 is an ongoing phase 2/3 study designed to evaluate the antiviral activity of LEN administered as an add-on to a failing regimen (functional monotherapy) for heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) people living with HIV (PLWH). Study 4334 is a phase 2 study conducted in a treatment-naïve patient population and serves as supplementary support for the efficacy and safety evaluation of LEN for the indication of treating the HTE HIV-1 population. Of note, the results of Studies 4625 and 4334 have been published [Week 26, (Segal-Maurer et al. 2022)] and presented at the Conference on Retroviral and Opportunistic Infections 2022 [Week 52, (Ogbuagu et al. 2022) and Week 54, (Gupta et al. 2022)], respectively.
L75: Other currently available therapies used as part of the standard of care for the treatment of HIV-1 are discussed in more detail in Section 2. When constructing an ARV regimen for HTE PLWH, as noted by the U.S. HIV Treatment Guidelines (DHHS 2022a), the expected potency and whether a new drug as part of a complete regimen has a new mechanistic action are important considerations. Currently, no other ARV product in the CA inhibitor class for HIV-1 has been approved, nor have any been approved with a dosing interval as long as every 6 months (DHHS 2022b).
L76: At the conclusion of the first NDA review cycle for NDAs 215973 and 215974 on February 28, 2022, Complete Response letters were issued to the Applicant as a result of product quality deficiencies including: 1) Incompatibility between drug product and borosilicate glass vials, and 2) incomplete information with respect to Container Closure Integrity Testing. On May 24, 2022, a Type A, postaction teleconference was held between the Applicant and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA; also, *the Agency*) for NDAs 215973 and 215974; the purpose of this
L77: meeting was to discuss the deficiencies noted in the Complete Response letters and to obtain feedback on the Applicant's plan for resubmission of NDAs 215973 and 215974. On June 27, 2022, Gilead resubmitted NDAs 215973 and 215974.
L78: The primary efficacy results from Study 4625 were confirmed during the first NDA review cycle. Superiority of LEN compared to placebo was demonstrated for the proportion of HIV-1 RNA reduction \ge 0.5 \log_{10} from baseline to the end of the functional monotherapy period (FMP) at Day 14. The Week 26 and Week 52 HIV-1 RNA were planned to be evaluated as secondary endpoints; however, the majority of subjects did not complete the Week 52 assessment at the time of the original NDA submissions. The resubmissions of NDAs 215973 and 215974 provide additional long-term safety and efficacy data (Week 52) from Study 4625, as well as safety and efficacy data from other ongoing and completed clinical studies with LEN.
L79: ## 3.1. Review Issue List
L80: Refer to Section 3.1 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle. During the first cycle, the review team identified five review issues relevant to the evaluation of benefit and three review issues relevant to the evaluation of risk.
L81: ## Key Review Issues Related to Evaluation of Benefit (First Cycle)
L82: - The baseline imbalances of HIV-1 RNA level and cluster of differentiation (CD) 4+ cell count for Cohort 1 between the two randomized arms. The conclusion was that these baseline imbalances did not impact the interpretability of the primary efficacy result.
- The Applicant proposed a simplified dosing regimen that was not studied during the LEN clinical development program. The review team concluded that the simplified dosing regimen was acceptable, and the label should include recommendations for both the simplified regimen and the regimen used in Study 4625.
- In a clinical study designed for study in an HTE patient population, it is important to determine if the subjects are truly failing on their pre-study ARV regimen rather than due to nonadherence to the ARV drugs with no evidence of resistance in their supposed “failing” regimen. If subjects are nonadherent to the regimen and do not have resistance to the “failing” regimen during the LEN functional monotherapy period, it will be difficult to determine the contribution of LEN to efficacy in the background of other active or partially active ARVs. Supplementary sensitivity efficacy analyses removing subjects that had evidence they were not failing on their background regimens at study entry confirmed the primary endpoint analysis of LEN.
- The proposed subcutaneous maintenance dosing interval and the approach to missed doses outside of the recommended window (\pm 2 weeks). The review team concluded that the optimal dosing interval for SC LEN injection is 26 weeks, and the \pm 2-week dosing window is acceptable to provide flexibility and facilitate adherence to the SC LEN regimen.
L83: ## **Key Review Issues Related to Evaluation of Risk (First Cycle)**
L84: - Emergence of resistance was assessed in virologic failures (VFs) of a LEN-containing ARV regimen. The review team concluded that LEN resistance emerges readily in VFs and thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen. LEN resistance substitutions do not confer cross-resistance to other ARVs, but longer-term data from all subjects are required to determine durability of LEN and the other ARVs in the optimized background regimen (OBR).
- Injection site reactions (ISRs) were identified as the most common adverse drug reaction (ADR) among subjects who received SC injections of LEN; however, long-term experience of subjects after multiple injections was limited in Studies 4625 and 4334. The review team concluded that additional information is needed to understand the contributing factors of ISRs with LEN, particularly for subjects who have prolonged time to resolution of nodules and indurations.
- The risk of supratherapeutic LEN exposures when LEN is combined with a background regimen containing boosted protease inhibitors was not prospectively assessed in Study 4625. The review team conducted a post hoc analysis and concluded that labeling for LEN should include the recommendation against concomitant administration of atazanavir/cobicistat or atazanavir/ritonavir. No clinically significant drug interactions were observed with darunavir/cobicistat.
L85: For the NDA resubmissions, the review team identified one review issue relevant to the evaluation of benefit (Section 6.3) and two review issues relevant to the evaluation of risk (Section 7.7).
L86: ## **3.1.1. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit**
L87: ## **3.1.1.1. Extended Efficacy Data From Study 4625 (Week 52 Interim Analyses for Cohorts 1 and 2)**
L88: The assessment of the durability of virologic response in HTE subjects is an important component of understanding the overall efficacy of LEN.
L89: ## 3.1.2. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L90: ## 3.1.2.1. Resistance Assessments of Virologic Failures at Week 52
L91: The assessment of resistance emergence in VFs of an LEN-containing ARV regimen is critical to interpreting the overall risk-benefit of LEN and understanding the durability of LEN as a component of an ARV regimen in a HTE patient population.
L92: ## 3.1.2.2. Injection Site Reactions
L93: ISRs were identified as the most commonly reported ADRs among subjects who received SC LEN injections; however, the long-term experience of subjects with multiple SC LEN injections was limited in Studies 4625 and 4334.

L172: ## 6.3. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L173: ## 6.3.1. Extended Efficacy Data From Study 4625 (Week 52 Interim Analyses for Cohorts 1 and 2)
L174: ## Issue
L175: Do the efficacy data from the Week 52 interim analysis demonstrate durability of the contribution of LEN?
L176: ## Background
L177: Prior to enrollment, the HTE population in Study 4625 had not been able to achieve virologic suppression with currently available therapy. Therefore, assessing the durability of virologic response in HTE subjects is an important component of understanding the overall efficacy of LEN.
L178: ## Assessment
L179: From Day 14 onward, all subjects in Cohort 1 were transitioned from their initial (failing) background regimen to an optimized regimen in combination with open-label LEN. There was no comparator arm during the maintenance period, and the interim analysis included follow-up through Week 52.
L180: The proportion of subjects in Cohort 1 who achieved HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL was 81% at Week 26 (presented at Cycle 1 of the review), and 83% at Week 52. The durability of virologic response was maintained. Details of the analyses for virologic outcomes at Week 52 for Cohorts 1 and 2 are presented in Table 8. Additional extended follow-up is anticipated (optional through 104 weeks).
L181: Comparing the virologic response of LEN to other drugs indicated for the HTE population, proportions of subjects who achieved HIV-1 RNA &lt;40 copies/mL was 54% at Week 48 for fostemsavir, and proportions of subjects who achieved HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL was 43% at Week 25 for ibalizumab-uiyk. These comparisons across these different studies, however, should be considered with caution.
L182: ## Conclusion
L183: Despite the limitations in the assessment of extended efficacy data, such as the lack of a comparator arm during the maintenance period and uncertainties associated with cross-study comparisons, the available data suggest that LEN contributes to the durable antiretroviral effect as part of an optimized background regimen.
L184: ## 7. Risk and Risk Management
L185: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L186: Refer to Section 7.1 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle. Please also refer to Section 13. No new potential risks were identified based on the Pharmacology Toxicology review of additional nonclinical data.
L187: ## 7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L188: Refer to Section 7.2 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle. LEN is the first in a new class of antiretroviral drugs; therefore, no previously described clinical experience is available to inform any specific safety concern regarding CA inhibitors.
L189: Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported with combination antiretroviral therapy, particularly in the initial phase of treatment, in patients whose immune systems develop an inflammatory response to indolent or residual opportunistic infections. This is also often particularly relevant in a HTE patient population.
L190: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L191: Loss of virologic response because of drug-drug interactions has been included as a warning in labeling for other ARVs.
L192: For other ARVs that are administered in an injectable form, such as CABENUVA (a long-acting formulation of two drugs, cabotegravir and rilpivirine), ISRs are the most commonly reported adverse reactions. The most commonly reported ISR that is included in the CABENUVA labeling is pain/discomfort (71% to 79% of subjects). The CABENUVA labeling also includes the following other ISRs: nodules (10% to 17% of subjects), induration (7% to 12% of subjects), swelling (5% to 8% of subjects), erythema (2% to 4% of subjects), pruritus (4% to 5% of subjects), bruising/discoloration (2% to 3% of subjects), and warmth (1% to 2% of subjects) (ViiV-Healthcare 2022).
L193: ## 7.3. Potential Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L194: During the current review cycle, the European Medicines Agency granted Marketing Authorization to LEN on August 17, 2022 (EMA 2022). Per the Applicant,
L195: (b) (4)
L196: no potential safety concerns have been identified through postmarket experience at this time. Following the priority review of New Drug Submissions, Sunlenca (LEN) was granted marketing authorization (Notice of Compliance) in Canada on November 2, 2022 (Health-Canada 2022).
L197: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L198: Refer to Section 7.4 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle.
L199: In the original NDA submissions, the primary safety data for LEN were derived from an ongoing phase 2/3 study of LEN in combination with an OBR in HTE PLWH (Study 4625). In addition, supportive safety data were derived from an ongoing phase 2 study of LEN in combination with other ARVs in treatment-naïve PLWH (Study 4334), and an Integrated Summary of Safety presenting a pooled analysis of two phase 1 studies evaluating the safety of LEN in healthy subjects (Study GS-US-200-4538 [Study 4538] and Study 5709). Of the two phase 1 studies, only Study 5709 was ongoing at the time of the original submission. Study 4538 had been completed, and the full clinical study report was included in the original NDA submissions.
L200: The review team did not identify any major data quality or integrity issues that preclude performing a safety review. No major issues were identified with respect to recording, coding, and categorizing AEs. The Applicant's translations of verbatim terms to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities preferred terms for the events reported in Studies 4625 and 4334 were reviewed and were found to be acceptable.
L201: This review summarizes the NDA resubmissions, which included additional longer-term safety data from the two studies included in the original NDA submissions:
L202: - The primary study, Study 4625 (a phase 2/3 study in HTE PLWH with multidrug resistance): analyses were conducted after all subjects in both Cohorts 1 and 2 had completed the Week 52 visit or prematurely discontinued study drug (February 2022 data cut date).
L203: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L204: - Study 4334 (a phase 2 study in treatment-naïve PLWH): Analyses were conducted after all subjects had completed the Week 54 visit (September 2021 data cut date).
L205: In addition, the Applicant included a summary of overall LEN exposure from all ongoing and completed studies.
L206: In the NDA resubmissions safety update report, updated cumulative safety data from the first dose of study drug through the safety update data cut date were provided for Studies 4625, 4334, and 5709. For Study 4625, the NDA resubmission safety update data-cut date was in February 2022, after all subjects in both Cohorts 1 and 2 had completed their Week 52 visit (i.e., 52 weeks after their first dose of SC LEN) or prematurely discontinued study drug. In addition, the safety update included safety data from six phase 1 studies with LEN that were not included in the original NDA submissions; these studies are evaluating the safety of SC, intramuscular, and oral LEN in healthy adult subjects. One of the six phase 1 studies (Study GS-US-536-5816 [Study 5816]) is evaluating the safety of SC LEN in combination with two broadly neutralizing anti-HIV-1 antibodies in virologically suppressed adults with HIV-1 infection. The studies providing data for this safety report are listed in Table 11.

L213: ## **Approach to Assessment of Clinical Trial Data**
L214: The review approach for assessment of risk consisted of the evaluation of safety data from Study 4625 and Study 4334 separately, as well as the pooled safety data from phase 1 studies. These
L215: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L216: studies were reviewed separately because the studies enrolled different patient populations. Study 4625 enrolled an HTE population, whereas Study 4334 enrolled a treatment-naïve population, and the phase 1 studies enrolled healthy adults. Results of individual studies are highlighted where important differences may have emerged.
L217: Clinical-study data from Studies 4635 and 4334 were independently analyzed using JMP v. 16.2.0, Analysis Studio v. 1.6.0, and JMP Clinical v. 8.0. Additional analyses were provided by the Clinical Data Scientist support team. All safety assessments and conclusions are those of the clinical review team unless otherwise specified. Prespecified hypothesis testing was not proposed for safety outcomes in Study 4625 or 4334; comparisons are therefore based on descriptive analyses.
L218: Comparisons across arms in Study 4625 were limited because assessment during the randomized portion of the study were limited to the 14-day FMP with only the oral administration of LEN. As a general approach, attribution of events due to LEN comparisons across study arms were derived largely from Study 4334 and selected cohorts from phase 1. For relevance to the proposed SC dosing, study arms that included SC LEN were combined and compared to another active control arm randomized to B/F/TAF. Because the pooled phase 1 data were placebo-controlled in healthy volunteers, comparisons across arms were generally more acceptable for the purpose of assessing contribution of LEN; however, the overall sample size achieved in this analysis was small and duration of follow-up was shorter.
L219: In the Applicant's proposed labeling for LEN, Adverse Reactions (Section 6.1) included only data from Study 4625 as this study included the relevant patient population (HTE) for the proposed indication, whereas Study 4334 included treatment-naïve subjects anticipated to have significant differences in underlying disease severity and comorbid conditions.
L220: ## 7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
L221: Refer to Section 7.5 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 from the first cycle.
L222: Overall, the safety database is adequate to assess the safety of LEN for the proposed indication, dosage regimen, and patient population (HTE).
L223: At the time of the NDA resubmissions, 1508 subjects were enrolled in clinical studies and received at least one dose of LEN, regardless of route (SC, by mouth, or intravenous), formulation, or population (healthy, PLWH). Excluding subjects who received LEN or LEN placebo for two ongoing blinded studies, the total number of subjects are at least 1272. A total of 797 subjects (healthy, PLWH) have received at least one subcutaneous dose of LEN, and a total of 303 subjects with HIV have received LEN (any route). The total number of PLWH who received one dose of 927 mg SC LEN, with the same proposed SC formulation or equivalent oral dose that is expected to achieve the targeted exposure for at least 6 months, was 195 (Table 12).

L246: ## 7.6. Safety Findings and Concerns Based on Review of Clinical Safety Database
L247: The demonstrated safety profile of LEN in HTE subjects with MDR HIV-1 infection is acceptable at the proposed doses by mouth and SC. Overall, there is no clear pattern of LEN-related safety issues considered severe or life-threatening (Grade 3 or 4). Deaths were uncommon, and there were no patterns observed among serious adverse events (SAEs). None of the deaths nor SAEs were considered to be study-drug related in Studies 4625 and 4334. A small number of subjects from Studies 4625 and 4334 experienced ISRs resulting in discontinuation of LEN, which is consistent with a long-acting injectable drug.
L248: ## 7.6.1. Safety Findings and Concerns, Studies 4625 and 4334
L249: ## 7.6.1.1. Overall Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event Summary, Studies 4625 and 4334
L250: An overview of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) in Study 4625 through at least the Week 52 visit date is shown in Table 15. Overall, 96% of subjects in the total LEN group experienced at least one TEAE.
L251: An overview of the TEAEs in Study 4334 through at least the Week 54 visit date is shown in Table 16. Overall, 88% of subjects in the total LEN group, and 84% of subjects in the B/F/TAF group experienced at least one TEAE.
L252: Across Studies 4625 and 4334, there were no drug-related SAEs, very few discontinuations because of AEs, and very few Grade \ge 3 AEs considered by the investigator to be study drug-related. Differences in AEs reported across these two studies likely reflect underlying differences in the patient populations.

L275: ## 7.6.1.3. Serious Adverse Events, Studies 4625 and 4334
L276: In Study 4625, since the Week 26 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), six additional subjects experienced the following SAEs: coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19; two subjects), genital herpes simplex (one subject), pneumonia (one subject), pneumonia mycoplasmal, pancytopenia, dehydration, and acute respiratory failure (one subject), and septic shock, renal impairment, shock (one subject).
L277: In Study 4334, after the Week 28 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), one subject experienced an SAE of uterine leiomyoma (SC LEN + emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide coformulated [F/TAF]→tenofovir alafenamide [TAF] group), and one subject experienced an SAE of hepatitis A (LEN + [F/TAF→bictegravir [BIC] group), which is discussed further in Section 7.6.4.6).

See Section 17.2 for additional details.

L296: ## 7.6.1.4. Dropouts and/or Discontinuations Due to Adverse Events, Studies 4625 and 4334
L297: In Study 4625, after the Week 26 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), one subject (1.4%) in Cohort 1 experienced a nonserious TEAE of injection site nodule (Grade 1) after receiving the Week 52 SC LEN injections, which led to premature discontinuation of LEN during the Extension Phase (data collected after Week 52). The TEAE of injection site nodule was assessed as related to LEN by the investigator and had not resolved by the data cut date. At the time of the original NDA submission, no subject had prematurely discontinued study drug because of an AE; however, this subject's premature discontinuation was included in the 90-Day Safety Update from the original NDA submissions. See Sections 7.6.3.4 and 7.7.2.
L298: In Study 4334, after the Week 28 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), one subject in the total SC LEN group experienced nonserious TEAEs of injection site erythema (Grade 1) and injection site swelling (Grade 1) that led to premature discontinuation of LEN. In total, 3 of 105 subjects (2.9%) in the SC LEN total group discontinued study drug due to ISRs (injection site induration [2 subjects], injection site erythema [1 subject], and injection site swelling [1 subject]); all the ISRs were nonserious and Grade 1 in severity. See Section 7.7.2.
L299: *Clinical Reviewer's Assessment: Nonserious, Grade 1 ISRs were the only AEs that led to the discontinuation of LEN in Studies 4625 and 4334. The LEN labeling includes the one subject from Study 4625 who discontinued LEN because of an AE (Grade 1 injection site nodule); in addition, ISRs are adequately described as adverse drug reactions (ADRs) associated with SC LEN in labeling. See Section 7.7.2 for details.*
L300: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Studies 4625 and 4334
L301: In Study 4625, a TEAE was defined as an AE that began on or after the first dose date of LEN; for participants who discontinued from the oral LEN, only AEs collected up to 60 days after the last dose date were considered treatment emergent. In Study 4334, TEAEs began on or after the first dose date of study drug up to last exposure date after permanent discontinuation of study drug, or led to premature study drug discontinuation.
L302: A combination of data from Studies 4625 and 4334 were used to assess the general AE profile of LEN. Although details of safety information from Study 4334 will not be presented in the LEN
L303: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use

L304: labeling, Study 4334 was important in this assessment because it serves as supplementary support for the safety evaluation of LEN.

L325: ## 7.6.2. Laboratory Findings Studies 4625 and 4334
L326: Most laboratory abnormalities in Studies 4625 and 4334 were generally not clinically significant (Grade 1 or 2), and occurred in subjects who had previous underlying conditions (e.g., diabetes), or there was an alternative explanation (e.g., creatine kinase elevation after strenuous activity).
L327: In Study 4625, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 18 (25.0%) of 72 subjects. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 5 (6.9%) of 72 subjects. Grade 3 or 4 abnormalities that occurred in more than two subjects included high creatinine, high fasting glucose, high nonfasting glucose, glycosuria, and proteinuria. The frequency of subjects with Grade 3 or Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities at Week 52 (23 subjects; 31.9%) was similar to Week 26 (19 subjects; 26.4%). See the discussion in Section 7.6.3.6.
L328: In Study 4334, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 26 (16.6%) of 157 subjects who received LEN (the total LEN group) and 6 (24.0%) of the 25 subjects in the B/F/TAF group. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 13 (8.3%) of 157 subjects in the total LEN group and no subjects in the B/F/TAF group. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 13 (8.3%) of 157 subjects in the total LEN group, including the following in more than one subject: high creatine kinase, high alanine aminotransferase (ALT), hyperbilirubinemia, and glycosuria. The frequency of subjects with Grade 3 or Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities at Week 54 (39 subjects; 24.8%) was similar to Week 28 (26 subjects; 16.6%). See the discussion in Section 7.6.4.6.
L329: Trends in vital signs and body weight in Studies 4625 (Week 52 analysis) and 4334 (Week 54 analysis) were also reviewed. There were no clinically relevant changes from baseline or in
L330: median values for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, pulse, respiration rate, or body temperature. In Study 4625, the median (quartile 1, quartile 3) increase in body weight was 1.3 (-2.0, 4.3) kg; only one subject had an ADR of weight increased (Grade 1). In Study 4334, the median increase in body weight was 2.6 (0.2, 6.8) kg and 2.3 (-3.1, 7.3) kg in the total LEN group and the B/F/TAF group, respectively; two subjects receiving LEN had ADRs of weight increased (oral LEN + F/TAF [Grade 1]; SC LEN + [F/TAF→TAF] [Grade 2]), and 1 subject receiving B/F/TAF had an ADR of weight increased (Grade 1).

L348: ## 7.6.3.2. Deaths
L349: After the Week 26 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), one additional death was reported and is summarized below; this death was not considered related to LEN by the investigator. In total, from both cohorts of Study 4625, two subjects (2.8%) who received LEN died (Table 24).
L350: **Subject** (b) (6)
L351: This was a 48-year-old female in the United States with an extensive ongoing medical history that included the following: hypertension, asthma, hyperlipidemia, colitis, depression, and esophageal candidiasis. At baseline, HIV-1 RNA was 880 copies/mL and CD4+ cell count was 495/µL (15.8%). The subject's HIV-1 background regimen included doravirine, BIC, emtricitabine (FTC), and TAF. On Study Day 514, experienced mycoplasma pneumonia (Grade 3, assessed as not related); Study Day 528, developed pancytopenia (Grade 3, assessed as not related); Study Day 543, developed dehydration (Grade 3, assessed as not related); and Study Day 553, developed acute respiratory failure (Grade 5, assessed as not related). The subject died on Day 568 of hypoxemic respiratory failure and mycoplasma pneumonia. Autopsy findings revealed “consolidated lungs with superimposed severe acute bronchopneumonia on pre-existing acute and organizing acute respiratory distress syndrome leading to respiratory failure and sepsis.”

The injection site nodules were assessed by the investigator as related to LEN and were ongoing as of the data cut date. L390: ## 7.6.3.6. Laboratory Findings
L391: Most laboratory abnormalities in Study 4625 were generally not clinically significant (Grade 1 or 2), and occurred in subjects who had previous underlying conditions such as diabetes.
L392: In Study 4625, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 15 (21%) of 72 subjects. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 4 (6%) of 72 subjects. Grade 3 and 4 abnormalities that occurred in more than two subjects included high creatinine and high fasting glucose.
L393: Since the Week 28 analysis, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported for an additional nine subjects (LEN total group: six subjects; B/F/TAF group: three subjects) and Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported for an additional six subjects in the LEN total group. No Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in the B/F/TAF group. None of these laboratory
L394: abnormalities were clinically relevant, as they were transient, subjects had a medical history of underlying conditions (e.g., diabetes), or there was an alternative explanation (e.g., creatine kinase or aspartate aminotransferase [AST] elevation after strenuous activity).

L404: ## Hepatic Safety
L405: Overall, there were no clinically relevant changes from baseline in ALT, AST, or total bilirubin. Subjects with marked elevations in hepatic transaminases and/or bilirubin were evaluated for potential drug-induced liver injury (DILI). The subjects were reviewed to determine the etiology of the biochemistry elevations. If no other likely causes of DILI could be found, the case could be attributed to LEN.
L406: Overall, two subjects in Cohort 2 (one in the Week 26 interim analysis and the other in the Week 52 interim analysis) each experienced a Grade 3 increase in ALT and a Grade 4 increase in AST. Both subjects had concurrent alternative etiologies and are described below.
L407: In a screening analysis for DILI from all subjects during Study 4625, one subject (b) (6) in Cohort 2 (large blue dot [●] in Figure 5, who was a 27-year-old Asian male, experienced a Grade 4 increase in AST, a Grade 3 increase in ALT, and a Grade 2 increase in total bilirubin; these increases were also reported as one TEAE of alcohol abuse (Grade 3) and three TEAEs of alcoholic hepatitis (Grade 2/3). Laboratory trends are shown in Figure 6. The increases in ALT, AST, and ratio of AST to ALT were not considered related to LEN by the investigator. Although not shown in Figure 6, additional information provided by the Applicant showed improvement in AST, ALT, and total bilirubin when the subject abstained from alcohol while LEN continued. Because of the alternative cause reported, the increases in ALT, AST, and total bilirubin were not considered related to LEN.

L461: ## 7.6.4.6. Laboratory Findings
L462: Since the Week 28 interim analysis (original NDA submissions), Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported for an additional nine subjects (total LEN group, six subjects; B/F/TAF group, three subjects) and Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported for an additional six subjects in the total LEN group only.
L463: None of these laboratory abnormalities were clinically relevant, as they were transient, subjects had a medical history of underlying conditions (e.g., diabetes), or there was an alternative explanation (e.g., creatine kinase or elevation after strenuous activity).
L464: ## Hepatic Safety
L465: Subjects with marked elevations in hepatic transaminases and/or bilirubin were evaluated for potential DILI. The subjects were reviewed to determine the etiology of the biochemistry elevations. If no other causes could be found, the case would be attributed to LEN. Since the Week 28 analysis, an additional three subjects experienced Grade 3 or 4 high ALT. Two of the three subjects also experienced high AST, and one of the three subjects also experienced hyperbilirubinemia and had a Grade 3 TEAE of hepatitis A (Subject # [REDACTED](b)(6); Figure 8). For all subjects, the laboratory abnormalities either improved or returned to normal while on study drug.

L483: ## 7.7. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L484: ## 7.7.1. Resistance Assessments of Virologic Failures (VFs) at Week 52
L485: ## Issue
L486: The assessment of resistance emergence in VFs of a LEN-containing ARV regimen is critical to interpreting the overall risk-benefit of LEN and understanding the durability of LEN as a component of an ARV regimen in an HTE patient population.
L487: ## Background
L488: Genotypic and phenotypic analyses of the HIV-1 protease, reverse transcriptase (RT), integrase, and capsid (CA) proteins were performed at screening for all subjects enrolled in Study 4625.
L489: Resistance testing at postscreening timepoints was performed for any subject meeting the criteria of the resistance analysis, which included any subject who received at least one dose of study drug and met one of the following VF criteria:
L490: - HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL and &lt;1 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA reduction from the start of oral LEN at the Week 4 visit, confirmed at a scheduled or unscheduled visit at least 2 weeks following Week 4.
- At any visit, after achieving HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL, a rebound in HIV-1 RNA to \ge 50 copies/mL, which was subsequently confirmed at the following scheduled or unscheduled visit; OR
L491: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L492: - At any visit, a &gt;1 \log_{10} increase in HIV-1 RNA from the nadir, which was subsequently confirmed at the following scheduled or unscheduled visit.
- Any study subject with HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL at the study endpoint or study discontinuation who did not meet any of the criteria above.
L493: Monogram Biosciences, Inc. (South San Francisco, CA, USA) was the designated reference laboratory for all resistance analyses at screening and virologic failure. The PhenoSense GT® assay (Monogram Biosciences), which determines the genotype for the entire HIV-1 protease and amino acids 1 to 305 of RT and measures the drug susceptibility of all marketed protease and RT inhibitors based on that sequence, was performed for all subjects at screening. The GeneSeq Integrase assay was used to determine the sequence of the entire IN protein, and the PhenoSense Integrase assay measured the drug susceptibility of all marketed integrase strand-transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) based on that sequence (Monogram Biosciences). In cases of assay failure, alternative assays such as GeneSeq, GenoSure mg, or GenoSure Integrase (Monogram Biosciences) were used to obtain genotypic information.
L494: HIV-1 CA genotype was determined using the GenoSure Gag-Pro assay, which uses next-generation sequencing (NGS) to detect codon variants present at &gt;10\% frequency (Monogram Biosciences). The PhenoSense Gag-Pro assay (Monogram Biosciences) was used to assess phenotypic response to LEN.
L495: The phenotypic susceptibility of screening samples from enrolled subjects to entry inhibitors (enfuvirtide, fostemsavir, ibalizumab, maraviroc) was analyzed at the end of the enrollment period. These analyses were conducted using a combination of the Trofile and PhenoSense Entry assays (Monogram Biosciences), which determine the coreceptor tropism and the susceptibility to the inhibitors, respectively, based on the HIV-1 envelope from the subject's sample.
L496: ## Assessment
L497: ## Week 52 Clinical Resistance Emergence
L498: In Study 4625, 31% (22 of 72) met the criteria for resistance analyses through Week 52 (HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL at confirmed VF [suboptimal virologic response at Week 4, virologic rebound, or viremia at last visit]) (Table 33 and Table 34; see also Table 54). The 22 confirmed VFs had postbaseline CA genotypic resistance data, comprising 11 from Cohort 1 (six in the LEN arm and five in the placebo arm) and 11 from Cohort 2. LEN resistance-associated substitutions in CA emerged in 41% (9 of 22) of the VFs (Table 33 and Table 34). The LEN resistance-associated CA substitution M66I was observed most frequently in six confirmed VFs (five with HIV-1 subtype B, one with HIV-1 subtype AE), alone or with other substitutions including Q67Q/H, Q67Q/H/K/N, K70K/R, K70N/S, N74D, N74N/H, A105T, and T107A. The other three VFs had emergent LEN resistance-associated CA substitutions Q67K+K70H, Q67H+K70R+T107S, and Q67Q/H. An independent assessment of NGS data was performed and in general, corroborated the genotypic results submitted in the NDA.

The remaining two VFs ( [REDACTED] (b) (6) ) had HIV-1 RNA resuppression with no change in their OBR after they experienced a viral load rebound at the time of LEN resistance emergence, suggestive of potential treatment adherence issues at the time of rebound.

L518: ## Emergence of Resistance Substitutions in Protease, RT, and Integrase
L519: Four virologic failures had emerging resistance substitutions to OBR components (Table 34):
L520: - Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) developed the K103N/S and M184M/I/V RT resistance substitutions while receiving an OBR composed of the non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) doravirine along with the INSTI/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) fixed-dose combination of BIC, FTC, and TAF. This subject met the criteria for resistance analysis due to suboptimal virologic response at Week 4 but was resuppressed to &lt;50 copies/mL by Week 52.
- Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) had the emergent NNRTI-resistance substitution V106M in addition to the LEN resistance substitutions M66I+T107A with doravirine plus FTC and ibalizumab in their OBR.
- Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) had the emergent resistance substitution K65K/R at Week 52 on a regimen including tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) (darunavir, dolutegravir, FTC, and TDF) as well as the emergent CA substitution T107S.
- Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) had emergent NRTI resistance substitutions K65R and S68N from mixtures at baseline in addition to the LEN resistance substitution M66I with TDF, plus FTC, dolutegravir, darunavir/cobicistat, and rilpivirine in their OBR and had 11,400 copies/mL HIV-1 RNA at Week 52.
L521: The Applicant stated that Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) developed the V82V/A resistance substitution in protease at Week 26 while receiving an OBR including the protease inhibitor darunavir along with the NNRTI doravirine, the NRTIs FTC and TAF, and the INSTI dolutegravir. However, this could not be confirmed in the submitted dataset. The subject was resuppressed to &lt;50 copies/mL at subsequent visits.
L522: ## NGS Analysis
L523: An independent resistance assessment was performed using the NGS data derived from subjects in Study 4625 who were determined to be VFs. Several CA amino acid substitutions were identified as treatment-emergent among multiple subjects from different genotypes and subgroups who experienced VF, including substitutions at positions M66 (six subjects: five B and one AE), Q67 (five subjects: three B, one BF, and one C), K70 (five subjects: three B, one AE, and one BF), N74 (four subjects: two B, one AE, and one C), A105 (four subjects: three B and one AE), and T107 (two subjects: two B). These treatment-emergent CA substitutions identified in the independent analysis were also reported by the Applicant and the phenotypic data were provided in the NDA submissions.
L524: ## Conclusion
L525: In Study 4625, 31% (22 of 72) of HTE subjects met the criteria for resistance analyses through Week 52 (HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL at confirmed VF [suboptimal virologic response at Week 4, virologic rebound, or viremia at last visit]) and were analyzed for LEN-associated substitution emergence. LEN resistance-associated CA substitutions were found in 41% (n=9) of the confirmed VF subjects with postbaseline CA genotypic resistance data (n=22). The M66I CA substitution was observed in 27% (6 of 22) of subjects, alone or in combination with other LEN resistance-associated CA substitutions, including Q67Q/H, Q67Q/H/K/N, K70K/R, K70N/S, N74D, N74N/H, A105T, and T107A. The other three VFs had emergent LEN resistance-associated CA substitutions Q67K +K70H, Q67H+K70R+T107S, and Q67Q/H. The treatment-emergent CA resistance substitutions were confirmed by FDA independent analyses.
L526: The VF isolates with emergent CA resistance-associated substitutions had reduced LEN susceptibility of 6- to &gt;1428-fold.
L527: Four VF subjects had emergent resistance substitutions to components of the OBR. Additionally, among the nine VFs who developed LEN resistance substitutions in CA, four received LEN in combination with a background regimen with no fully active ARVs based on the baseline genotypic and/or phenotypic resistance. Therefore, given the higher risk of developing resistance to LEN, careful consideration should be given to inclusion of active drugs in addition to LEN in the treatment regimen.
L528: - LEN resistance emerges readily in VFs and thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen.
- LEN resistance substitutions do not confer cross-resistance to other ARVs.
L529: ## 7.7.2. Injection Site Reactions
L530: ## Issue
L531: ISRs were identified as the most commonly reported ADRs among subjects who received SC injections of LEN; however, long-term experience of subjects after multiple SC injections of LEN was limited in Studies 4625 and 4334.
L532: ## **Background**
L533: For other ARVs administered in an injectable form, such as CABENUVA (a long-acting formulation of two drugs, cabotegravir and rilpivirine), ISRs are the most commonly reported ADRs. ISRs associated with intramuscular CABENUVA were most commonly described as localized pain/discomfort (71% to 79% of subjects). The CABENUVA label also includes the following other ISRs: nodules (10% to 17% of subjects), induration (17% to 12% of subjects), swelling (5% to 8% of subjects), erythema (2% to 4% of subjects), pruritus (4% to 5% of subjects), bruising/discoloration (2% to 3% of subjects), and warmth (1% to 2% of subjects). Anesthesia, abscess, cellulitis, and hemorrhage at the injection site were each reported in less than 1% of subjects (ViiV-Healthcare 2022). Serious postinjection reactions were reported within minutes after the injection of rilpivirine and began to resolve within a few minutes after the injection (&lt;1% of subjects). These reactions were characterized by signs and symptoms including dyspnea, bronchospasm, agitation, abdominal cramping, rash/urticaria, dizziness, flushing, sweating, oral numbness, changes in blood pressure, and back pain (e.g., back and chest). These events may have been associated with accidental intravenous administration during the intramuscular injection procedure (ViiV-Healthcare 2022).
L534: Injection site nodules have been reported with a number of other drug classes, including glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists used for treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes. General ISRs (e.g., erythema, pain, or rash) have been reported with all commercially available glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (i.e., exenatide, lixisenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide) (Hearn and Sherman 2021). Injection site nodules have rarely been described with other long-acting or extended-release drug products, such as exenatide. Although the mechanism for development of such nodules is not entirely clear, available histopathology data reveal the presence of eosinophils and granuloma at these sites, and therefore, hypersensitivity to the formulation is a plausible mechanism (Jones et al. 2015). Surgical excision or some other medical intervention, such as serial intralesional corticosteroid injections, may be required for treatment of persistent lesions.
L535: LEN is a CA inhibitor with not only a new mechanism of action but also unique, albeit not fully understood, physical properties when injected (b) (4)
L536: ## **Assessment**
L537: ISRs were the most commonly reported ADRs with SC LEN injections. Preferred terms related to ISRs in Studies 4625 and 4334 are listed in Table 35. Injection site swelling, erythema, pain, nodule, and induration were the most frequently (&gt;10%) reported preferred terms. None of the ISRs was considered serious.
L538: - In Study 4625, 47 of 72 (65.3%) subjects experienced ISRs assessed as related to SC LEN; most ISRs were Grade 1 or 2 in severity. Three subjects (4.2%) experienced nonserious, Grade 3 ISRs that were considered by the investigator to be related to SC LEN and are described below:Subject (b) (6) experienced two Grade 3 ISRs: “bilateral swelling at injection site max diameter cm 10” reported on Day 16 and ending on Day 19 (Injection site swelling); “bilateral redness at the injection site max diameter cm 10” reported on Day 16 and ending on Day 23 (Injection site erythema).
L539: - Subject (b) (6) experienced two Grade 3 ISRs: “pain at injection site (1st)” on Day 16 and ending on Day 16 (Injection site pain); “pain at injection site (2nd)” on Day 16 and ending on Day 16 (Injection site pain).
- Subject (b) (6) experienced five Grade 3 ISRs: “injection site redness” on Day 380 and ending Day 394 (Injection site erythema); “injection site redness” on Day 380 and ending Day 394 (Injection site erythema); “injection site pain bilateral” on Day 380 and ending Day 394 (Injection site pain); “swelling dx injection site” on Day 380 and ending Day 394 (Injection site swelling); “swelling sx injection site” on Day 380 and ending Day 394 (Injection site swelling).
- One subject (1.4%) reported nonserious, Grade 1 injection site nodules that led to SC LEN discontinuation and is described below:Subject (b) (6) experienced two Grade 1 ISRs: “right sided injection site nodules” reported on Day 18 and are ongoing (*Injection site nodule*); “right abdomen injection site nodules” on Day 380 and are ongoing (*Injection site nodule*).
- In Study 4334, 57 of 103 (55.3%) of subjects who received SC LEN experienced ISRs assessed as related to SC LEN; most ISRs were Grade 1 or 2 in severity. One subject (1.0%) experienced a nonserious, Grade 3 ISR that was considered by the investigator to be related to SC LEN and is described below:Subject (b) (6) experienced one Grade 3 ISR: “injection site nodule” reported on Day 194 and is ongoing (*Injection site nodule*).

In summary, the Applicant stated that their review of ISRs and pH for various SC ARVs as well as other LEN formulations did not identify a clear association between high pH of a formulation and ISRs. The Applicant states that their available nonclinical data suggest that chronic granulomatous inflammation and foreign body response at the SC injection site are expected to occur due to the presence of a SC drug depot, and irrespective of the pH of the formulation. Finally, the Applicant believes that the ISRs observed in clinical studies with SC LEN, including nodules and indurations, are likely associated with the expected host foreign

L583: ## Conclusion
L584: ISRs can be characterized as having a short-term phase lasting a few days (e.g., pain, swelling, and erythema) or a long-term phase (e.g., indurations and nodules), some of which were still resolving over a period of weeks to months. Indurations and nodules were generally described as palpable and elongated (1 to 4 cm), not painful, and not associated with any erythema. Nodules were more visible in subjects who were leaner with little fat tissue in the abdomen. Several subjects in Study 4625 had indurations or nodules that had not fully resolved at the time of the interim data cut dates. Overall, it appears nodules tend to resolve more slowly than indurations; however, there may be overlap in choice of preferred terms used by investigators that could also be characterized similarly by terms such as “mass” or “granuloma”. Due to the lack of understanding of the histopathology at the injection sites in patients who experienced longer times to resolution of indurations and nodules, and the relationship with the unique properties of the drug product solution, it is unclear what is driving persistence in some subjects. Given the concern about the incompatibility of LEN with the borosilicate glass, compatibility with the (b) (4) was further evaluated. The available nonclinical and clinical data do not support that the presence of particulates are responsible for the development or persistence of ISRs. The available dermatopathology has revealed expected responses to foreign body that are also expected from the presence of the SC LEN drug depot.
L585: Overall, DDD agrees with the Applicant's assessment, that ISRs most likely the result of the presence of the drug depot, and the proposed labeling describing ISRs, including injection site nodules and indurations. In addition, DDD continues to recommend that human histopathology (e.g., punch biopsy) be obtained in ongoing or future clinical trials; the presence of findings such as necrosis, hypersensitivity, granulomas, foreign bodies, fibrous tissue, etc. can aid in understanding the pathophysiology of nodule formation. Additionally, where possible, injection site nodules should be followed to resolution or stabilization. Please also refer to the DDD Memorandum completed November 18, 2022 for additional details.
L586: During the initial exchange of updates to the draft labeling in the first cycle for LEN, DAV requested additional description of ISRs similar to the presentation in the Cabenuva labeling (ViiV-Healthcare 2022), with the additional description of nodules and induration and details of time to resolution provided as a separate subsection entitled “Injection-Associated Adverse Reactions” in Section 6 (Adverse Reactions) of the proposed label. During the NDA resubmissions, a similar exchange of updates to the draft labeling for LEN occurred. Initially, DAV requested the additional description of ongoing and resolved injection site nodules and
L587: NDA 215973 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) injection, for subcutaneous use
NDA 215974 Sunlenca (lenacapavir) tablets, for oral use
L588: indurations, including the time to resolution in Section 6 (Adverse Reactions). Later in the review cycle, DAV requested the addition of ISRs in Section 5 (Warnings and Precautions) to address the concern of persistent injection site nodules and indurations. The Product Quality team has also recommended that the provider carefully inspect the syringe after withdrawing the LEN solution from the vial for visible particulates.
L589: Based upon our assessment of the available data, including the addendum submitted by the Applicant on December 14, 2022, the potential of risk of ISRs associated with SC LEN do not outweigh the benefit for the treatment of MDR HIV-1 infection in HTE subjects with the appropriate labeling as mentioned above. From a clinical safety perspective, however, additional information is needed to fully understand if there are any contributing factors of injection site reactions with LEN, particularly for subjects who have prolonged resolution with nodules and indurations. The Clinical team has recommended a PMR to assess the completion of long-term follow-up of ISRs in Studies 4625 and 4334, and the Product Quality team has recommended postmarketing commitments (PMCs) to further assess vial and [REDACTED] (b) (4) compatibility, and evaluate an alternative device for withdrawing the LEN injection from the vial.

L600: This is the second CMC review of this NDA. In the original submission, Gilead proposed borosilicate and aluminosilicate glass vials for the packaging of LEN injection. However, the proposed drug product formulation was found incompatible with borosilicate glass vials, leading to the generation of glass lamellae. Due to the lack of sufficient data to support the compatibility of lenacapavir injection with aluminosilicate vials, a CR was issued.
L601: The delamination is suspected to occur as a result of (b) (4) of the formulation (b) (4). Significant pitting was observed with (b) (4) the originally proposed borosilicate vials. Scanning electron microscopy and optical microscopy images were submitted late in the previous review cycle to support the use of the aluminosilicate vials; however, unexplained particles were observed and the data was not sufficient to mitigate concerns for the potential interaction of the formulation with the vials.
L602: In addition, the stability data submitted in the first review cycle for the aluminosilicate vials only included 9 months long-term (and 6 months accelerated) results, which did not allow final assessment of the proposed drug product expiry period.
L603: The deficiency included in the CR for vial incompatibility is as follows: "Your data demonstrate that the drug product solution is incompatible with the proposed commercial borosilicate glass vials. The data provided in support of the compatibility of the alternative aluminosilicate glass vials are incomplete and ambiguous. As evidenced by your data and glass particles found in the clinical batches, glass containers are (b) (4) (w) (4). In order to resolve this deficiency, we require a comprehensive study report with unambiguous data and fully validated methods to demonstrate the compatibility of the drug product solution with your proposed primary container closure system."
L604: In the resubmission, Gilead submitted the vial compatibility data (optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry) data for three registration batches stored in aluminosilicate glass vials for up to 18 months under long term storage conditions (30°C/75% relative humidity). The data do not show any evidence of glass incompatibility of LEN formulation with the proposed aluminosilicate glass vials. In addition, the FDA Office of Translational Research laboratory analysis (report no. FY22-114-OTR-DPQR-T) of registration and clinical batches also demonstrated the compatibility of proposed vials with LEN injection. The proposed analytical methods were also found acceptable. The additional data from registration stability batches and three production batches will be reviewed as it will be submitted postapproval as CBE-0 supplements to further confirm the suitability of the proposed vials with the LEN injection solution.

L610: ## Drug Substance
L611: The drug substance review was adequate in the previous review cycle, and no new drug substance information was provided in the resubmission. The NDA is recommended for approval from the drug substance perspective.
L612: ## Drug Product
L613: The submission is adequate from a drug product perspective. LEN Injection is sterile, preservative-free, for subcutaneous administration. Marketing of a single strength is proposed (463.5 mg/1.5 mL [309 mg/mL]) in a glass vial. The dosage strength is based on the lenacapavir free acid. Each vial contains a nominal 1.5 mL clear, yellow (b) (4) solution consisting of 473.1 mg of lenacapavir sodium, 896.3 mg polyethylene glycol 300, and (b) (4) water for injection. Each vial contains sufficient volume ((b) (4) mL with (b) (4) mL overfill) to allow withdrawal of 1.5 mL.
L614: Drug product kit: The proposed container closure system for the drug product consists of a single-dose, clear glass vial. Each vial is sealed with an (b) (4) closure and aluminum overseal with flip-off cap. The drug product is supplied as a co-packaged kit which includes all the components needed for healthcare professionals to administer the injection; i.e., two lenacapavir filled vials, two vial access devices, two disposable syringes, and two injection safety needles.
L615: ## Devices
L616: All components (devices) of the proposed kit are 510(k) cleared; therefore, the CDRH determined that no additional review is needed. There is no change in the device design since that determination (February 2021), thus no additional review was needed from the DMEPA team and their review will be limited to the labeling.

These considerations were discussed during the review cycle with the Office of New Drugs review team, including the Clinical and Pharmacology-Toxicology teams as well as Office of New Drugs leadership.
L632: In addition to the above factors, the review discussions highlighted the following relevant factors for consideration:
L633: - Nonclinical studies were performed using container closures using borosilicate vials with a synthetic [REDACTED] (b) (4) [REDACTED] (b) (4) [REDACTED] (b) (4), and demonstrated injection site reactions (chronic granulomatous inflammations) for dose groups but not vehicle control groups in the same container closures. This suggests that [REDACTED] (b) (4) particulates are not responsible for the ISRs in animal studies, although it does not rule out that glass lamellae could have contributed. To note, the studies used a needle to withdraw the vial contents.
- Phase 1 clinical studies, although some were conducted with a different formulation/pH and not all subjects were followed to resolution, were all performed with a container closure sealed with a [REDACTED] (b) (4) and demonstrated a decreased frequency and duration of injection site nodules and induration in patients who received placebo versus in patients who received lenacapavir. This again suggests that [REDACTED] (b) (4) particulates may not be responsible for the ISRs. Likewise, if [REDACTED] (b) (4) is responsible for the glass delamination observed in borosilicate vials, the ISRs may not be related to glass lamellae but rather drug depot formation or other characteristics of the formulation.
- Although evidence of foreign body reaction were obtained in available biopsy results, the above studies indicate that the subcutaneous depot of the drug may be responsible.
- The intended population for the product is treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment experienced patients with multi-drug resistance, for which the product has breakthrough designation.

L701: ## 13. Pharmacology Toxicology: Additional Information and Assessment
L702: Please refer to Section 13 of the Integrated Review dated February 28, 2022 for the Nonclinical review from the first cycle. Additional data submitted in this cycle include a 26-week carcinogenicity study in transgenic mouse and a single-dose intramuscular local tolerance study in rabbit.
L703: ## 13.1. Carcinogenicity
L704: ## GS-6207(b) (4): A 26-Week Subcutaneous Carcinogenicity Study in 001178-T (Hemizygous) RasH2 Mice (TX-200-2068)
L705: The carcinogenic potential of lenacapavir (LEN) was tested via subcutaneous (SC) administration in a 26-week mouse study. RasH2 hemizygous mice were administered 0, 30, 100, or 300 mg/kg/dose of LEN formulated in (b) (4)% polyethylene glycol (PEG)-300 and (b) (4)% sterile water for injection once every 13 weeks for 26 weeks (two total doses).
L706: There were no variations of tumor incidences considered related to administration of LEN based on the FDA statistical review. The Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee concurred that this study was negative.
L707: ## 13.2. Other Toxicology Studies
L708: ## A Single-Dose Intramuscular Injection Local Tolerance Study of GS-6207(b)(4) in Male New Zealand White Rabbits with a 28- or 90-Day Observation Period (TX-200-2074)
L709: The effects of three formulations of LEN on local tolerance were evaluated in male rabbits via a single intramuscular injection followed by a 28- or 90-day observation period. The vehicle control formulations were as follows:
L710: There were no marked differences among the different vehicle formulations.
L711: Injection site reactions of granulomatous inflammation and minimal to slight mineralization were detected in all animals across doses and controls 28 days postdose (necropsy 1). Slight to moderated myofiber necrosis and minimal to slight hemorrhage was detected at 400 mg/kg LEN.
L712: At necropsy 2, granulomatous inflammation at dosing-site B was still detected but at a lower incidence and severity compared to necropsy 1. Other histopathology findings detected at necropsy 1 were no longer detected at necropsy 2.
