L1645: ## I. Executive Summary
L1646: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L1647: These new drug applications (NDAs) for both oral (NDA 215974) and injectable formulations (NDA 215973) of lenacapavir (LEN) were submitted by Gilead Sciences. LEN is a first-in-class human immunodeficiency type 1 (HIV-1) capsid inhibitor with Breakthrough Therapy Designation. These NDAs were reviewed by the interdisciplinary review team.
L1648: The intended indication for LEN is to be used in combination with other antiretroviral(s) for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment-experienced adult patients with multidrug resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current antiretroviral regimen due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations.
L1649: The clinical, virology, clinical pharmacology, pharmacology/toxicology, statistics, and regulatory disciplines did not identify issues that preclude approval. Product quality deficiencies were identified which include: (1) product quality information to support the proposed container presentation in borosilicate glass vials was not acceptable for commercial use due to delamination of the vial containers and concern for glass particulate contamination, (2) data supporting aluminosilicate glass vials as an alternative were insufficient for full review. The Product Quality assessment team recommends a complete response based on these deficiencies. I, the signatory authority for these applications, concur with the complete response recommendation and therefore the Agency will issue a complete response for both NDAs because the approval of NDA 215974 is dependent on the approval of NDA 215973. The proposed proprietary name, Sunlenca, was found acceptable only pending approval of the application; therefore, the Applicant will need to resubmit their proposed name when the deficiencies are addressed. Please refer to the Complete Response letter for further details.
L1650: The Applicant submitted one adequately designed phase 2/3 trial, Study 4625, that provided substantial evidence of efficacy for the proposed indication. Supportive evidence of efficacy was provided by Study 4334.
L1651: The available safety data from the clinical trials demonstrate that LEN is safe for its intended use. I concur that the risks identified in the review of the clinical trials' data can be mitigated through labeling and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.
L1652: The long-acting properties of the LEN injectable formulation have potential advantages and disadvantages. The long-acting injectable formulation can be administered every 6 months in combination with other active antiretrovirals. However, because residual concentrations of LEN can remain for prolonged periods, careful selection of patients who agree to the injection dosing schedule is imperative. Nonadherence to the injection dosing schedule can lead to loss of virologic response and development of resistance to this new drug class.
L1653: For detailed information supporting the basis for the benefit-risk assessment please refer to the details in this Integrated Assessment document. Please also refer to the Product Quality Reviews for the deficiencies observed resulting in the overall Complete Response action.
L1654: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L1655: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L1656: Table 3. Benefit-Risk Framework
L1657: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of Condition	Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is a transmissible virus that attacks and weakens the immune system. Without effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV-1 infection leads to progressive destruction of the immune system, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illnesses, and premature death in almost all cases.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that approximately 1.2 million people in the U.S. are living with HIV. In 2019, there were 15,815 deaths among people diagnosed with HIV (CDC 2021).
Maximal and durable suppression of HIV-1 RNA restores and/or preserves the immune system and reduces HIV-associated morbidity and mortality. Most treatment-adherent patients with limited previous HIV treatment experience can maximally and durably suppress HIV-1 RNA using a combination of two or more commercially available drugs from different drug classes.
Treatment failure occurs as a result of drug resistance, drug intolerance, and suboptimal adherence. Resistance-associated substitution(s) selected by one drug often confer(s) resistance to other drugs within that drug class, which further limits treatment options.
Heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) patients have limited remaining options for constructing a fully suppressive antiretroviral (ARV) regimen due to multidrug resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations.
HTE patients with limited treatment options and evidence of ongoing HIV replication despite ART are at high risk of AIDS-related morbidity and mortality.
L1658: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1659: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1660: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current Treatment Options	For patients with multidrug resistant (MDR) HIV-1 infection, providers must individually tailor combination treatment regimens based on previous antiretroviral (ARV) exposure, cumulative viral resistance testing, drug safety and tolerability, and comorbid conditions.
The resulting ARV regimens are often burdensome, less well-tolerated, and associated with inadequate HIV-1 RNA suppression.
HTE patients with limited treatment options need new and effective therapies that lack cross-resistance with commercially available products, have a favorable tolerability profile, and allow for convenient dosing.

Benefit	Efficacy of lenacapavir (LEN) in HTE patients who were failing treatment due to multidrug resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations was established in Study GS-US-200-4625 (Study 4625), a phase 2/3 trial conducted in two cohorts.
The Study 4625 trial design was consistent with FDA's Guidance for Industry Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 Infection: Developing Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment (November 2015).
Cohort 1 of Study 4625 was divided into two periods. During the first period, the Functional Monotherapy Period (FMP), 36 subjects in Study 4625 were randomized 2:1 to receive 14 days of oral LEN or placebo, respectively, in addition to their failing regimen. During the second period, the Maintenance Period, all subjects were unblinded and dosed with LEN (via subcutaneous injection following the 14-day oral lead-in) plus an optimized background regimen (OBR) through at least 52 weeks of follow-up. A second cohort enrolled 36 subjects, all of whom received open-label LEN plus an OBR, in parallel with Cohort 1.
The primary efficacy endpoint for Study 4625 was the proportion of subjects in Cohort 1 achieving a reduction in HIV-1 RNA of \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL from baseline at the end of the 14-day FMP. The difference in proportions in HIV-1 RNA \log_{10} copies/mL from Day 1 to Day 14 (LEN minus placebo) was -70.8 (95% CI, -34.9, -90.0), demonstrating statistical superiority of LEN compared to placebo.
Early HIV-1 RNA decreases of > 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL in prior trials have been associated with reduction in clinical disease progression according to the FDA's Guidance for Industry,
LEN has demonstrated virologic activity in HTE patients with MDR HIV-1 infection who have limited treatment options.
The clinical trial design and endpoints were appropriate for the HTE population with limited treatment options.
Reductions in HIV-1 RNA levels are highly predictive of meaningful clinical benefit, and LEN functional monotherapy was superior to placebo for reducing HIV-1 RNA over 14 days.
Because Study 4625 was uncontrolled during the maintenance period and the interim analysis included follow-up through only Week 26, there is some uncertainty surrounding the contribution of LEN to the durability of virologic response.
Availability of LEN would provide a new and effective first-in-class treatment option for HTE patients with HIV-1 infection and limited alternative options due to multidrug resistance, intolerance or safety considerations. Patients who achieve virologic suppression with LEN plus an OBR would have a reduced risk of HIV/AIDS-related morbidity and mortality.
L1661: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1662: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1663: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Risk and Risk Management	
Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 Infection: Developing Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment (November 2015).
The key secondary efficacy endpoints assessed durability of virologic response following the FMP; however, the majority of subjects had not yet completed their Week 52 visits. Based on an interim analysis, 81% of subjects in Cohort 1 maintained HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at the Week 26 visit.
Supplemental efficacy data was provided by a phase 2 trial, Study GS-US-200-4334 (Study 4334). A total of 183 treatment-naïve people living with HIV (PLWH) were randomized to receive one of three regimens containing LEN or an active comparator (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide, [B/F/TAF]). At the Week 28 interim analysis, 94% (147/157) of the subjects who received a regimen containing LEN and 100% (25/25) of the subjects who received B/F/TAF maintained HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL.
Study 4625 enrolled 72 subjects from the HTE patient population, and the safety database that included subjects exposed to at least one 927 mg subcutaneous dose of LEN with the same proposed formulation for marketing was 232 subjects. This safety database is smaller than the minimum recommended sample size of 300 to 500, as outlined by FDA's Guidance for Industry Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 Infection: Developing Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment (November 2015); however, the overall clinical experience in PLWH and healthy volunteers was 803.
The most common adverse drug reaction during treatment with LEN was injection site reactions (ISRs). Injection site pain, swelling, and erythema were the most common specific ISRs reported, and typically lasted no more than a few days; however, indurations and nodules were reported to have longer durations, and approximately 7-19%, respectively, of cases had not fully resolved following up to 1 year of follow-up.
Based on the available clinical data, LEN has an acceptable safety profile. Additional information, however, is needed to understand the contributing factors of ISRs with LEN, particularly for subjects with nodules and indurations that have slow or no documented resolution.
LEN resistance emerges readily in virologic failures and thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen.
LEN resistance substitutions do not confer cross-resistance to other currently FDA-approved ARVs.
Longer term data are required to determine durability of LEN and the other ARVs in the OBR.
The product quality information to support the proposed container presentation in borosilicate glass vials was not acceptable for commercial or investigational use due to delamination of the vial containers and concern for glass particulate contamination. The data supporting aluminosilicate glass vials as an alternative was insufficient for full review.
L1664: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1665: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1666: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
A review of deaths, serious adverse events (SAEs), and clinically significant laboratory abnormalities did not reveal any patterns to suggest a significant safety risk attributable to LEN; however, all three subjects who prematurely discontinued study drug due to an adverse event were due to injection site nodules or indurations and were considered related to LEN SC injection.
Resistance to LEN occurred frequently in virologic failures.
The LEN resistance substitutions selected in virologic failures did not confer cross-resistance to other current ARVs.
There are not enough data on the durability of LEN as a component of an ARV regimen. Longer-term data from all subjects after Week 26 are needed to determine if resistance to other drugs in the OBR occur.
In the assessment of product quality, the proposed commercial glass vial presentation was found to be incompatible with the drug product solution as glass particles were found in the solution. Combined with concerns for (b) (4) the lack of details provided from container closure integrity testing, lack of intrinsic release controls, and additional information required to determine the acceptability of a proposed alternative aluminosilicate glass vial, the application for LEN for injection was determined to be deficient from the product quality perspective.
L1667: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L1668: Infection with HIV-1 continues to be a significant public health concern both domestically and internationally. Although the HIV treatment armamentarium is robust, additional effective ARV treatment options that provide greater flexibility in meeting patients' individual needs and facilitating their tolerance for and adherence to lifelong HIV-1 treatment are needed.
L1669: HTE patients infected with MDR HIV-1 represent a rare but important subset of patients living with HIV. Patients with MDR HIV-1 who cannot achieve complete virologic suppression with antiretroviral therapy (ART) are at high risk for AIDS-related morbidity and mortality. This population needs new and effective ARV products that lack cross-resistance with commercially available products, have a favorable tolerability profile, and allow for convenient dosing. LEN, a first-in-class HIV-1 capsid inhibitor with Breakthrough Therapy Drug designation, is one such product. The injectable formulation of LEN provides an option with the advantage of providing a new mechanism of action and maintenance dosing every six months following a lead-in with oral tablets. However, the prolonged residual exposure is an important consideration when LEN is combined with background regimens that have a different dosing schedule and reduced antiviral activity due to resistance or concerns with adherence.
L1670: The submitted evidence clearly demonstrates LEN is effective in combination with an OBR in patients with limited options due to multi-drug resistance, intolerance or safety concerns with other ARVs. The pivotal trial, Study 4625 (CAPELLA), demonstrated superiority of LEN compared to placebo, when added to a failing regimen, for the proportion of subjects achieving a reduction in HIV-1 RNA of \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL after 14 days of treatment. The lack of a control group after Day 14 in Study 4625 limits the ability to precisely quantify the contribution of LEN to long-term virologic suppression. However, the contribution of LEN is reflected by the relatively high rate of virologic suppression achieved with LEN plus an optimized background regimen (OBR) through the Week 26 interim analysis in a population previously unable to achieve virologic suppression. Additional supportive data from the phase 2 study in treatment-naïve PLWH, Study 4334, demonstrated that regimens containing LEN achieved and maintained virologic suppression through the Week 28 interim analysis.
L1671: The safety evaluation for LEN was adequate and the demonstrated clinical safety profile of LEN is acceptable for the proposed indication, dose and HTE population. With the exception of local ISRs, treatment-emergent resistance to LEN, and [REDACTED] (b) (4)
L1672: [REDACTED], the safety profile of LEN was generally favorable. Injection site indurations and nodules remained persistent in several cases and were a significant cause of study drug discontinuations. The rate of virologic failure reported in Study 4625 reflects the targeted patient population: heavily treatment-experienced patients with advanced HIV/AIDS who are failing current ART and have very few remaining treatment options. Longer-term data will be needed to determine durability of LEN and the other ARVs in the OBR.
L1673: With all factors considered, the benefits of LEN when administered with other ARVs clearly outweigh the risks; however, the product quality information to support the proposed container presentation in borosilicate glass vials was not acceptable due to incompatibility of the LEN solution with the vial containers and concern for glass particulate contamination. In addition, there was lack of sufficient data to rule out any contribution of the product quality issues to ISRs.
L1674: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1675: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1676: Given the safety concerns raised by the product quality issues, the applications for LEN were determined not to be approvable.
L1677: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L1678: ## 3. Introduction
L1679: The Applicant has submitted two new drug applications (NDAs) for lenacapavir (LEN) seeking the indication of treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral(s) (b) (4).
L1680: LEN is a first-in-class human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) capsid inhibitor and has been formulated for subcutaneous injection and as a tablet for oral use. The Applicant previously submitted an original investigational new drug (IND) application in 2017 to investigate LEN for injection and in 2018 to investigate LEN for oral use for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. (Refer to Section III.12 for additional regulatory history.) This interdisciplinary assessment combines the review of NDA 215973 for LEN subcutaneous injection and NDA-215974 for LEN oral tablets.
L1681: The Applicant conducted two clinical trials in support of the findings of safety and efficacy for LEN, Study GS-US-200-4625 (Study 4625, also referred to as CAPELLA) and Study GS-US-200-4334 (Study 4334, also referred to as CALIBRATE). Study 4625 is an ongoing phase 2/3 trial designed to evaluate the antiviral activity of lenacapavir administered as an add-on to a failing regimen (functional monotherapy) for heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) people living with HIV (PLWH). Study 4334 is a phase 2 trial conducted in a treatment-naïve patient population that serves as supplementary support for the efficacy and safety evaluation of LEN for the indication of treating the HTE HIV-1 population.
L1682: Other currently available therapies used as part of the standard of care for the treatment of HIV-1 are discussed in more detail in Section I.2 and are listed in Section III.12.1. When constructing an ARV regimen for heavily-treatment experienced (HTE) PLWH, as noted by the U.S. HIV Treatment Guidelines (NIH 2022), the expected potency and whether a new drug as part of a complete regimen has a new mechanistic action are important considerations. Currently, no other ARV products HIV-1 have been approved in the capsid inhibitor class, nor have any been approved with a dosing interval as long as every 6 months.
L1683: ## 3.1. Review Issue List
L1684: The review team identified five review issues relevant to the evaluation of benefit (Section II.6.3) and three review issues relevant to the evaluation of risk (Section II.7.7).
L1685: ## 3.1.1. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L1686: ## 3.1.1.1. Imbalance in Study 4625 Baseline Characteristics
L1687: - More subjects in the LEN arm of Cohort 1 in Study 4625 had baseline HIV-1 RNA \le100,000 copies/mL compared to the placebo arm.
- The mean baseline CD4+ cell count and CD4+ percentage were higher in the LEN arm than those in the placebo arm.
L1688: ## 3.1.1.2. Justification for the Proposed Simplified Dosing Regimen
L1689: - The Applicant is proposing a simplified dosing regimen that was not studied during the phase 2/3 LEN clinical development program.
- The Applicant used PK data to support the proposed simplified regimen.
L1690: ## 3.1.1.3. Impact of Subjects Not Maintaining Eligibility Criteria: Not Failing on Background Regimen or Nonadherence to Background Regimen
L1691: - Several subjects did not meet the established enrollment criteria for Study 4625, including resistance to at least two ARVs from each of at least three of the four main classes or demonstration of virologic failure despite adherence to a failing background regimen.
L1692: ## 3.1.1.4. Dosing Interval and Approach to Missed Subcutaneous Maintenance Doses
L1693: - The Applicant proposed that during the LEN SC maintenance period, if more than 28 weeks have elapsed since the last LEN SC injection and if it is clinically appropriate to continue LEN treatment, then the indicated dosing regimen should be reinitiated.

L1700: ## 3.1.2.1. Resistance Assessments of Virologic Failures
L1701: - The assessment of resistance emergence in virologic failures of an LEN-containing ARV regimen is critical to interpreting the overall risk-benefit of LEN and understanding the durability of LEN as a component of an ARV regimen in a heavily treatment-experienced patient population.

L1704: ## 3.1.2.2. Injection Site Reactions
L1705: - Injection site reactions were identified as the most common adverse drug reaction among subjects who received subcutaneous injections of lenacapavir; however, long-term experience of subjects after multiple injections was limited in Studies 4625 and 4334.
L1706: ## 3.1.2.3. Background Regimens Containing Boosted Protease Inhibitors
L1707: - The risk of supratherapeutic LEN exposures when LEN is combined with a background regimen containing boosted protease inhibitors was not prospectively assessed in Study 4625.

L1730: **Table 6. Summary of General Clinical Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetics of LEN**
L1731: Characteristic	Drug Information
Pharmacologic Activity
Established pharmacologic class (EPC)	A human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) capsid inhibitor.
Mechanism of action	Lenacapavir (LEN) is a multistage selective inhibitor of HIV-1 capsid function that directly binds to the interface between capsid protein subunits. LEN inhibits HIV-1 replication by interfering with multiple essential steps of the viral lifecycle, including capsid-mediated nuclear uptake of HIV-1 linear unintegrated DNA (by blocking nuclear import proteins binding to capsid), virus assembly and release (by interfering with Gag/Gag-Pol functioning, reducing production of capsid protein subunits), and capsid core formation (by disrupting the rate of capsid subunit association, leading to malformed capsids).
Antiviral activity	In MT-4 cells, LEN demonstrated antiviral activity with an EC50 value of 0.19nM and a selectivity index (CC50 value/EC50 value) of 140,000. LEN predominately targets at least one essential capsid-mediated step involved in the early stages of HIV replication with an EC50 value of 0.023nM. LEN also showed an antiviral effect against at least one capsid-mediated process essential for the late stages of HIV replication with a mean late stage EC50 value of 0.439nM.
Active moieties	LEN
QT prolongation	At LEN concentrations nine-fold higher than the therapeutic concentrations from the Applicant's proposed dosing regimen, LEN does not prolong the QT interval to any clinically relevant extent.

L1739: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L1740: ## 5.1.1. Antiviral Activity Against HIV-1 Subtypes
L1741: LEN displayed antiviral activity against 23 diverse HIV-1 clinical isolates representing all major subtypes with a median 50% effective concentration (EC_{50}) value of 0.04nM (range 0.02 to 0.16nM) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) (Table 124). LEN also showed antiviral activity against two HIV-2 isolates but was 15- to 25-fold less active relative to HIV-1. In a separate study testing the activity of LEN against 40 clinical HIV-1 isolates of diverse subtypes using the PhenoSense Gag-Pro Antiviral Assay, the range of means across subtypes was 0.166 to 0.297nM, with less than two-fold difference in activity across subtypes (Table 125). The range of means for subtype B isolates was 0.03 to 0.08nM with a median of 0.04nM.
L1742: ## 5.1.2. Antiviral Activity of Lenacapavir Against Non-HIV Viruses
L1743: LEN was tested against hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), human rhinovirus (HRV), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in cell-based assays. LEN did not display selective antiviral activity in cell culture against HCV or HRV up to the highest concentration tested (44 to 50\muM) (Table 129). However, LEN did demonstrate antiviral activity against HBV and RSV at low micromolar concentrations, with EC_{50} values and corresponding 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC_{50})/EC_{50} ratios of 1.5\muM and &gt;34, and 8.2\muM and &gt;6.1, respectively. These data indicate that LEN is approximately 25,000-fold more active against HIV as compared to HBV. However, a proper clinically active therapy against HBV should be used in HIV/HBV-coinfected patients to maintain the HBV suppression.
L1744: ## 6. Assessment of Effectiveness
L1745: ## 6.1. Dose and Dose Responsiveness
L1746: ## 6.1.1. Study 4625 (CAPELLA)
L1747: The dose selection for LEN in this study was based on data from nonclinical and clinical studies. Prior to initiation of Study 4625, phase 1 PK and safety data were available in healthy subjects in Studies GS-US-200-4071 and GS-US-200-4538 (Studies 4071 and 4538) where LEN was administered as a single oral dose of up to 1800 mg, a multiple oral daily dose of up to 100 mg, or a single SC dose of up to 927 mg.
L1748: In in vitro studies, LEN was tested at concentrations corresponding to tissue culture equivalent inhibitory quotients (IQs) of 4, 8, 16, and 24, with an IQ of 1 defined as a concentration corresponding to the protein-adjusted 95% effective concentration (paEC_{95}) for wild-type HIV-1 (paEC_{95} 3.87 ng/mL in MT-4 cells). In Study GS-US-200-4072 (Study 4072), the mean maximum HIV-1 RNA decline over 10 days was 1.8 to 2.2 \log_{10} copies/mL in HIV-1-infected subjects administered LEN monotherapy as a single SC dose of 50 to 450 mg (Figure 1). All subjects achieved at least 1 \log_{10} copy/mL decline in their HIV-1 RNA at Day 10. Day 10

L1802: ## 6.2. Clinical Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L1803: ## 6.2.1. Study 4625 (CAPELLA)
L1804: ## 6.2.1.1. Study Design
L1805: Results from Study 4625 serve as the basis of the efficacy evaluation. This trial was designed in accordance with the recommendations set forth in FDA's Guidance for Industry *Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 Infection: Developing Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment* (November 2015).
L1806: Study 4625 had two cohorts. Eligible subjects who were HTE people living with HIV-1 (PLWH) with multidrug resistance were screened and then had a Cohort Selection visit 14 to 30 days after the Screening visit. During the Cohort Selection visit, if the subject's HIV-1 RNA was \ge 400 copies/mL and had &lt;0.5 \log_{10} decline from Screening, the subject would be enrolled into Cohort 1 for randomization. If Cohort 1 was fully enrolled or the criteria for Cohort 1 were not met, the subject would be enrolled into Cohort 2.
L1807: Cohort 1 was a randomized, placebo-controlled, superiority trial in which subjects were randomized to receive 14 days of oral LEN or placebo in addition to their failing ARV regimen (functional monotherapy period [FMP]). At the end of the FMP, subjects who were randomized to receive oral LEN received SC LEN and initiated their optimized background regimen (OBR) on Day 1 SC (defined as 14 days after the first dose of oral LEN). Subjects who were randomized to placebo arm received oral LEN and initiated their OBR on Day 15, and then received SC LEN at Day 1 SC while continuing their OBR. Subjects enrolled in Cohort 2 received oral LEN for 14 days together with an OBR on Day 1. At Day 1 SC, Cohort 2 subjects received SC LEN and continued their OBR (Figure 7).
L1808: Figure 7. Study Design Schema, Study 4625
L1809: Source: Figure 1 of the Applicant's Clinical Summary.
L1810: Eligible subjects were enrolled into Cohort 2 if Cohort 1 was fully enrolled.
L1811: Abbreviations: GS-6207, lenacapavir; HIV, human immunodeficiency virus; OBR, optimized background regimen; SC, subcutaneous

L1813: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1814: ## 6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria
L1815: Key eligibility criteria are summarized in this section, and the full criteria are available in Section III.15.
L1816: The study enrolled subjects who met the following inclusion criteria:
L1817: - Adults aged \ge 18 years or adolescents aged \ge 12 years and weighing \ge 35 kg, receiving a stable failing ARV regimen for &gt;8 weeks before screening.
- Have HIV-1 RNA \ge 400 copies/mL at screening.
- HIV resistance reports showing resistance to \ge 2 antiretroviral medications from each of \ge 3 of the 4 main classes of antiretroviral medications (integrase strand-transfer inhibitor [INSTI], non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor [NNRTI], nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor [NRTI], protease inhibitor [PI]).
- Have \le 2 fully active ARV remaining from the 4 main classes that can be effectively combined to form a viable regimen.
- Willing to receive an optimized background regimen together with LEN.
L1818: Subjects who met the following exclusion criteria were excluded from the study:
L1819: - An opportunistic illness requiring acute therapy within the 30 days prior to screening.
- Active and serious infections (other than HIV-1 infection) requiring parenteral antibiotic or antifungal therapy within 30 days before screening.
- Acute hepatitis.
- Untreated or newly treated HBV infection.
- HCV infection.
- Clinical decompensated liver cirrhosis.
- Active malignancy requiring acute therapy.
- Current alcohol or substance use.
- Clinically significant abnormal electrocardiogram (ECG).
- Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) \le 50 mL/min.
- Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) &gt;5 \times the upper limit of normal (ULN).
- Direct bilirubin &gt;1.5 \times ULN.
- Platelets &lt;50,000/\text{mm}^3.
- Hemoglobin &lt;8.0 g/dL.
- Use or planned use of exclusionary medications.
L1820: ## 6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan
L1821: The Applicant and the review division agreed on the statistical analysis plan prior to trial completion.
L1822: The primary efficacy endpoint for Study 4625 was the proportion of subjects in Cohort 1 achieving a reduction in HIV-1 RNA of \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL from baseline at the end of the FMP. The efficacy analysis population included all subjects who were randomized in the FMP and received at least one dose of blinded study drug (full analysis set [FAS]). Only data collected up to Day 1 SC or Day 15 visit were included in the primary efficacy analysis. For subjects with missing HIV-1 RNA values at the end of the FMP, the value was imputed using the last observation carried forward method. The difference in proportions between two treatment groups were compared using an unconditional exact method with two inverted 1-sided tests at alpha
L1823: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1824: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1825: level 0.05 to evaluate superiority. The p-value and 95% exact confidence interval (CI) for the point estimate of treatment difference in proportions were provided.
L1826: The secondary efficacy endpoints were the proportions of subjects in Cohort 1 with HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 and &lt;200 copies/mL at Weeks 26 and 52 using the U.S. FDA-defined snapshot algorithm. Analyses were based on the all LEN population that was defined as all subjects who were enrolled in the study and received at least one dose of SC LEN. Only results at Week 26 were included as the majority of subjects had not reached Week 52 at the time of NDA submission.
L1827: Subgroup analyses were planned for the proportion of subjects with HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 26 as determined by the U.S. FDA-defined snapshot algorithm. Subgroups of interest included age group, sex, race, region, baseline cluster of differentiation (CD)4^{+} categories, baseline viral load categories, baseline INSTI resistance categories, genotypic sensitivity score, phenotypic sensitivity score, and overall susceptibility score.
L1828: ## 6.2.1.4. Results of Analyses of Clinical Trial Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy, Study 4625 (CAPELLA)
L1829: This section summarizes the subject disposition, baseline demographics, clinical characteristics, and primary and key secondary efficacy results to support the efficacy of LEN in HTE subjects with multidrug resistant (MDR) HIV-1 infection. Data from Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 are often shown side-by-side for ease of presentation. However, the two cohorts represent discrete groups with different populations and are not intended to be compared to one another.
L1830: ## 6.2.1.4.1. Disposition, Baseline Demographics, and Baseline Clinical Characteristics
L1831: ## Disposition
L1832: The study screened a total of 144 subjects. Among them, 72 were enrolled in the study (Table 9). All of the 72 subjects completed the FMP and received SC LEN injection on Day 1 SC. All of the Cohort 1 subjects also completed the Week 26 assessment. One subject in Cohort 2 prematurely discontinued study drug in the maintenance period due to death.
L1833: ## Baseline Demographics and Clinical Characteristics
L1834: The majority of subjects in the trial (Cohort 1 and Cohort 2) were male (75%) and white (40%), the median age was 52 years ranging from 23 to 78 years, and the median body mass index (BMI) was 26 kg/m^{2} ranging from 15 to 43 kg/m^{2} (Table 10).
L1835: For Cohort 1, notably more subjects in the LEN arm had baseline HIV-1 RNA \le 100,000 copies/mL (96%) compared to the placebo arm (50%). The mean baseline CD4^{+} cell count and CD4^{+} percentage were higher in the LEN arm. The median number of prior ARV medications was nine for both arms. Further discussion of Cohort 1 baseline differences between the LEN and placebo arms is discussed in Section 6.3.1.
L1836: Compared to Cohort 1, Cohort 2 subjects had more prior antiretroviral (ARV) regimens, higher mean baseline CD4^{+} percentage and CD4^{+} cell count.

L1850: ## 6.2.1.4.2. Primary and Key Secondary Efficacy Results
L1851: ## Primary Endpoint
L1852: The Applicant's primary efficacy results were confirmed by the statistical review team, and the results demonstrate superiority of LEN compared to placebo for the endpoint of proportion of HIV-1 RNA reduction \ge 0.5 \log_{10} from baseline to the end of the FMP at Day 14. The 95% CI for the difference in the proportions (LEN – placebo) excluded zero and the p-value was statistically significant (p&lt;0.0001), indicating superiority (Table 11).
L1853: **Table 11. Primary Efficacy Endpoint of HIV-1 RNA Reduction \ge 0.5 \log_{10} at the End of Functional Monotherapy Period, Study 4625**
L1854: Parameter	LEN	Placebo	Difference and 95% CI	p-Value
HIV-1 RNA reduction \ge 0.5 \log_{10}	21/24 (87.5%)	2/12 (16.7%)	70.8 (34.9, 90.0)	<0.0001
L1855: Source: Statistical reviewer's analysis.
L1856: The 95% CI of the difference in proportions between groups and the corresponding p value were calculated based on an unconditional exact method using two invert one-sided tests.
L1857: Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; HIV-1, human immunodeficiency virus 1; SD, standard deviation
L1858: ## Secondary Endpoints
L1859: Assessing the durability of virologic response in HTE subjects is an important component of understanding the overall efficacy of LEN. At the end of the FMP, all subjects were transitioned from their initial (failing) background regimen to an optimized regimen in combination with open-label LEN. It was planned that the Week 26 and Week 52 HIV-1 RNA would be evaluated as secondary endpoints. The majority of subjects did not complete the Week 52 assessment at the time of NDA submission; thus, only Week 26 data are presented (Table 12). Approximately 81% subjects in Cohort 1 achieved HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 26: 66.7% and 87.5% for subjects in the placebo arm who later switched to LEN and the LEN arm, respectively. We did not find imbalances in baseline characteristics that account for the numerical difference between the two groups (see Section 6.3.1). In addition, variations between the two groups could happen due to the small sample size. In Cohort 2 only six subjects completed the Week 26 evaluation, therefore, the review team will revisit this analysis once more data are received.

L1881: ## 6.2.2. Study 4334 (CALIBRATE)
L1882: ## 6.2.2.1. Study Design
L1883: Results from Study 4334 serve as supplementary data for the efficacy and safety evaluation of LEN for the indication of treating the HTE HIV-1 population. This was a phase 2, randomized, open-label, active-controlled study conducted in the treatment-naïve PLWH population. Eligible subjects were randomized in a 2:2:2:1 ratio to SC LEN + (emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide [F/TAF] \to tenofovir alafenamide [TAF]), SC LEN + (F/TAF \to bictgravir [BIC]), Oral LEN + F/TAF, or bictgravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (B/F/TAF) group (Figure 9). Randomization was stratified by HIV-1 RNA level (\le 100,000 copies/mL or &gt; 100,000 copies/mL) at screening.
L1884: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1885: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1886: Figure 9. Study Design Schema, Study 4334
L1887: Source: Figure 2 of the Applicant's Clinical Summary.
L1888: During the induction period for the first two arms, in addition to the oral daily DVY, subjects also took oral LEN 600 mg on days 1 and 2, then 300 mg on day 8, followed by SC LEN 927 mg on day 15.
L1889: Abbreviations: B/C, bictegravir; BL, baseline; F/TAF, emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide; LEN, lenacapavir; QD, once daily; SC, subcutaneous; TAF, tenofovir alafenamide; B/F/TAF, bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide; Tx, treatment; Wk, week
L1890: ## 6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria
L1891: Key eligibility criteria are summarized in this section and the full criteria are available in Section III.15. Subjects with HIV who met the following criteria were included:
L1892: - Aged ≥18 years.
- ARV naïve (no use of any ARV within 1 month of screening).
- Plasma HIV-1 RNA ≥200 copies/mL and CD4+ cell count ≥200 cells/µL at screening.
L1893: The major exclusion criteria were:
L1894: - An opportunistic illness requiring acute therapy.
- Active and serious infections requiring parenteral antibiotic or antifungal therapy.
- HBV.
- HCV.
- Clinical decompensated liver cirrhosis.
- Malignancy requiring acute therapy.
- Alcohol or substance use.
- Significant abnormal ECG.
- eGFR ≤50 mL/min.
- ALT &gt;5× ULN.
- Direct bilirubin &gt;1.5× ULN.
- Platelets &lt;50,000/mm3.
- Hemoglobin &lt;8.0 g/dL.
- Use or planned use of exclusionary medications.
L1895: ## 6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan
L1896: The Applicant and the review division agreed on the interim analysis (IA) plan prior to the Week 28 IA.
L1897: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1898: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1899: The study had four prespecified IAs: Week 28, Week 38, Week 54 (primary analysis), and Week 80. The Week 28 IA was conducted when all subjects completed the Week 28 evaluation. The results of this analysis were used to supplement the efficacy and safety of LEN for the HTE population. There were no multiplicity adjustments planned because this was stated as a phase 2, non-confirmatory study.
L1900: The primary endpoint of this study was the proportion of subjects with HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 54 as determined by the U.S. FDA-defined snapshot algorithm. Because the majority of subjects had not yet reached Week 54 at the time of the NDA submission, the primary endpoint was not analyzed.
L1901: A secondary endpoint was the proportion of subjects with HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 28, as determined by the U.S. FDA-defined snapshot algorithm. The FAS was used as the analysis population. Point estimates and 95% CI for the difference in the response rates between each of the LEN-containing regimen groups (Treatment Groups 1 to 3) and the B/F/TAF group (Treatment Group 4) were constructed using stratum-adjusted Mantel-Haenszel proportion as described in Chapter 13 of *Categorical Data Analysis* (Koch et al. 1989), stratified by baseline HIV-1 RNA level (\le 100,000 copies/mL or &gt; 100,000 copies/mL).

L1923: ## 6.2.2.4.2. Secondary Efficacy Results

L1942: ## 6.3. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L1943: ## 6.3.1. Imbalance in Study 4625 Baseline Characteristics
L1944: ## Issue
L1945: The baseline imbalance of HIV-1 RNA and CD4+ cell count for Cohort 1 between the two randomized arms may impact the interpretability of the primary efficacy results.
L1946: ## Background
L1947: In Cohort 1, the mean baseline CD4+ cell count and CD4+ percentage were higher in the LEN arm than those in the placebo arm (199 versus 85 cells/µL CD4+ cell counts, and 10.8% versus 5.9% CD4+ percentages, respectively).
L1948: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1949: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1950: In the LEN arm, 46% (11/24) had baseline HIV-1 RNA &gt;20,000 copies/mL with one subject having &gt;100,000 copies/mL. Additionally, seven (29%) LEN-treated subjects had baseline HIV-1 RNA &lt;2000 copies/mL with five (21%) having &lt;1000 copies/mL, and four (17%) subjects did not maintain the eligibility entry criterion of &lt;400 copies/mL through their Baseline visit. In the placebo arm, all 12 subjects (100%) had baseline HIV-1 RNA &gt;20,000 copies/mL with 6 (50%) subjects having &gt;100,000 copies/mL (Table 17).
L1951: **Table 17. Number of Subjects With High Baseline Viral Loads, Study 4625**
L1952: Number of Subjects	LEN Cohort 1A	Placebo Cohort 1B
N=24	N=12

L1953: Source: FDA Clinical Virology reviewer's analysis.
L1954: Abbreviations: HIV, human immunodeficiency virus; LEN, lenacapavir
L1955: This finding suggests that subjects in the LEN arm may have had an advantage with regard to their baseline status, and therefore, may have had improved efficacy outcomes compared to subjects in the placebo arm.
L1956: ## Assessment
L1957: Post hoc analyses were conducted to explore the association between baseline HIV-1 RNA and CD4+ imbalance across Cohort 1 treatment arms and the outcome of HIV-1 RNA reduction of \ge 0.5 \log_{10}. The distributions of baseline HIV-1 RNA by arm and by outcome are presented in Table 18. Within each arm, subjects who had reduction \ge 0.5 \log_{10} at the end of the functional monotherapy period generally had higher baseline HIV-1 RNA. Therefore, it appears that the lower baseline HIV-1 RNA level in the LEN arm is not likely associated with more reduction in HIV-1 RNA at the end of the functional monotherapy period. In addition, subgroup analyses (Table 13) showed that the effects of LEN were consistent across the subgroups of HIV-1 RNA \le 100,000 copies/mL and &gt;100,000 copies/mL, and the subgroups of CD4+ &lt;200 cells/\muL and \ge 200 cells/\muL.

L1962: ## Conclusion
L1963: The baseline imbalance of HIV-1 RNA and CD4+ cell count did not impact the interpretability of the primary efficacy result.
L1964: ## 6.3.2. Justification for the Proposed Simplified Dosing Regimen
L1965: ## Issue
L1966: The Applicant proposes a simplified dosing regimen that was not studied during the LEN clinical development program.
L1967: ## Background
L1968: The LEN dosing regimen evaluated in the phase 2/3 study allowed for a 14-day oral lead-in period, where subjects received oral LEN on Day 1 (600 mg), Day 2 (600 mg), and Day 8 (300 mg) before SC LEN injection on Day 15 (927 mg), then every 26 weeks thereafter. The oral lead-in period enabled an assessment of safety and tolerability of LEN prior to SC LEN administration. Given the established safety profile and lack of exposure-safety relationship from the phase 2 and phase 2/3 trials, the Applicant proposed a simplified dosing regimen as a strategy to potentially improve adherence. The following simplified regimen is proposed: oral LEN 600 mg and SC LEN injection 927 mg on Day 1, oral LEN 600 mg on Day 2, followed by SC LEN injection 927 mg every 26 weeks thereafter.
L1969: ## Assessment
L1970: The Applicant performed population PK simulations using their final PK model (see Section III.14.3 for further details on the population PK) to compare LEN PK from both the phase 2/3 dosing regimen and the proposed simplified regimen. The simulated LEN concentration-time profiles and the predicted exposure metrics (AUC_{\tau}, C_{max}, and C_{trough}) indicated that the simplified regimen has a similar LEN PK profile compared to that evaluated in the phase 2/3 study (Figure 12 and Table 19). Similar LEN accumulation is expected after the second SC and the seventh SC dose after administration of either regimen (Figure 12).

L1992: ## Conclusion
L1993: Based on observed and predicted data, the exposures of LEN are anticipated to be similar between the regimen used in Study 4625 and the proposed simplified regimen. The review team agreed that the proposed label should include recommendations for both the simplified regimen and the regimen used in Study 4625.
L1994: ## 6.3.3. Impact of Subjects Not Maintaining Eligibility Criteria: Not Failing on Background Regimen or Nonadherence to Background Regimen
L1995: ## Issue
L1996: In a clinical trial designed for study in an HTE patient population, it is important to determine if the subjects are truly failing on their pre-trial ARV regimen rather than due to nonadherence to the ARV drugs with no evidence of resistance in their supposed “failing” regimen. If subjects are nonadherent to the regimen and do not have resistance to the “failing” regimen during the LEN functional monotherapy period, it will be difficult to determine the contribution of LEN to efficacy in the background of other active or partially active ARVs.
L1997: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L1998: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L1999: ## Background
L2000: The entry eligibility criteria for Study 4625 included:
L2001: - Resistance to \ge 2 ARVs from each of \ge 3 of the 4 main classes of ARV drugs (INSTI, NNRTI, NRTI, PI), which could include historical reports.
- Plasma HIV-1 RNA \ge 400 copies/mL at the screening visit while taking a failing background regimen.
L2002: ## Assessment
L2003: Eligibility criteria for Cohort 1 included 0.5 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA decline compared to the Screening visit and HIV-1 RNA \ge 400 copies/mL at the Cohort Selection visit. There were subjects who did not maintain eligibility criteria for Cohort 1 because of the following reasons:
L2004: - There was evidence that a subject was not failing background regimen:Day 1 viral load &lt;400 copies/mL.
- Decline in viral load from the Screening visit to Baseline.
- There was evidence that a subject was nonadherent to background regimen:&lt;3 class resistance (by genotype, phenotype, or historical)
- No reported resistance to drugs in failing background regimen

L2025: The efficacy (proportion of subjects achieving \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL reduction from baseline in HIV-1 RNA) of Cohort 1A and 1B was assessed after removing the subjects who had evidence they were not failing their background regimen or were nonadherent to the background regimen. After removing the five subjects who had evidence they were not failing their background regimen, 95% (18/19) of subjects in Cohort 1A (LEN) achieved \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL reduction in HIV-1 RNA from baseline compared to 17% (2/12) in the placebo Cohort 1B arm (difference of 78%) (Table 24). Removing the six subjects with evidence of nonadherence narrowed the difference between groups (86% [18/21] versus 22% [2/9]; difference of 63.5%) but was still significantly different. Removing both the subjects with evidence of not failing background regimen and subjects with evidence of nonadherence showed efficacy of 94% (15/16) versus 22% (2/9) (difference of 72%) compared to the overall efficacy of 88% (21/24) versus 17% (2/12) (difference of 71.5%). Thus, this supplementary sensitivity analysis confirmed the efficacy of LEN in comparison to placebo and was consistent with the primary endpoint analysis.

L2030: Although the sample size of Cohort 1 was small, and decreased further following sensitivity analysis exclusions, the demonstrated treatment effect for this efficacy analysis remains large. Of note, recent prior studies in the HTE patient population had a similar sample size (e.g., 40 HTE subjects in the phase 3 trial TMB-301 for ibalizumab-uiyk), which may reflect the challenge of enrolling trials in this limited patient population.
L2031: ## Conclusion
L2032: Five subjects (21%) in LEN Cohort 1A had evidence that they were not failing on their regimen at study entry, four of whom had &lt;400 copies/mL on Day 1. Additionally, three subjects in each LEN Cohort 1A and placebo Cohort 1B had evidence that they were nonadherent to their “failing” background regimen based on genotypic and phenotypic susceptibility to their background drugs. Supplementary sensitivity efficacy analyses removing these subjects confirmed the primary endpoint analysis of LEN.
L2033: ## 6.3.4. Dosing Interval and Approach to Missed Subcutaneous Maintenance Doses
L2034: ## Issues
L2035: - Is administration of SC LEN within the Applicant's proposed dosing window of \pm 2 weeks expected to compromise the safety or efficacy of LEN?
L2036: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2037: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2038: - Is reinitiating therapy with the indicated regimen in patients who did not receive SC LEN up to 28 weeks since the previous SC LEN dose expected to compromise the safety of LEN?
L2039: ## Background
L2040: The Applicant has proposed a dosing window of 26\pm 2 weeks (i.e., 24 to 28 weeks) after the previous SC injection. In phase 2 and phase 2/3 studies, SC LEN doses were to be administered within 24 to 28 weeks after the previous SC LEN dose as per protocol.
L2041: The Applicant proposes to restart LEN regimen with the oral loading dose, if more than 28 weeks have elapsed since the previous SC LEN injection. For subjects in phase 2 and phase 2/3 studies who were not dosed by Week 28 and continued in the studies, the protocol indicated that the regimen be reinitiated with oral LEN followed by SC LEN administration (oral LEN 600 mg daily for 2 days followed by oral LEN 300 mg on Day 8, with SC LEN injection 927 mg restarting 1 week later) with the intent to rapidly correct LEN concentrations.
L2042: ## Assessment
L2043: ## Applicant's Proposed \pm 2-Week Dosing Window
L2044: The Applicant predicted the following arithmetic mean C_{\text{trough}} (90% CI of mean) in adult patients at Weeks 24, 26, 28, 30 and 32, following the phase 2/3 dosing regimen: 34.6 (29.4, 38.5), 29.2 (24.6, 32.5), 24.5 (20.4, 27.3), 20.6 (17.0, 23.1), and 17.3 (14.2, 19.7) ng/mL, respectively. According to the analysis conducted by the Applicant (Figure 13), the lower bound of the 90% CI of the simulated arithmetic mean C_{\text{trough}} was consistently above the IQ4 threshold of 15.5 ng/mL, indicating that LEN will maintain efficacious concentrations when dosed within the proposed \pm 2 week dosing window.
L2045: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2046: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2047: **Figure 13. Predicted LEN Arithmetic Mean C_{\text{trough}} (90% CI of Mean) on Weeks 24 to 32 After the First SC Injection in Adult Patients Receiving the Phase 2/3 Dosing Regimen**
L2048: \text{IQ}4 = inhibitory quotient 4; LEN = lenacapavir; PWH = people with HIV; SC = subcutaneous
The points and error bars represent mean and 90% CI simulated LEN C_{\text{trough}} exposures. The horizontal dashed line represents the \text{IQ}4 threshold at 15.5 ng/mL. Weeks 24 to 32 indicate the number of weeks after SC administration.
Source: Applicant's Summary of Clinical Pharmacology Studies, Figure 13, page 77.
Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; C_{\text{trough}}, minimum concentration; \text{IQ}4, inhibitory quotient 4
L2049: According to the phase 2 study (4334) and phase 2/3 study (4625) protocols, SC LEN doses were to be administered with a dosing window of 24 to 28 weeks, and the regimen was to be restarted (with oral lead-in) for dosing delays longer than 28 weeks from the last SC injection. However, &gt;75% of the subjects were evaluated for PK or efficacy endpoints 26 weeks after the first SC injection, hence there were insufficient data to assess the appropriateness of the proposed dosing window based on observed LEN PK data.
L2050: The review team assessment of the dosing window found that unlike arithmetic mean C_{\text{trough}} (as shown in Figure 14), the geometric mean C_{\text{trough}} (Figure 15) and the median C_{\text{trough}} (Figure 16) showed that at Week 28, after the first SC injection, the average C_{\text{trough}} is expected to be around the \text{IQ}4 (15.5 ng/mL). Therefore, about 50% of subjects are expected to be below \text{IQ}4 at Week 28 (Figure 16, lower panel), which is lower than the predicted average C_{\text{trough}} and \text{IQ}4 attainment for Week 26 (reference dosing interval, Figure 15 and Figure 16). The discrepancy between the arithmetic mean C_{\text{trough}} (as shown by the Applicant in Figure 14) and the geometric mean or median C_{\text{trough}} (Figure 15 and Figure 16) is likely, in part, due to the imbalance in LEN exposure between BMI groups in studied patients (4334 and 4625), with underweight patients having higher LEN exposure and overweight/obese patients having lower LEN exposure compared to patients with normal BMI. In addition, as depicted in Figure 16 the difference in the average C_{\text{trough}} between Study 4334 (in treatment-naïve patients with HIV) and Study 4625 (in HTE patients with HIV), due to drug-drug interactions (co-medications with cobicistat or ritonavir) in Study 4625, likely contributed to the discrepancy between the overall mean and geometric mean or median C_{\text{trough}} (calculated from both studies). The exclusion of subjects with interacting co-medication from Study 4625 decreased the average C_{\text{trough}} to levels similar to those observed in Study 4334 (see Section III.14.3 for further details).
L2051: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2052: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2053: The geometric (\pm 90\% CI) LEN C_{\text{trough}} after administration of the LEN second SC dose either 24 or 26 weeks after the first SC dose is expected to be above IQ4 (Figure 15 and Figure 16, middle column of each panel; data not shown for Week 24). By contrast, dosing at 28 weeks (Figure 15 and Figure 16, right column of each panel) is expected to maintain the geometric (\pm 90\% CI) C_{\text{trough}} either closer to or at the IQ4 threshold, particularly for overweight and more likely obese patients, as depicted by the lower right panel of Figure 15.
L2054: In conclusion, a second injection given 26 weeks instead of 28 weeks after the first injection is more likely to ensure that the geometric mean LEN C_{\text{trough}} is well above the IQ4 threshold in all BMI groups. A second injection given 28 weeks after the first injection is expected to maintain the geometric mean C_{\text{trough}} either closer to IQ4 or at the IQ4 for a long period of time (due to slower accumulation), particularly in overweight/obese patients. Because most patients in phase 2 and phase 2/3 studies received SC LEN at Week 26, the clinical implications of LEN concentrations falling below IQ4, especially in a subset of overweight/obese patients, at Week 28 are unknown.
L2055: ## Conclusion
L2056: The optimal dosing interval for SC LEN injection is 26 weeks, particularly in overweight and obese patients to maintain LEN geometric mean C_{\text{trough}} and its 95% CI well above the IQ4 threshold. However, \pm 2 weeks dosing window is acceptable to provide flexibility and facilitate adherence to the SC LEN regimen.

L2075: ## **Applicant's Proposal of Reinitiating the Indicated Regimen in Patients Who Did Not Receive SC LEN Up To 28 Weeks After the Previous SC LEN Dose**
L2076: The Applicant proposed that during the LEN SC maintenance period, if more than 28 weeks have elapsed since the last LEN SC injection and if it is clinically appropriate to continue LEN treatment, then reinitiate the indicated dosing regimen.
L2077: PK simulations were performed for different dosing delays (Weeks 30 to 48) after the last SC injection followed by either the administration of an SC LEN injection or the reinitiation of the dosing regimen starting with oral loading.
L2078: **Figure 17** (upper panel) shows that the median LEN concentration from the previous LEN injection stays above IQ4 as long as the next LEN SC injection is administered within the dosing window (\pm 2 weeks).
L2079: The lower panel of **Figure 17** shows that reinitiation of the dosing regimen (starting with oral loading) for dosing delays &gt;28 weeks and up to 32 weeks is expected to yield a median C_{\text{trough}} and SC C_{\text{max}} comparable to the second SC injection from the regular 24 to 28-week dosing window. However, the median C_{\text{max}} resulting from the oral loading dose is anticipated to be relatively higher than the median C_{\text{max}} observed and predicted with the indicated regimen. Even though the median C_{\text{max}} from the loading dose is relatively higher, it remains within acceptable safety ranges and well below the LEN concentrations and C_{\text{max}} values observed in the thorough QT study (Study 4332).

L2085: ## **Conclusion**
L2086: The Applicant's proposal to reinstitute the indicated dosing regimen if more than 28 weeks have elapsed since the last LEN SC injection, and if it is clinically appropriate to continue LEN treatment, is acceptable.
L2087: ## 7. Risk and Risk Management
L2088: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L2089: Nonclinical studies were conducted using both the oral and subcutaneous routes of exposure to assess both systemic and local toxicity of lenacapavir. Both routes of exposure were used in clinical trials; the oral as a lead-in and the subcutaneous route for maintenance given once every 6 months. Nonclinical safety studies with lenacapavir included good laboratory practice (GLP) single and repeat-dose toxicology studies in rats and dogs; reproductive and developmental toxicology studies in rats and rabbits; and in vitro and in vivo safety pharmacology and genotoxicology studies. Thirteen-week and 2-year carcinogenicity studies in mice and rats, respectively, are currently ongoing and will be part of a future postmarketing requirement (PMR). Overall, the nonclinical safety assessment for lenacapavir was considered acceptable to support marketplace approval from a pharmacology/toxicology perspective. Exposure multiples mentioned in the summary text are based on total lenacapavir concentration. All pertinent studies and findings are summarized in the following section. Full reviews for all studies are located in Section III.13.2.
L2090: ## Safety Pharmacology and Pharmacokinetics
L2091: Please see the clinical virology review (Section III.19) for studies on mechanism of action and antiviral activity.
L2092: In safety pharmacology studies, other than a slight decrease in respiration rate at 100 mg/kg, lenacapavir had no adverse effects on other respiratory parameters, neurological functions or changes in electrocardiogram parameters tested in rats and dogs.
L2093: The pharmacokinetic profile of lenacapavir (GS-6207) following IV or oral administration was evaluated in portal vein cannulated male Cynomolgus monkeys and Beagle dogs with or without the cytochrome P450 (CYP) inhibitor, aminobenzotriazole, to understand the role of CYP metabolism of lenacapavir. The results from these studies indicated that pretreating dogs and monkeys with aminobenzotriazole did not change lenacapavir oral exposure in dogs or monkeys, but showed the role of intestinal metabolism of lenacapavir.
L2094: Lenacapavir was \ge 98\% protein-bound in all animals and humans (unbound fraction was 0.13, 0.83, 1.11, 1.45, and 1.46% in rats, dogs, cynomolgus monkey, Rhesus monkey, and human, respectively) at a concentration of 10mM.
L2095: The highest tissue concentration of lenacapavir was detected in the liver up to 42 days followed by kidney cortex, kidneys, pancreas, kidney medulla, brown fat, and thyroid in both intact and bile duct-cannulated nonpigmented male Wister Hanover rats and intact pigmented Long Evans rats. LEN was cleared from all organs by 28 days and from the liver by 56 days.
L2096: Several metabolites resulting from glutathione conjugation, pentose conjugation, and glucuronidation were identified in isolated liver microsomes and hepatocytes, plasma, urine,
L2097: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2098: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2099: feces, bile, and/or liver samples from rats, dogs, monkeys, and humans. Oxidative metabolites were not detected. No new or additional metabolites were observed in human plasma or tissues that were not identified in human isolated microsomes and hepatocytes or in other animal species.
L2100: The major routes of elimination in rats and dogs is feces resulting from lenacapavir excretion into the intestines by the p-glycoprotein transporter.
L2101: ## General Toxicology
L2102: Repeat-dose toxicology studies were conducted with oral and subcutaneous formulations of lenacapavir to evaluate toxicity from systemic and local toxicity and irritation. The most common toxicity noted among all of the toxicology studies was injection site reactions.
L2103: The acute toxicity and tolerability of lenacapavir was evaluated in single dose intravenous studies in both Wister Hanover rats and Beagle dogs up to 30 mg/kg. Infusion site reactions (cellular inflammation, thrombus, congestion/hemorrhage, edema, and fibrosis) were noted at all doses. Additionally, clinical signs of toxicity in rats included: red urine, ataxia, hypoactivity, vocalization, squinting and/or pale eyes, audible/labored/irregular breathing, and sternal recumbence. Clinical signs of toxicity in dogs included: skin lesions, intermittent tremors, vocalization, and/or discharge of the left eye and front foot.
L2104: Pivotal repeat-dose toxicology evaluation for lenacapavir included GLP studies of up to 6-month duration in rats and 9-month duration in dogs via oral or subcutaneous administrations. The skin at the injection site was the target organ of toxicity in both animal species. Additionally, in the 9-month dog study using the clinical formulation, the liver and kidney were also identified as targeted organs of toxicity.
L2105: Based on systemic exposure in the repeat-dose studies in rats via subcutaneous administrations, there was no target organ identified at doses up to 100 mg/kg. However, based on local toxicity, the injection site was the target organ identified in the rat studies via subcutaneous administrations in all studies. These injection site reactions were observed after the recovery periods, albeit at a lesser degree of intensity. Toxicities at the injection sites included necrosis, granulomatous inflammation, mixed cell inflammation, and/or macrophage infiltration.
L2106: Based on systemic exposure in the repeat-dose studies in dogs via subcutaneous administrations, there was no target organ identified at doses up to 100 mg/kg up to 2 months. However, repeat-dose studies up to 9 months in dogs identified the liver, gall bladder, kidneys, and stomach as targeted organs of toxicity. Liver findings included bile duct degeneration and cell/bile ductule hyperplasia. Gallbladder findings included edema and hyperplasia detected at doses up to 411 mg/kg. Kidney findings included tubule degeneration and dilatation, and findings in the stomach included degeneration/atrophy of mucosa at the highest dose of 411 mg/kg. Additionally, based on local toxicity, the injection site was the target organ identified in all repeat-dose dog studies via subcutaneous administrations up to 411 mg/kg. Toxicities at the injection sites included necrosis, granulomatous inflammation, mixed cell inflammation, and/or macrophage infiltration. These injection site reactions were observed after the recovery periods, albeit at a lesser intensity. Based on systemic exposure, at the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL), lenacapavir was 32-fold the human exposure at the recommended human dose (RHD) in the 2-month rat study and 6- to 8-fold in the 6-month rat study. Additionally, based on
L2107: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2108: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2109: systemic exposure, at the NOAEL in the 2- and 9-month dog studies, lenacapavir was 24- and 9-fold the human exposure at the RHD.
L2110: In clinical trials, the most notable adverse events (AEs) associated with lenacapavir were nodules that formed at the injection sites, thus reflecting the main toxicities of injection site reactions observed in nonclinical species.
L2111: ## Genotoxicology and Carcinogenicity
L2112: Lenacapavir was negative for mutagenesis in the in vitro reverse mutation assay, negative for clastogenicity in the in vitro assay using human peripheral lymphocytes, and negative for genotoxicity in the in vivo micronucleus assay in rats. Additionally, several impurities were identified and tested in a battery of genotoxicology studies for mutagenesis and clastogenicity. Overall, the weight of evidence indicates that lenacapavir does not exhibit genotoxic potential.
L2113: The carcinogenicity potential of lenacapavir is being evaluated in a 26-week study (single subcutaneous injection given once every 13 weeks for a total of two doses) in 001178-T (hemizygous) RasH2 mice and a 2-year study (single subcutaneous injection given once every 13 weeks for a total of eight doses) in Wister Hanover rats. These studies are ongoing at the time of NDA submission and will be part of a future PMR.
L2114: ## Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology
L2115: No lenacapavir-related effects on male and female fertility parameters occurred with up to 100 mg/kg lenacapavir when administered via a single subcutaneous injection to rats at exposures seven- and five-fold (in males and females, respectively) the RHD. No lenacapavir-related effects on embryo-fetal development (EFD) occurred at doses up to 30 mg/kg lenacapavir when orally administered to rats once daily from gestation day (GD) 6 to 17 at exposures 16-fold the RHD.
L2116: In the rabbit EFD study, lower body weight gains at doses up to 20 mg/kg correlated to a dose-dependent decrease in food intake following intravenous administration of lenacapavir. Body weights returned to those of controls levels after 9 days without treatment. No other maternal or fetal toxicity occurred with up to the highest intravenous administration of 20 mg/kg at exposures 39-fold the RHD.
L2117: In the pre-and postnatal development (PPND) toxicity study, lenacapavir was administered to pregnant rats via a single subcutaneous injection of doses of 30 and 300 mg/kg on GD 6. There were no maternal toxicities or effects on PPND at doses up to 300 mg/kg at exposures five-fold the RHD. Lactation endpoints were not measured in the PPND study.
L2118: ## Additional Toxicology Studies
L2119: Lenacapavir resulted in local toxicity at the injection sites at concentrations up to 500 mg/mL in rabbits. Lenacapavir was not phototoxic, cytotoxic, or considered an eye irritant. Using in vitro skin models, lenacapavir was not considered corrosive but was considered positive in two of three skin sensitization assays. However, in the in vivo assessment, lenacapavir was considered negative for sensitization potential. In the clinical formulation for marketing, the hemolytic potential of lenacapavir is low.

L2121: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use

L2140: ## 7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L2141: Lenacapavir is the first in a new class of antiretroviral drugs, so no previously described clinical experience is available to inform any specific safety concern regarding capsid inhibitors.
L2142: Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported with combination antiretroviral therapy, particularly in the initial phase of treatment, in patients whose immune systems develop an inflammatory response to indolent or residual opportunistic infections. This is also often particularly relevant in a heavily treatment-experienced patient population. Loss of virologic response due to drug-drug interactions has been included as a warning in labeling for other ARVs.
L2143: For other ARVs that are administered in an injectable form, such as Cabenuva (a long-acting formulation of two drugs, cabotegravir and rilpivirine), injection site reactions are the most common adverse reactions. These were described usually (79%) as localized pain or discomfort. The Cabenuva label notes that “Other manifestations included nodules (14%), induration (12%), swelling (8%), erythema (4%), pruritus (4%), bruising (3%), warmth (2%), and hematoma (2%). Abscess and cellulitis at the injection site were each reported in less than 1% of subjects” (Cabenuva 2021). Serious post-injection reactions were reported in less than 1% of subjects within minutes after the injection of rilpivirine and begin to resolve within a few minutes after the injection. These reactions were characterized by signs and symptoms including dyspnea, agitation, abdominal cramping, flushing, sweating, oral numbness, and changes in blood pressure.
L2144: Additionally, given the long-acting properties of Cabenuva, the label notes that “residual concentrations of both cabotegravir and rilpivirine may remain in the systemic circulation of patients for prolonged periods”; therefore, a warning is included that nonadherence could lead to loss of virologic response and development of resistance.
L2145: ## 7.3. Potential Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L2146: Lenacapavir has not been approved in any country; therefore, there has been no postmarketing experience with lenacapavir.
L2147: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L2148: ## Adequacy of Applicant's Clinical Safety Assessments
L2149: The review team did not identify any major data quality or integrity issues that preclude performing a safety review. No major issues were identified with respect to recording, coding, and categorizing AEs. The Applicant's translations of verbatim terms to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities preferred terms for the events reported in Studies 4625 and 4334 were coded according to Version 23.1 and reviewed and were found to be acceptable.
L2150: AEs were protocol-defined as: "any untoward medical occurrence in a clinical study participant administered an investigational product, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment."
L2151: Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined in the Applicant's analysis, and for the purpose of this review, as any AE that occurred on or after the day of treatment initiation.
L2152: Adverse drug reactions were defined for the purpose of this review as any TEAE that was considered by the investigator to be related to the study drug with reasonable possibility. "Reasonable possibility" is meant to convey that there are facts or evidence or arguments to suggest a causal relationship, rather than a relationship cannot be ruled out.
L2153: Serious adverse events (SAEs) were protocol-defined as any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose, resulted in:
L2154: - Death.
- Was life-threatening (note: the term "life-threatening" in the definition of "serious" refers to an event in which the subject was at risk of death at the time of the event; it does not refer to an event that hypothetically might have caused death if it were more severe).
- In-patient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization.
- Persistent or significant disability/incapacity.
- A congenital anomaly/birth defect.
- A medically important event or reaction: such events may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalization but may jeopardize the subject or may require intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes constituting SAEs. Medical and scientific judgment must be exercised to determine whether such an event is reportable under expedited reporting rules. Examples of medically important events include intensive treatment in an emergency room or at home for allergic bronchospasm; blood dyscrasias or convulsions that do not result in hospitalization; and development of drug dependency or drug abuse.
L2155: Severity grades were defined by the Division of AIDS Table for Grading the Severity of Adult and Pediatric Adverse Events (corrected Version 2.1, July 2017) (NIAID 2017).

L2165: ## Approach to Assessment of Clinical Trial Data
L2166: The review approach for assessment of risk consisted of evaluation of the safety data from the phase 2/3 trials separately as well as the pooled safety data from phase 1 studies. These trials were reviewed separately because the studies enrolled different patient populations. Study 4625 included an HTE population, while Study 4334 enrolled a treatment-naïve population, and the phase 1 studies were healthy adults. Results of individual trials are highlighted where important differences may have emerged.
L2167: Clinical trial data from Studies 4635 and 4334 were independently analyzed using JMP and JMP Clinical software. Additional analyses were provided by the Clinical Data Scientist support team. All safety assessments and conclusions are those of the clinical review team unless otherwise specified. Prespecified hypothesis testing was not proposed for safety outcomes in Studies 4625 or 4334. Comparisons are therefore based on descriptive analyses.
L2168: Comparisons across arms in Study 4625 were limited because assessment during the randomized portion of the study were limited to the FMP with only the oral administration of LEN. As a general approach, attribution of events due to LEN comparisons across study arms were derived largely from Study 4334 and selected cohorts from phase 1. For relevance to the proposed SC dosing, study arms that included SC LEN were combined and compared to another active control arm randomized to B/F/TAF. Because the pooled phase 1 data were placebo-controlled in healthy volunteers, comparisons across arms were generally more acceptable for the purpose of assessing contribution of LEN; however, the overall sample size achieved in this analysis was small and duration of follow-up was shorter.
L2169: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2170: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2171: In the Applicant's proposed label, Adverse Reactions (Section 6.1) included only data from Study 4625, as this study included the relevant patient population for the proposed indication, whereas Study 4334 included treatment-naïve subjects that were anticipated to have significant differences in underlying disease severity and comorbid conditions.
L2172: ## 7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
L2173: Overall, the safety database is adequate to assess the safety of lenacapavir for the proposed indication, dosage regimen, and patient population. See Table 27.

A total of 284 subjects received at least one dose of 927 mg SC LEN (with same proposed SC formulation or equivalent oral dose that is expected to achieve the targeted exposure for at least 6 months). A total of 232 subjects received at least one 927 mg SC dose of LEN with the same proposed formulation for marketing. The total number of PLWH who received SC LEN at the proposed dose/duration (LEN exposures \ge26 weeks) was 177.

L2222: ## 7.6. Safety Findings and Concerns Based on Review of Clinical Safety Database
L2223: ## 7.6.1. Safety Findings and Concerns, Studies 4625 (CAPELLA) and 4334 (CALIBRATE)
L2224: ## 7.6.1.1. Overall Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event Summary
L2225: An overview of the TEAEs in Studies 4625 and 4334 through at least the Week 26 and Week 28 visit dates, respectively, is shown in **Table 33**. While the comparisons across the grouped study arms (total LEN in Study 4625 and Study 4334) revealed a trend of higher incidence of AEs as compared with the oral-only regimen of B/F/TAF, there were no serious AEs and very few moderate to severe (Grades 3 to 5) AEs that were considered by the investigator to be study-drug related in any of the studies. Overall, these trends suggest that differences in AEs reported across studies likely reflect underlying differences in patient populations.

L2259: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
L2260: In Study 4625, TEAEs were defined as an AE that began on or after the first dose date of blinded study drug and prior to the first dose date of the open-label study drug. Table 36 includes TEAEs occurring at 5% or higher frequency in Study 4625. The most common TEAEs were injection site reactions (ISRs) in the SC LEN arms. The B/F/TAF arm, however, did not include any injectable study drug. Other frequent TEAEs in LEN arms of Studies 4625 and 4334 included nausea, headache, and diarrhea.

L2270: ## 7.6.2. Laboratory Findings
L2271: Most laboratory abnormalities in Studies 4625 and 4334 were generally not clinically significant (Grade 1 or 2), and occurred in subjects who had previous underlying conditions such as diabetes.
L2272: In Study 4625, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 15 (21%) of 72 subjects. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported in four (6%) subjects. Grade 3 and 4 abnormalities that occurred in more than two subjects included high creatinine and high fasting glucose. None of the subjects had Grade 3 or higher increase in creatine kinase (CK) or CK-associated AEs such as rhabdomyolysis. Please see additional discussion in Section 7.6.3.6.
L2273: In Study 4334, Grade 3 laboratory abnormalities were reported in 19 (12%) of the 157 subjects who received LEN (the total LEN group) and 3 (12%) of the 25 subjects in the B/F/TAF group. Grade 4 laboratory abnormalities were reported for seven (5%) subjects in the total LEN group, including three subjects with high CK and one subject each with the following abnormalities: high alanine aminotransferase (ALT), hyperbilirubinemia, fasting triglycerides, high lipase, and nonfasting hyperglycemia. The Grade 4 high ALT was attributed by the investigator to the use of Bactrim for the treatment of *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia. The Grade 3 and 4 CK elevations were all attributed to strenuous activity, dehydration, or use of creatine, and the levels returned to normal at a later visit. Please see additional discussion in Section 7.6.4.6.
