L2327: ## 7.6.3.2. Deaths
L2328: One treatment-emergent adverse event resulting in death was reported in Study 4625. This event was not considered related to LEN. No additional deaths were reported with follow-up through July 27, 2021 in the Applicant's 90-Day Safety Report.
L2329: Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 61-year-old white male in the United States. At baseline, he had a prior history of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, his HIV-1 RNA was 112,000 copies/mL, and his CD4+ cell count was 7/µL (0.8%). His background regimen included ibalizumab, dolutegravir, emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide fumarate, and fosamprenavir. On Study Day 15, his HIV-1 RNA was 1250 copies/mL but rebounded to 101,000 copies/mL on Day 50.
L2330: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2331: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2332: On Day 38 the subject experienced serious dizziness of Grade 3. LEN dose was not changed. The event was considered not related to study drug and resolved on Day 43.
L2333: On Day 80 the subject experienced a Grade 5 SAE of “neoplasm malignant”. Due to deteriorating clinical status during hospitalization, the subject was transferred to hospice, where he subsequently died. His cause of death was updated to “metastatic cancer”, and this was a suspected recurrence of his prior non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. He expired prior to biopsy of the new lesions, no autopsy was performed, nor was any further specific diagnosis on the type of cancer provided by the investigator.
L2334: *Reviewer comment: Given the prior history and timing of the onset of symptoms, the actual start of the adverse event of “metastatic cancer” was likely prior to the time of study enrollment and was not related to LEN.*
L2335: ## 7.6.3.3. Serious Adverse Events
L2336: No SAEs were reported during the FMP of Study 4625. Serious AEs were reported for 5.6% (4 of 72 subjects); no SAEs were reported in more than one subject. No SAEs were considered related to study drug. As discussed above in Section 7.6.3.2, one SAE (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6)) resulted in death. See Table 42.

L2344: - Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 24-year-old male in Cohort 1 who had COVID-19. The event started on Day 266, resolved/recovered on Day 275, and was considered to be unrelated to the study drug.
- Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 50-year-old male in Cohort 1 who had the SAE of pneumonia (reported term: multifocal pneumonia). The event started on Day 465, resolved/recovered on Day 467, and was considered to be unrelated to the study drug.
- Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) was a 51-year-old female in Cohort 2 who had a baseline CD4+ cell count of 14 cells/\muL experienced the SAEs of septic shock (Days 177 to 197), and renal impairment and shock (both events, Days 221 to 236). The SAEs of renal impairment and the second event of shock were initially considered related to the study drug by the investigator. Renal function improved promptly while LEN exposure continued, and both
L2345: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2346: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2347: SAEs resolved in 6 days. The Applicant noted that after the data cut for this NDA Safety Update, based on emerging clinical information regarding these SAEs for this subject, the investigator no longer considered them to be related to study drug.
L2348: Additional details of the subjects in the original NDA submission with nonfatal SAEs were provided:
L2349: - Subject [REDACTED](b) (6), who had a history of intermittent proctalgia due to prior rectal surgery for squamous cell carcinoma, experienced the unrelated SAE of proctalgia (Days 288 to 289), which was reported in the initial submission, and the additional unrelated SAEs of anal squamous cell carcinoma (Days 257 to 259) and impaired healing (reported term: nonhealing perianal wound; Days 351 to 358) since the NDA submission. In the investigator's opinion, all three SAEs were likely to be related to the subject's underlying conditions.
- In the original NDA submission, subject [REDACTED](b) (6) experienced the SAEs of pancreatic mass (Day 36, ongoing), abdominal pain (Days 77 to 115), and Clostridium difficile colitis (Days 240 to 242). An additional SAE of angina pectoris (Days 367 to 368) was reported and was considered unrelated to the study drug.
L2350: ## 7.6.3.4. Dropouts and/or Discontinuations Due to Adverse Events
L2351: No TEAEs were reported in Study 4625 that led to discontinuation through follow-up period ending April 01, 2021. Since the original NDA data cut date through follow-up period ending July 27, 2021, one subject prematurely discontinued study drug due to TEAEs of injection site nodules, both of which were Grade 1 and were ongoing with follow-up through June 25, 2021.

L2477: Although not part of the Applicant's Integrated Summary of Safety (ISS) analysis for Studies 4538 and 5709, in Cohort 3 of Study GS-US-200-4329 (Study 4329; a phase 1 study evaluating the safety, tolerability, PK, metabolism, and excretion of LEN following a single IV dose in healthy subjects), one subject who received LEN 20 mg had a Grade 4 SAE of rhabdomyolysis which was considered related to study drug and resolved during continued exposure to LEN. The serum creatine phosphokinase level elevated to a peak of 380,000 U/L (normal range 0 to 250 U/L), which was accompanied by increased lactate dehydrogenase (585 U/L), but the subject remained asymptomatic. There were no reports of recent strenuous exercise, trauma, illicit substance use, or prior creatine phosphokinase elevations. The time of onset of the rhabdomyolysis (Day 22) for this subject was 21 days after the Cmax of LEN was reached (within 1 hour of dosing), and the LEN concentration was approximately 150-fold lower on Day 22 than Cmax on Day 1 (Day 1: 210 ng/mL; Day 22: 1.43 ng/mL). In addition, creatine phosphokinase levels for this subject continued to decrease in the presence of ongoing LEN exposure.
L2478: *Clinical reviewer's comment: Given the lack of presenting symptoms, delayed time of onset, and resolution despite continued LEN exposure, this presentation would be unusual for drug-induced rhabdomyolysis.*
L2479: ## 7.7. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L2480: ## 7.7.1. Resistance Assessments of Virologic Failures
L2481: ## Issue
L2482: The assessment of resistance emergence in virologic failures of an LEN-containing ARV regimen is critical to interpreting the overall risk-benefit of LEN and understanding the durability of LEN as a component of an ARV regimen in an HTE patient population.
L2483: ## Background
L2484: Genotypic and phenotypic analyses of the HIV-1 protease, reverse transcriptase (RT), integrase, and capsid (CA) proteins were performed at screening for all subjects enrolled in Study 4625.
L2485: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2486: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2487: Resistance testing at postscreening timepoints was performed for any subject meeting the criteria of the resistance analysis, which included any subject who received at least one dose of study drug and met one of the following virologic failure (VF) criteria:
L2488: - HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL and &lt;1 log_{10} HIV-1 RNA reduction from the start of oral LEN at the Week 4 visit, confirmed at a scheduled or unscheduled visit at least 2 weeks following Week 4.
- At any visit, after achieving HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL, a rebound in HIV-1 RNA to \ge 50 copies/mL, which was subsequently confirmed at the following scheduled or unscheduled visit; OR
- At any visit, a &gt;1 log_{10} increase in HIV-1 RNA from the nadir, which was subsequently confirmed at the following scheduled or unscheduled visit.
- Any study subject with HIV-1 RNA \ge 50 copies/mL at the study endpoint or study discontinuation who did not meet any of the criteria above.
L2489: Monogram Biosciences, Inc. (South San Francisco, CA, USA) was the designated reference laboratory for all resistance analyses at screening and virologic failure. The PhenoSense GT^{\text{®}} assay (Monogram Biosciences), which determines the genotype for the entire HIV-1 protease and amino acids 1 to 305 of RT and measures the drug susceptibility of all marketed protease and RT inhibitors based on that sequence, was performed for all subjects at screening. The GeneSeq Integrase assay was used to determine the sequence of the entire IN protein, and the PhenoSense Integrase assay measured the drug susceptibility of all marketed INSTIs based on that sequence (Monogram Biosciences). In cases of assay failure, alternative assays such as GeneSeq, GenoSure mg, or GenoSure Integrase (Monogram Biosciences) were used to obtain genotypic information.
L2490: HIV-1 CA genotype was determined using the GenoSure Gag-Pro assay, which uses next-generation sequencing (NGS) to detect codon variants present at &gt;10\% frequency (Monogram Biosciences). The PhenoSense Gag-Pro assay (Monogram Biosciences) was used to assess phenotypic response to LEN.
L2491: The phenotypic susceptibility of screening samples from enrolled subjects to entry inhibitors (enfuvirtide, fostemsavir, ibalizumab, maraviroc) was analyzed at the end of the enrollment period. These analyses were conducted using a combination of the Trofile and PhenoSense Entry assays (Monogram Biosciences), which determine the co-receptor tropism and the susceptibility to the inhibitors, respectively, based on the HIV-1 envelope from the subject's sample.
L2492: ## Assessment
L2493: ## **Key Capsid Resistance-Associated Substitutions Selected in Cell Culture**
L2494: LEN-resistant viruses were selected with increasing concentrations of LEN in MT-2 cells following 19 to 103 days in cell culture passage (see Section III.18).
L2495: - At low concentrations, LEN selected for N74D, which conferred 16-fold decreased susceptibility to LEN.
- At higher drug concentrations, LEN selected for Q67H+N74D, which conferred &gt;2757-fold decreased susceptibility to LEN.
L2496: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2497: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2498: - For the LEN selected resistance substitutions, there was no change in susceptibility to any of the tested inhibitors from other antiretroviral classes (atazanavir [PI], dolutegravir [INSTI], efavirenz [NNRTI], and elvitegravir [INSTI]).
L2499: LEN-resistant viruses were selected at fixed LEN concentrations in PBMCs over 35 days (See Section III.18).
L2500: - Within the projected human plasma exposure range, breakthrough viruses exhibited 5.5- to &gt;200-fold decreases in LEN susceptibility and encoded substitutions N74D (16-fold), L56I (204-fold), Q67H (5-fold), Q67H + N74S (20-fold), or T107N (87-fold).
- At higher concentrations, the treatment-emergent viruses encoded substitutions M66I (&gt;2757-fold), L56I (204-fold), K70N (assay failure), or M66I+Q67H (1594-fold).
L2501: Variants containing single or double substitutions conferred reduced susceptibility to LEN (3.8- to &gt;2757-fold) with highest reductions seen with L56I (204-fold), M66I (&gt;2757-fold), M66I +Q67H (1594-fold), Q67H+N74D (&gt;2757-fold), and Q67H+T107N (87-fold) (Table 51 and Section III.18). These mutant viruses were fully susceptible to PIs atazanavir (fold-change range: 0.9- to 1.5) and darunavir (fold-change range: 0.9- to 1.7), indicating the absence of cross-resistance to PIs for these LEN-resistant mutants.

L2509: ## **Screening Resistance in Study 4625**
L2510: The target population for Study 4625 was HTE HIV-1 subjects with resistance to at least two ARV medications from each of at least three of the four main classes of ARV medications (INSTI, NNRTI, NRTI, PI). In the presence of the RT substitution M184V/I, resistance to lamivudine and emtricitabine did not count towards the total number of drugs with resistance for the NRTI drug class per protocol requirements. Resistance reports were obtained prior to enrollment to confirm that the resistance criteria for enrollment in the study were met. These reports were either generated from the screening visit (Monogram genotypic and phenotypic assays, n=45 of 72) or from historical reports supplied by the investigators (various assays, n=27 of 72). For a subset of subjects, both historical reports and screening reports were used to evaluate the baseline resistance (n=15).
L2511: Based on the phenotypic resistance data provided, 78% (28/36) of subjects in Cohort 1 (79% in 1A and 75% in 1B) had greater than three-class resistance (Table 52) with 51% (18/35) showing resistance to the INSTI DTG and 50% (16/32) showing resistance to the PI DRV. Additionally, 84% (27/32) of the subjects in Cohort 1 had C-X-C motif chemokine receptor (CXCR)-4 tropism impacting maraviroc efficacy. Fewer subjects showed resistance to the gp120-directed attachment inhibitor fostemsavir, the CD4+-directed post-attachment inhibitor ibalizumab, or the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide (Table 52).
L2512: The presence of resistance substitutions to the four main ARV drug classes was consistent with the high level of resistance observed from phenotypic data. No subject harbored lenacapavir-associated resistance substitutions at study entry.

The three subjects who did not meet the primary endpoint were also virologic failures at Week 26. In Cohort 1B, where subjects received placebo

L2529: Of the 11 virologic failures, 3 did not have postbaseline resistance data and 4 had no genotypic or phenotypic evidence of LEN resistance emergence. The other four VFs (one from the LEN functional monotherapy arm [Subject (b) (6)] and three from the placebo functional monotherapy arm [Subjects (b) (6)]) had evidence of genotypic LEN resistance emergence in capsid (Table 54). All four virologic failure isolates had emergent capsid substitution M66I, which was selected by LEN in cell culture selection experiments and conferred &gt;2757-fold reductions in LEN susceptibility. Other capsid substitutions that emerged with M66I included K70N/R/S, N74D, A78S, A105T and conferred 46- to &gt;1428-fold reduced susceptibility in the three isolates that had postbaseline phenotypic data (Table 54). We note that S41T in combination with other polymorphisms (S41T+Q50A/S+T107S, S41T+T54M, S41T+H87Q) was associated with virologic failure and emergence of CA resistance substitutions (Subjects (b) (6)) (Table 55) (see Section III.19).

L2542: ## Next-Generation Sequencing Analysis
L2543: An independent assessment was performed by Dr. Eric Donaldson, clinical virology reviewer, using the next-generation sequencing data derived from subjects in clinical Study 4625 who were determined to be treatment failures (Section III.19). The independent analysis compared the capsid gene changes from baseline and postbaseline samples for each virologic failure subject (Table 55). This independent assessment confirmed the emergent substitutions shown in Table 55. Based on the next-generation sequencing analysis, the A78S substitution appears to be polymorphic, because it is present at baseline and later timepoints in several subjects.
L2544: ## Resistance to Drugs in Optimized Background Regimen
L2545: Of the subjects who had postbaseline OBR resistance data (two in the LEN arm and five in the placebo arm), none had evidence of resistance emergence to the drugs in the OBR (Table 56). However, three virologic failure subjects (one in the LEN arm [Subject (b) (6)] and two in placebo arm [Subjects (b) (6)]) had no active drugs in their OBR based on baseline and postbaseline genotypic and phenotypic data. We note that two of these subjects (Subjects (b) (6)) also had emergent LEN resistance.
L2546: Most of the virologic failures had BIC or DTG (82%; 9/11) or DRV (63%; 7/11) as a component of their OBR with 45% (5/11) using DRV plus BIC or DTG (Table 56). In addition, ibalizumab and maraviroc were each used in two different virologic failures and one virologic failure had both ibalizumab and maraviroc in their OBR. Three of the virologic failures had resistance to
L2547: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2548: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2549: BIC, DTG and/or DRV with no active drugs in their OBR. However, the other eight had susceptibility to their OBR containing BIC, DTG, or DRV. Of note, five of these eight virologic failures with susceptible OBR drugs had HIV-1 RNA &lt;400 copies/mL at Week 4 (n=4) or Week 26 (n=1). Of the other three virologic failures with active OBR who had HIV-1 RNA &gt;400 copies/mL at Week 4 (n=2) or Week 26 (n=1), two had emergent LEN resistance.

L2554: ## **Effect of Optimized Background Regimen on Efficacy**
L2555: Given that OBR was added with LEN at the end of the FMP, the ARVs in the OBR were critical to the durability of the LEN-containing regimen. As shown in Table 57, the INSTIs BIC and DTG were used in the OBR of 69% (25/36) of the subjects and the PI DRV was used in the OBR of 58% (21/36) of the subjects with 36% (13/36) of the subjects having both DRV plus BIC or DTG as components of their OBR. Only 8% (3/36) of subjects in Cohort 1 did not have DTG, BIC, or DRV as a component of their OBR. Additionally, 28% (10/36) were taking IBL, 8% (3/36) were taking FTR, and 3% (3/36) were taking ENF, as a component of their OBR.
L2556: The effect of these anchor drugs as components of the OBR on efficacy at Week 26 was assessed. Sixty-four percent (16/25) of subjects with DTG or BIC, 67% (14/21) of subjects with DRV, and 62% (8/13) of subjects with DRV+DTG or BIC in the OBR had HIV-1 RNA &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 26 (Table 57). Only three subjects did not have BIC, DTG or DRV as components in their OBR and all three had &lt;50 copies/mL at Week 26. One of these subjects (Subject [b] (6)) had a baseline viral load of only 274 copies/mL, which indicates they were not failing on their background regimen. The other two subjects were resistant to BIC, DTG and ibalizumab, but one was taking fostemsavir (Subject [b] (6)) and the other was taking maraviroc (Subject [b] (6)). Longer term data from all subjects after Week 26 is required to determine the durability of LEN as a component of a regimen with other ARVs.

L2564: ## Cross-Resistance
L2565: Lenacapavir demonstrated antiviral activity in cell culture against a broad spectrum of HIV-1 site-directed mutants and patient-derived HIV-1 isolates with resistance to the four main classes of antiretroviral agents (INSTIs, NNRTIs, NRTIs, and PIs; n=58), and to viruses resistant to fostemsavir (gp120-directed attachment inhibitor), ibalizumab (CD4-directed postattachment inhibitor), maraviroc (C-C chemokine receptor [CCR5] coreceptor inhibitor), and enfuvirtide (gp41 fusion inhibitor) (n=42) (Section III.18). In addition, the antiviral activity of LEN in patient isolates was unaffected by the presence of naturally occurring Gag polymorphisms at gag cleavage sites with or without PI resistance.
L2566: PIs (atazanavir, darunavir, nelfinavir, and saquinavir) showed wildtype antiviral activity against LEN site-directed mutants with capsid substitutions Q67H or Y, Q67H+N74D, Q67H+N74S, and Q67H+T107N, N74D, and T107N indicating a lack of cross-resistance with PIs.
L2567: ## Conclusion
L2568: HIV-1 variants with reduced susceptibility to lenacapavir have been selected in cell culture. Resistance selections with lenacapavir identified seven substitutions in capsid: L56I, M66I, Q67H, K70N, N74D/S, and T107N singly or in dual combination. Phenotypic susceptibility to lenacapavir was reduced 4- to &gt;3,226-fold, relative to wild-type virus.
L2569: In the randomized Cohort 1 of CAPELLA, 31% (11/36; six in LEN Cohort 1A and five in placebo Cohort 1B) of heavily treatment-experienced subjects were virologic failures at Week 26 (confirmed HIV-1 RNA \ge50 copies/mL). Lenacapavir resistance-associated capsid substitutions were found in 36% (n=4) of the 11 virologic failure subjects with the M66I CA substitution emerging in all 4 virologic failures, alone or in combination with other lenacapavir resistance-associated capsid substitutions including Q67Q/H, K70K/N/R/S, N74D, and A105T. These treatment-emergent capsid resistance substitutions were confirmed by FDA independent analyses. The virologic failure isolates with emergent capsid resistance-associated substitutions had reduced lenacapavir susceptibility ranging from 46- to &gt;1428-fold. There were no treatment-emergent resistance substitutions to components of the optimized background regimen in the
L2570: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2571: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2572: virologic failures, but based on genotypic and phenotypic data, three virologic failures had no active drugs in their OBR.
L2573: - LEN resistance emerges readily in virologic failures and thus it is important to use LEN as a component of a complete active ARV regimen.
- LEN resistance substitutions do not confer cross-resistance to other ARVs.
- Longer term data from all subjects after Week 26 is required to determine durability of LEN and the other ARVs in the OBR.
L2574: ## 7.7.2. Injection Site Reactions
L2575: ## Issue
L2576: Injection site reactions were identified as the most common adverse drug reaction among subjects who received subcutaneous injections of lenacapavir; however, long-term experience of subjects after multiple injections was limited in Studies 4625 and 4334.
L2577: ## Background
L2578: Other prior experience with long-acting subcutaneously injectable antiretrovirals that have a similar dosing regimen includes Cabenuva (cabotegravir and rilpivirine). Injection site reactions were the most common adverse reactions reported with Cabenuva and were described usually (79%) as localized pain or discomfort (Cabenuva 2021). Fuzeon (enfuvirtide) is another injectable antiretroviral drug with 98% of subjects experiencing at least one injection site reaction (described as pain, discomfort, erythema, nodules and cysts, and ecchymosis) (Fuzeon 2019); however, this product is indicated to be administered twice daily.
L2579: Injection site nodules have been reported with a number of other drug classes, including glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists used for treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes. General injection-site reactions (e.g., erythema, pain, or rash) have been reported with all of the commercially available GLP-1 receptor agonists (i.e., exenatide, lixisenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide (Hearn and Sherman 2021). Injection site nodules have rarely been described with other long-acting or extended-release drug products, such as exenatide. Although the mechanism for development of such nodules is not entirely clear, available histopathology data reveal the presence of eosinophils and granuloma at these sites, and therefore, hypersensitivity to the formulation may be one plausible mechanism (Jones et al. 2015). Surgical excision or some other medical intervention, such as serial intralesional corticosteroid injections, may be required for treatment of persistent lesions.
L2580: Lenacapavir is a capsid inhibitor with not only a new mechanism of action, but also unique, albeit not fully understood, physical properties when injected that provide its sustained exposure.
L2581: ## Assessment
L2582: Injection site reactions were the most common adverse reaction reported with LEN SC injection. Preferred terms related to injection site in Studies 4625 or 4334 were further explored in the following table (Table 58). Injection site swelling, erythema, pain, nodule, and induration were the specific MedDRA preferred terms that were most frequently (&gt;10%) reported. None of the ISRs were considered serious.
L2583: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2584: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2585: In Study 4625, 61.1% of subjects reported any ISR (54.2% considered related to study drug), and most ISRs were Grade 1 or 2 severity. Two subjects (2.8%) reported Grade 3 ISRs (Subjects
L2586: and ) that were considered by the investigator to be related to LEN. Subject had “bilateral swelling at injection site max diameter cm 10” reported on Day 16 and ending on Day 19. Subject experienced “pain at injection site (1st)” on Day 16 and ending on Day 19.
L2587: In Study 4334, 43.8% of subjects who received SC LEN reported any ISR (39.0% considered related to study drug). Subject experienced injection site induration, which was considered Grade 1 in severity, on Day 15 (same day as the first SC injection). The subject discontinued treatment due to the ISR on Day 211. L2644: No biopsies or histopathologic examinations were obtained from any clinical study subjects experiencing injection site nodules or indurations; however, nonclinical studies of rats (TX-200-2014), rabbits (TX-200-2033) and dogs (TX-200-2047) demonstrated “granulomatous inflammation” (please see Section III.13.2.3 for additional discussion). “Inflammation and foreign body response” to the LEN SC depot was considered an expected host response similar to observations with SC and intramuscular implantation of bioactive material, including those for HIV treatment. Of note, however, these nonclinical studies were not likely to have used the same drug products as presented in borosilicate glass vials that were used in the clinical studies.

L2654: A consultation request was submitted to the Division of Dermatology and Dentistry in the Office of New Drugs that requested any recommendations for additional clinical safety information to be submitted regarding these reactions and recommendations for communication of injection site reactions in labeling. The Division of Dermatology and Dentistry recommended that in ongoing trials, where possible, injection site nodules be followed to resolution or stabilization. Human histopathology should be obtained to rule out the presence of findings such as necrosis, hypersensitivity, granulomas, foreign bodies, and fibrous tissue. In addition, the Division of Dermatology and Dentistry agreed with the expanded characterization of injection site reactions in Section 6 (Adverse Reactions) of the label, and that elevation to Section 5 (Warnings and Precautions) was not necessary at this time given there were no reports to date of AEs that were considered serious or life-threatening.
L2655: As discussed in further detail in the Integrated Quality Review, the LEN injectable drug substance has a high pH (&gt;9) and no intrinsic release controls. Additionally, the proposed vial containers (borosilicate), which were also used in clinical trials, demonstrated incompatibility with the drug product, degradation of the vial surface, and glass particles found in the solution.
L2656: ## Conclusion
L2657: Injection site reactions can be characterized as having a short-term phase lasting a few days (e.g., pain, swelling, and erythema) or a long-term phase (e.g., indurations and nodules), some of which were still resolving over a period of weeks to months. Indurations and nodules were generally described as palpable with an elongated shape (up to 1 to 4 cm), not visible, not painful, and not associated with any erythema. Nodules were more visible in subjects who were
L2658: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2659: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2660: leaner with little fat tissue in the abdomen. Several subjects in Study 4625 had indurations or nodules that had not fully resolved at the time of the last safety update. Due to the lack of understanding of the histopathology at the injection sites in patients who experienced longer times to resolution of indurations and nodules, and the relationship with the unique properties of the drug product solution, it is unclear whether these subjects may have experienced permanent tissue damage. Additionally, given the concern about the incompatibility of the drug substance with borosilicate glass and resulting delamination of the vial containers (please refer to the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review), contribution of glass particulate contamination cannot be ruled out.
L2661: During the initial exchange of updates to the draft labeling for LEN, the Division of Antivirals (DAV) requested additional description of injection site reactions similar to the presentation in the Cabenuva label, with additional description of nodules and induration and details of time to resolution provided as a separate subsection entitled “Injection-Associated Adverse Reactions” in Section 6 (Adverse Reactions) of the proposed label.
L2662: From a clinical safety perspective, additional information is needed to understand the contributing factors of injection site reactions with LEN, particularly for subjects who have prolonged resolution with nodules and indurations. Where clinically indicated, at the discretion of an independent dermatologist, DAV requested that the Applicant obtain human histopathology (e.g., punch biopsy), and specimens should be examined by an independent dermatopathologist.
L2663: From a product quality perspective, several deficiencies, including [REDACTED] (b) (4), and glass particle contamination, were the basis for the recommendation of nonapproval. Additional concerns included [REDACTED] (b) (4) and the atypical mechanism of release following injection of the drug product. Although the Applicant has withdrawn the proposal for the borosilicate glass vial presentation, the proposal for aluminosilicate glass vials lacked a comprehensive and validated study to support this alternative presentation through the drug product expiry period. Of note, on 20 December, 2021, a supporting investigational new drug (IND) application for these NDAs (IND 136260), as well as IND [REDACTED] (b) (4) (with ongoing clinical studies for pre-exposure prophylaxis of HIV-1), were placed on Full Clinical Hold due to the lack of information needed to assess risks of lenacapavir injection and the extent to which glass particulate contamination, including subvisible particles, may be associated with injection site nodules, indurations, or other clinical effects.
L2664: ## 7.7.3. Background Regimens Containing Boosted Protease Inhibitors
L2665: ## Issue
L2666: The risk of supratherapeutic LEN exposures when LEN is combined with a background regimen containing boosted protease inhibitors was not prospectively assessed in Study 4625.
L2667: ## Background
L2668: Most regimens containing boosted protease inhibitors (BPIs) are typically used as second-line options, or when INSTIs are not available. The HTE patient population by definition has limited alternative options to construct a complete regimen; therefore, BPIs may be an important component of an optimized background regimen.
L2669: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2670: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2671: Based on in vitro data, LEN was found to be a substrate of cytochrome P450 (CYP)3A and uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase (UGT)1A1 enzymes and p-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporters. In the dedicated DDI study, Study GS-US-200-4333 (Study 4333), an approximate two-fold increase in LEN exposures was observed with mixed CYP3A/P-gp inhibition associated with cobicistat, and an approximate four- to six-fold increase LEN exposure was observed with mixed CYP3A/P-gp/UGT) inhibition associated with atazanavir/cobicistat; therefore, given the potential for clinically significant drug-drug interactions with LEN due to the combined strong inhibition of CYP3A, P-gp, and UGT1A1 together, Study 4625 did not allow concomitant use of atazanavir (ATV, an inhibitor of CYP3A and UGT1A1) when boosted with either cobicistat (COBI) or ritonavir (RTV). The results from Study 4333 also showed an 84% decrease in LEN AUC when LEN was coadministered with rifampin, a strong CYP3A inducer; and 56% decrease in LEN AUC when LEN was coadministered with efavirenz, a moderate CYP3A inducer. CYP3A inducers (e.g., rifampin, efavirenz, tipranavir) were disallowed in Study 4625. Background regimens with other BPIs were allowed. Please refer to Section 8.2.2 for additional discussion of drug interactions.
L2672: ## Assessment
L2673: ## Clinical Safety Experience With Supratherapeutic Doses of LEN
L2674: Clinical safety experience was reviewed from two clinical studies where doses of LEN were predicted to provide higher exposures than what was studied in Study 4625. Study 4332 was a phase 1 QT study, which evaluated a 600 mg dose of LEN (2×300 mg tablets) taken orally twice-daily for 8 days to achieve supratherapeutic exposure. Study 5709 was a phase 1 PK study, and Cohort 3 evaluated a 600 mg dose of LEN (2×300 mg tablets) taken orally twice daily for 10 days. Although direct comparisons between these studies are limited (because they are in different patient populations: healthy volunteers versus treatment-naïve and heavily treatment-experienced subjects), the clinical safety experience from this analysis may be informative regarding potential exposure-related effects attributable to LEN.

L2706: ## Conclusion
L2707: Analysis of safety experience with LEN and regimens containing BPIs revealed adverse event and laboratory profiles previously anticipated with BPIs. With the exception of regimens containing ATV/COBI or ATV/RTV, no additional significant safety concerns were revealed with dose exploration studies and similar supratherapeutic exposures of LEN (up to approximately two-fold higher) that would be expected when combined with BPIs.
L2708: Labeling for LEN should include the recommendation against concomitant administration with ATV/COBI or ATV/RTV, but no clinically significant drug interactions have been observed with DRV/COBI.
L2709: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L2710: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L2711: ## 8.1.1. Renal Impairment
L2712: Results from Study 4329 (mass balance study) showed that renal excretion is a minor excretion pathway of LEN, representing 0.237% of total dose. However, severe renal impairment (RI) may affect uptake and efflux transporters and metabolic enzymes in the liver and gastrointestinal tract. Increases in exposure in subjects with severe RI for drugs that are not renally excreted may be due to the effects of uremic toxin on either intestinal or hepatic cell transporters, metabolizing enzymes, or both. This phenomenon has been observed for other drugs, such as raloxifene and revefenacin, which show significantly higher exposures in subjects with severe RI despite not being primarily eliminated renally.
L2713: In the RI Study 4330, subjects with severe RI (estimated creatinine clearance \ge15 mL/min) were administered 300 mg single oral dose of LEN. LEN geometric least-squares mean (GLSM) AUC
L2714: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2715: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2716: and C_{max} were 162% and 84% higher, respectively, in subjects with severe renal impairment compared to subjects with normal renal function. As LEN has linear PK, these results can be extrapolated to the recommended dosing regimen. Based on cross-study PK comparisons, even larger exposure increases were observed without safety concerns in other studies. As shown in Table 65, in Studies 4332 and 5709, the magnitude of increase in LEN C_{max} and AUC following 600 mg BID relative to the therapeutic exposure was higher compared with the magnitude of increase in LEN C_{max} and AUC in Study 4330. Therefore, the impact of RI on LEN PK is not considered clinically significant.

L2722: The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposed labeling that no dose adjustment of LEN is required in patients with mild, moderate, or severe RI, and that LEN has not been studied in patients with end-stage renal disease (estimated creatinine clearance &lt;15 mL/min) (Section III.13.2).
L2723: ## 8.1.2. Hepatic Impairment
L2724: In vitro studies indicated that LEN is a substrate of enzymes CYP3A5 and UGT1A1. In addition, metabolism of LEN was also observed in the clinical Study 4329. Therefore, hepatic impairment (HI) is expected to have an impact on LEN PK.
L2725: In HI Study 4331, subjects with moderate HI (Child-Pugh Class B) were administered a 300 mg single oral dose of LEN. GLSM LEN AUC and C_{max} were 47% and 161% higher, respectively, in subjects with moderate HI compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. As shown in Table 65, in Studies 4332 and 5709, the magnitude of increase in GLSM mean C_{max} and AUC following 600 mg BID relative to the therapeutic exposure was higher compared with the magnitude of increase in C_{max} and AUC in Studies 4331. Therefore, the impact of moderate HI on LEN PK is not considered clinically significant.
L2726: The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposed labeling that no dose adjustment of LEN is required in patients with mild or moderate HI (Child-Pugh Class A or B), and that LEN has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) (Section III.13.2).
L2727: ## 8.1.3. Other Intrinsic Factors
L2728: Population PK analyses indicate that sex, race, age (18 to 78 years), and body weight do not have a clinically significant effect on LEN PK. No subjects &gt;78 years old were enrolled in the clinical studies (see Section III.14.3).
L2729: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2730: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2731: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L2732: ## 8.2.1. Food Effect
L2733: Study GS-US-200-4071 evaluated the impact of a standard light meal (400 kcal and 25% fat) and the impact of a high-fat meal (1000 kcal and 50% fat) on LEN PK. Two LEN solution-in-capsule formulations and the to-be-marketed oral tablet formulation were used in the study.
L2734: Regardless of the calorie and fat content of the meal, food had no significant effect on plasma LEN PK. LEN was given without regard to food in the Phase 3 trials CAPELLA and CALIBRATE. The review team agrees with the Applicant's proposed labeling that LEN can be administered with or without food (see Section III.14.2).
L2735: ## 8.2.2. Drug-Drug Interactions
L2736: ## Effects of Other Drugs on LEN
L2737: In vitro studies (see Section III.13.1 for details) indicate that LEN is a substrate of CYP3A, P-gp and UGT1A1, but not a substrate of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, breast cancer resistance protein, or organic anion transporter polypeptide (OATP)1B1 and OATP1B3. In vitro studies to evaluate if LEN is a substrate of renal transporters were not conducted because the absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion data suggest that active renal secretion is not expected to be significant.
L2738: Drug-drug interaction Study 4333 (see Section III.14.2 for details) was conducted in healthy volunteers to evaluate the effect of CYP3A, P-gp, and UGT1A1 modulators as well as the effect of an acid-reducing agent on the PK of LEN.

L2746: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2747: ## **Coadministration With Inhibitors of CYP3A, P-gp, and/or UGT1A1**
L2748: Coadministration of drugs that are inhibitors of CYP3A (strong), P-gp, and UGT1A1 together (i.e., atazanavir [ATV]/COBI or ATV/RTV) with LEN during treatment is not recommended. Of note, use of ATV was not allowed in Studies 4625 and 4334. Clinical DDI results confirmed the in vitro findings and showed that an inhibitor of CYP3A (strong), P-gp, and UGT1A1 together (ATV/COBI) increased LEN concentrations to a larger degree than coadministration with an inhibitor of CYP3A (strong) and P-gp (COBI and DRV/COBI) or a strong CYP3A inhibitor alone (voriconazole) (Table 67).
L2749: Coadministration of LEN with a strong inhibitor of CYP3A and P-gp (e.g., DRV/RTV, DRV/COBI) together, a strong CYP3A inhibitor alone, or a P-gp inhibitor alone is not expected to result in a clinically significant effect on LEN concentrations. In Study 4625, 18 (29%) subjects coadministered LEN with COBI, 19 (30.6%) subjects with RTV, and 19 (30.6%) with DRV. In addition, the increase of LEN C_{max} (&lt;3-fold) due to coadministration with a strong inhibitor of CYP3A and P-gp together, a strong CYP3A inhibitor alone, or a P-gp inhibitor alone is much less than the 9-fold higher C_{max} observed following oral LEN 600 mg BID (Studies 5709 and 4332, up to 11 days) versus the C_{max} observed with the regimen studied in the pivotal trial without safety concerns. Safety data from Cohort 3 of Study 4334 (LEN oral 600 mg on day 1 and day 2, and oral 50 mg once daily starting day 3), which provided comparable C_{max} and C_{trough} but about 2-fold higher AUC_{0-6month} as compared to the proposed regimen, also supports coadministration of LEN with a strong inhibitor of CYP3A and P-gp together, a strong CYP3A inhibitor alone, or a P-gp inhibitor alone.
L2750: ## **Coadministration With Inducers of CYP3A**
L2751: Coadministration of strong inducers of CYP3A during treatment with LEN is contraindicated and coadministration of moderate inducers of CYP3A during treatment with LEN is not recommended. Drugs that are strong inducers of CYP3A (e.g., rifampin), or that are moderate inducers of CYP3A (e.g., efavirenz), may significantly decrease plasma concentrations of LEN, which may result in loss of therapeutic effect of LEN and development of resistance. A strong inducer of CYP3A is expected to be an inducer of P-gp and UGT1A1 with lower potency because CYP3A, P-gp, and UGTs are all regulated by the pregnane X receptor. Therefore, other strong inducers of CYP3A are expected to decrease LEN concentrations by a similar magnitude as rifampin. Although exposure-response (E-R) relationship analyses for Study 4625 indicated that there was no clear E-R relationship identified for efficacy or safety (see Section 6.1), strong or moderate CYP3A inducers were not allowed in pivotal trials. In addition, although based on the exploratory E-R relationship analysis (Study 4072), near maximum efficacy is expected in the lowest quartile of C_{trough} (see Section III.25). A decrease in LEN exposures by strong or moderate CYP3A inducers will most likely result in LEN exposures in the range for which the current E-R relationships may not be applicable.
L2752: ## **Coadministration With Acid-Reducing Agents**
L2753: LEN is practically insoluble in aqueous media, gastric fluid, or intestinal fluid and exhibits higher solubility at pH \ge 6. The effect of famotidine LEN exposures was assessed. Administration of a single dose of LEN 2 hours after famotidine did not result in clinically
L2754: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2755: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2756: significant changes in LEN PK (28% increase in mean LEN AUC_{inf}). Accordingly, there are no restrictions for use of LEN with acid-reducing agents.
L2757: ## **Effect of LEN on Other Drugs**
L2758: Considering the results of both in vitro and in vivo DDI studies, LEN is a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A and is an inhibitor of P-gp.
L2759: The DDI potential evaluation was based on FDA Guidance for Industry: *In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies—Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions* (January 2020). In vitro studies indicate that LEN is an inhibitor of both gut and hepatic CYP3A, mainly due to time-dependent or mechanism-based inhibition. Using static mechanistic models, the ratio of LEN AUC (AUC_r) of oral LEN coadministered with a CYP3A inhibitor to oral LEN alone is predicted to be approximately 5-fold, with about 1.7-fold due to gut CYP3A inhibition and 2.9-fold due to hepatic CYP3A inhibition. The predicted AUC_r is about 2.8-fold following coadministration of a CYP3A inhibitor with SC LEN compared to SC LEN alone. In vitro studies also indicate that LEN is not expected to inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 or UGT 1A1. LEN is an inhibitor of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3, but is not likely to inhibit P-gp, breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), OAT1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT)1, OCT2, multidrug and toxin extrusion protein (MATE)1, or MATE2K. In vitro studies indicate LEN is not expected to be an inducer of CYP enzymes.
L2760: As shown in Table 67, DDI Study 4333 showed that LEN is a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A (as observed by coadministration of LEN with midazolam [MDZ] resulting in a 259% increase in mean AUC_{inf}). MDZ administered 1 day after LEN resulted in a similar magnitude of effect on MDZ concentrations, indicating that the effect of LEN on MDZ concentrations is mainly through hepatic CYP3A inhibition.
L2761: Concomitant use of LEN with CYP3A substrates can increase the exposures and risk of adverse reactions of these substrates. Avoid coadministration of LEN with CYP3A substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities.
L2762: Study 4333 also showed that LEN appeared to inhibit P-gp transporter (as observed by coadministration of LEN with TAF resulting in a 32% increase in AUC_{inf}) and BCRP transporter (as observed by coadministration of LEN with rosuvastatin resulting in a 31% increase in AUC_{inf}). Although in vitro data suggested that LEN is a weak inhibitor of OATP1B1, LEN does not inhibit OATP transporters in vivo (based on no significant changes in PIT exposures). Therefore, substrates of BCRP and OATP can be coadministered with LEN while therapeutic monitoring of digoxin (a P-gp substrate) concentrations is recommended when LEN is coadministered with digoxin.

L2771: If LEN is discontinued, residual concentrations of LEN may remain in the systemic circulation of patients for prolonged periods. These concentrations may affect the exposures of other drugs (i.e., sensitive CYP3A substrates) that are initiated within 9 months after the last subcutaneous dose of LEN. Using a static mechanistic model, the Applicant concluded that inhibition of CYP3A is possible only at LEN concentrations above 14.9 ng/mL and LEN concentrations are predicted to decline below this value by approximately 8.3 months after the last LEN SC injection, thereby suggesting a low likelihood of LEN to be a significant perpetrator of DDIs 9 months after the last LEN SC dose.
L2772: ## 8.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
L2773: - The NDAs for lenacapavir trigger PREA as a new active ingredient.
- In their Agreed Amended initial Pediatric Study Plan, the Applicant requested a partial waiver for pediatric HTE patients from birth to &lt;12 years, because studies in this patient population are impossible or highly impracticable.
- There are no nonclinical or clinical safety issues that indicate a concern for continuing the study of LEN specifically in adolescents, but the lack of enrollment in Study 4625 likely reflects the lack of a sufficient number of adolescents to target this patient population (i.e., heavily treatment experienced with multidrug resistance) for further clinical study.
- The next studies anticipated to enroll adolescents are ongoing studies for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
- DAV met with the PeRC on 16 November, 2021. The PeRC agreed with the plan to request partial waiver of pediatric patients from birth to &lt;12 years of age studies because necessary studies are impossible or highly impracticable.
- The PeRC also agreed to grant deferred studies for pediatrics 12 to 18 years of age who weigh at least 35 kg.
- Similar to the approach taken with Rukobia (fostemsavir), DAV proposed considering the following Pediatric Research Equity Act PMR language: "Conduct a clinical study to evaluate week 24 safety of lenacapavir in adolescents from 12 years to less than 18 years of age who weigh at least 35 kg." The PeRC agreed with this plan.
L2774: ## 8.4. Pregnancy and Lactation
L2775: The reproductive and development toxicology studies with lenacapavir are summarized in Section 6.1. In the fertility study, lenacapavir was administered to male and female rats via a single subcutaneous injection of 20 or 100 mg/kg at 4 and 6 weeks prior to pairing to male and female rats, respectively. LEN had no effect on male or female fertility in rats, at doses up to
L2776: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2777: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2778: 100 mg/kg, at exposures 7- and 5-fold (in males and females, respectively) those observed at the RHD.
L2779: No significant toxicological effects on embryo-fetal growth or development were observed in rats when lenacapavir was administered at oral doses up to 30 mg/kg from GD 6 to 17, at exposures 16-fold the RHD.
L2780: Lower body weight gains that correlated with a decrease in food intake was observed in rabbits when lenacapavir was administered intravenously at doses up to 20 mg/kg from GD 7 to 19, at exposures 39-fold the RHD.
L2781: In the PPND toxicity study, lenacapavir was administered to pregnant rats via a single subcutaneous injection on GD 6. Lactation was not measured in the PPND study. There were no maternal toxicities or effects on PPND that occurred up to 300 mg/kg at exposures 5-fold the RHD.
L2782: ## 9. Product Quality
L2783: The Quality Assessment team completed an integrated assessment from the drug substance, drug product, manufacturing, microbiology, biopharmaceutics and environmental disciplines. The team determined that NDA 215794, for oral LEN tablet, was approvable from the product quality perspective; however, NDA 215793, for LEN injection, was found to be deficient from a product quality perspective. One of the proposed commercial vial containers (borosilicate) was not compatible with the drug product solution. Degradation of the vial surface was evident from microscopic imaging, and glass particles were found in the solution. Considering [REDACTED] (b) (4)
L2784: [REDACTED] (b) (4) and concern for glass particle contamination, approval of the proposed alternative aluminosilicate glass vial will require a comprehensive validated study. Further, data supporting the container closure integrity testing remained outstanding despite numerous information requests to the Applicant. The Quality Assessment team also notified the OND review team about the atypical nature of this product, including the lack of intrinsic release controls and the concern about a subcutaneous product with a pH &gt;9. Please refer to the integrated reviews for both NDAs, 215973 and 215974, completed January 12, 2022, for additional details.
L2785: Although each discipline recommended approval for NDA 215794, both NDA 215793 and NDA 215794 will receive a Complete Response action. As stated above, deficiencies were identified in the product quality information for the LEN injection NDA. The approval of the oral LEN NDA is contingent on the approval of the LEN injection NDA; therefore, the LEN injection NDA deficiencies must be adequately addressed before the oral LEN NDA can be approved.

L2799: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L2800: Lenacapavir (LEN), formerly known as GS-6207, is a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-1 capsid inhibitor that is being developed as a solution for subcutaneous injection under investigational new drug (IND) 136260 and as a tablet for oral use under IND 138311. The dosage forms were intended to be used in conjunction for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
L2801: On 30 August, 2017, Gilead Sciences submitted a meeting request under Pre-IND 136260 for LEN, injection. Pre-IND guidance on the nonclinical studies needed to support the alternative injectable formulations of LEN that Gilead planned to use in their clinical trials was provided to Gilead on 25 October, 2017 via a Written Response correspondence.
L2802: IND 136260 was submitted 21 December, 2017 and the Agency deemed it safe-to-proceed on 20 January, 2018. Fast Track Designation was granted on 23 March, 2018 for the treatment of HIV-1 infection on the basis that the submitted information was sufficiently likely to support use of LEN as [REDACTED] (b) (4) parenteral formulation with a new mechanism of action, and therefore, LEN demonstrated the potential to address an unmet medical need.
L2803: On 20 March, 2018, Gilead submitted a new IND 138311 for lenacapavir tablets, for the treatment of HIV-1 infection and the Agency deemed the IND safe to proceed on 19 April, 2018. Fast Track Designation was granted on 19 September, 2018 for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
L2804: On 30 May, 2019, the development program for LEN (IND 136260) for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) patients with multidrug resistant (MDR) virus was granted Breakthrough Therapy Designation. The decision was based upon the need for an antiretroviral agent with a new mechanism of action and no overlapping resistance with any approved agent that could potentially meet the high unmet medical need in HTE patients with limited treatment options. A Type B, Initial Breakthrough Therapy meeting was held on 6 August, 2019 during which the phase 2/3 development program and proposed registration plan to support an indication for treatment of HIV-1 infection in HTE patients with MDR HIV-1 was discussed. The Agency generally agreed with the proposed phase 2/3 Study 4625 to support the submission of a new drug application (NDA). The clinical trial would investigate the use of a 14-day lenacapavir oral lead-in dosing, followed by LEN, subcutaneous injections on Day 15 and every 6 months.
L2805: On 19 March, 2020, a rat carcinogenicity Special Protocol Assessment was submitted to IND 136260; and on 26 June, 2020, a mouse carcinogenicity Special Protocol Assessment was submitted. The Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee agreed with the Special Protocol Assessments, but they provided recommendations on the design of the studies.
L2806: An Agreed initial Pediatric Study Plan was issued by the Agency on 27 May, 2020. The agreed initial Pediatric Study Plan covered [REDACTED] (b) (4) HTE adolescents \ge 35 kg with MDR HIV would be enrolled in Study 4625. However, difficulties in enrollment of this population were anticipated, [REDACTED] (b) (4)
L2807: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2808: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2809: (b) (4). A plan to seek a waiver for HTE children &lt;12 years of age was included.
L2810: On September 6, 2020, Meeting Preliminary Comments were issued for a Type C Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) meeting requested to discuss the proposed excess volume for LEN 300 mg/mL and the design validation strategy for the lenacapavir vial kit. The meeting was canceled by the firm following receipt of preliminary comments.
L2811: On January 13, 2021, the Agency issued Preliminary Comments for a Type B Pre-NDA meeting requested under INDs 136260 and 138311, the purpose of which was to discuss the strategy for submission of NDAs for lenacapavir, key aspects related to content and format of the NDAs, to obtain feedback on the proposed content of the NDA Safety Update, and to seek feedback and agreement on the revisions to the dosing regimen used in the Phase 3 clinical trial. In the Preliminary Comments, the Agency agreed that clinical studies 4625 (primary registrational study in intended population), 4334 (supportive efficacy and safety study), and 4538 and 5709 (supportive safety studies) were appropriate to submit in the initial NDAs. Regarding the proposal to submit a simplified regimen that would include oral loading dose on Day 1 and Day 2 with the injection administered on Day 1, the Agency stated that the acceptability of the dosing regimen is contingent upon availability of adequate pharmacokinetic (PK), safety and efficacy data and would be a review issue. The Agency further agreed that having a single U.S. Prescribing Information for both injection and tablet dosage forms is appropriate. Regarding a transgenic mouse study draft report and SEND databases, the Agency requested that these be submitted either with the NDA or after approval. Following receipt of the Preliminary Comments the meeting was canceled.
L2812: On 11 February, 2021, the Agency provided the firm with Human Factors Validation Study Protocol Advice containing recommended protocol revisions in response to a Human Factors Validation Protocol submitted 11 December, 2020, regarding a co-package kit containing injection vials, syringes, vial access devices, and injection needles.
L2813: On 31 March, 2021, a Proprietary Name Request Unacceptable letter was issued by the Agency, detailing that the proposed proprietary name, SUNLENCA, could result in medication errors due to confusion with another product currently under review. Ultimate acceptability of the proposed name would be dependent upon which underlying application is approved first.
L2814: On 25 May, 2021, a Final Written Response was issued by the Agency in response to a type B, meeting, the purpose of which was to discuss phase 2/3 clinical data from Studies 4625 and 4334 in advance of NDA filing. The Agency agreed that the preliminary data from these studies were appropriate to support the firm's proposed initial NDAs.

Respiratory system function via SC injection (PC-200-2014)
Wister Han rats, males
0, 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg
Single dose	LEN administration resulted in a 5% increase in tidal volume at 30 mg/kg and a 11% increase in the 100 mg/kg compared to controls that lasted up to 72 hours postdose. There was no effect on respiration rate at 10 or 30 mg/kg compared to controls but there was a 6% decrease at 100 mg/kg. Although GS-6207 related differences in mean tidal volume and respiration rate were noted in the high dose groups, these differences were not statistically significant. The NOAEL for respiration is 30 mg/kg based on the GS-6207 related decrease in respiration rate at 100 mg/kg.
L2849: Source: Reviewer.
L2850: Abbreviations: LEN, lenacapavir; NOAEL, no observable adverse effect level; SC, subcutaneous
L2851: ## 13.2.2. Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion/PK
L2852: ## Absorption
L2853: ## In Vitro
L2854: - The bidirectional permeability of GS-6207 was investigated using monolayers of the human colon carcinoma cell line (Caco-2). Refer to Section 14.1.1 for more information.
L2855: ## In Vivo
L2856: Oral single dose absorption studies were conducted in Sprague Dawley rats (5 mg/kg), Beagle dogs (4 mg/kg), and Cynomolgus and Rhesus monkeys (4 mg/kg) following oral administration of GS-6207.
L2857: - The time to maximum concentration (T_{max}) ranged from 8.7 to 18.7 across species.
- An exposure (area under the concentration-time curve [AUC_{INF}]) was not determined for Cynomolgus monkeys. However the exposure in Rhesus monkeys was 1133nM\cdoth. In rats and dogs, the exposure was 25,200 and 16,533nM\cdoth, respectively. In addition, the C_{max} was 336, 471, 17.7, and 29.4nM in rats, dogs, Cynomolgus and Rhesus monkeys, respectively.

The oral routes in these studies were administered formulations for liquid capsules, liquid-filled capsules, and tablets. The subcutaneous routes of administration were different formulations

L2912: The PK profile of GS-6207 following intravenous (IV) or oral administration was evaluated in portal vein cannulated male Cynomolgus monkeys and Beagle dogs with or without the cytochrome P450 (CYP) inhibitor, aminobenzotriazole, to understand the role of CYP metabolism of GS-6207. The results from these studies indicated that pretreating dogs and monkeys with aminobenzotriazole did not change GS-6207 oral exposure in dogs or monkeys, suggesting role of intestinal metabolism of GS-6207.
L2913: ## Distribution
L2914: ## In Vitro
L2915: - Protein binding was evaluated in plasma from CD-1 mice. GS-6207 was 99.8% protein-bound (unbound fraction was 0.18%) at a concentration of 2\muM.
- The distribution between the cellular and soluble fractions of blood was evaluated in whole blood from Sprague Dawley rats, Beagle dogs, Cynomolgus and Rhesus monkeys, and humans. At an initial concentration of 0.5\muM, GS-6207 was nearly excluded from the blood cellular fraction with the blood:plasma concentration ratios in animals being 0.59 to 0.67 and 0.64 in human.
- Protein binding was evaluated in plasma from Sprague Dawley rats, Beagle dogs, Cynomolgus and Rhesus monkeys, and humans. GS-6207 was \ge98% protein-bound in all animals and human (unbound fraction was 0.13, 0.83, 1.11, 1.45, and 1.46% in rat, dogs, Cynomolgus monkey, Rhesus monkey, and human, respectively) at 10mM.
L2916: ## In Vivo
L2917: - The absorption, tissue distribution and excretion of [14C]GS-6207 was evaluated following a single IV (3 mg/kg-IV; n=3 to 26) dose of GS-6207 in both intact and bile duct-cannulated nonpigmented male Wister Hanover and intact pigmented Long Evans rats. The highest concentration was in the liver in both species of rats up to 1008 hours (42 days) followed by kidney cortex, kidneys, pancreas, kidney medulla, brown fat, and thyroid. GS-6207 was cleared from all organs by 672 hours and in the liver by 1344 hours (56 days).
L2918: ## Metabolism
L2919: ## In Vitro
L2920: - The metabolic profile of GS-6207 was evaluated in Wistar Han rat, Beagle dog, cynomolgus and Rhesus monkey, and human microsomes and hepatocytes in vitro.In all animal species and human microsomes, 90 to 94% of radioactivity detected was from unchanged [14C]GS-6207. In microsomes, [14C]GS-6207 metabolism occurred via oxidation, reduction, defluorination, and glutathione conjugation.
L2921: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2922: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2923: - Metabolism in hepatocytes occurred via glutathione conjugation, pentose conjugation, and glucuronidation. Oxidative metabolites were not detected.
- There were no unique human metabolites.
L2924: ## In Vivo
L2925: - The metabolism of [^{14}\text{C}]GS-6207 was evaluated in plasma, urine, bile, and feces from intact and bile duct-cannulated Sprague Dawley rats and Beagle dogs.
- The proposed metabolic pathways in the rat, dog and human are presented in Figure 33.

L2929: ## Excretion
L2930: - The excretion of GS-6207 was evaluated following a single 30-minute IV infusion (1 mg/kg; n=3) in male bile-duct cannulated male Sprague Dawley rats. The results indicate that GS-6207 is excreted into the intestines by the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporter and excreted in rat feces.
- The absorption and excretion of [^{14}\text{C}]GS-6207 was evaluated following a single 1 mg/kg IV dose in intact and bile-duct cannulated Beagle Dogs and a 2 mg/kg oral dose in intact dogs. The results indicated that GS-6207 was primarily excreted in the feces.
L2931: ## 13.2.3. General Toxicology
L2932: ## 13.2.3.1. Single-Dose Toxicology/Toxicokinetics
L2933: A single dose subcutaneous (SC) dose range-finding toxicology study was conducted to determine the doses to use in future carcinogenic studies to characterize the potential long-term carcinogenic effects of GS-6207. The study was evaluated in rasH2 Transgenic mice (0, 30, 99, or 300 mg/kg) with a 13-week recovery period.
L2934: - The skin at the injection site and the liver appeared to be the targeted organs of toxicity.
- The liver weight was increased at 99 and 300 mg/kg and was correlated with slight centrilobular hepatocyte vacuolation, an increased incidence of minimal hepatocyte degeneration/necrosis, and an increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 300 mg/kg.
- Injection site reactions were observed in various animals at each dose in females and at 300 mg/kg in males; a palpable mass was detected at 300 mg/kg.
- Hematology findings (increases in white blood cells, lymphocytes, and eosinophils in males and leukocytes) were detected sporadically in males and females at each dose.
- The no observable adverse effect level (NOAEL) was 300 mg/kg in males and 99 mg/kg in females due to clinical observations and gross and histopathology findings at the injection site and histopathology findings in the liver at 300 mg/kg.
L2935: A single dose intravenous toxicology study to characterize potential systemic effects of GS-6207 was evaluated via a 30-minute IV infusion to Wister Han rats (0, 3, 10, or 30 mg/kg) with a 15-day recovery period.
L2936: - Several rats dosed with GS-6207 or control had to be euthanized early because of declining health due to the infusion procedure.
- Clinical observations were noted in various rats at each dose (red urine, ataxia, hypoactivity, vocalization, squinting and/or pale eyes, audible/labored/irregular breathing, and sternal recumbence).
- Decrease in body weight gain was observed in male rats at 30 mg/kg.
- Increases in neutrophil counts, ALT, creatine kinase (CK), positive blood urine, and liver weights were observed at 10 and/or 30 mg/kg.
- Hemorrhage of valve leaflets, mixed cell inflammation, and myocardial degeneration/necrosis was found in dosed and control animals.
- Infusion site reactions (cellular inflammation, thrombus, congestion/hemorrhage, edema, and fibrosis) were noted at all doses.
L2937: To characterize potential systemic effects, GS-6207 was evaluated via a single 30-minute IV infusion to Beagle dogs (0, 3, 10, or 30 mg/kg) with a 15-day recovery period.
L2938: - Clinical observations (skin lesions, intermittent tremors, vocalization, and/or discharge of the left eye and front foot) were observed at all doses and in controls. These observations were unlikely related to GS-6207 and IV dosing procedure because they were noted in controls.
- A GS-6207-related decrease in body weight gain was observed in all dogs at doses \ge 3 mg/kg that only correlated with a decrease in food consumption in female dogs. The decrease in weight in dogs lasted throughout recovery.
L2939: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L2940: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L2941: - Hematology findings (red blood cell count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit), prothrombin time or activated partial thromboplastin time prolongation, and an increase in hepatic enzymes were noted at 30 mg/kg.
- Histopathology findings in the liver included hepatocyte degeneration (at \ge 3 mg/kg in males and \ge 10 mg/kg in females), individual necrosis (30 mg/kg in two males and at 10 mg/kg in one female), mixed cell infiltrate (at \ge 10 mg/kg in males and females), and hemorrhage (one male and three females and 30 mg/kg and one female at \ge 3 mg/kg). The GS-6207-related liver findings at Day 2 were not detected at Day 15.

L2947: ## A 4-Week Oral Gavage Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study of GS-6207 in Wister Han Rats (TX-200-2011)
L2948: ## **Key Study Findings**
L2949: - No target organ of toxicity was identified.
- Longer clotting time (activated partial thromboplastin time) in males was noted at all doses and an increase in cholesterol was noted in females at all doses. These findings were not considered adverse and the significance of these findings is unclear as there was no other data to correlate with the findings.
- The NOAEL was 30 mg/kg.The Day 28 AUC0-24hr (male and female combined) was 34,500 ng•h/mL.
- The exposure margin was 26× based on predicted human exposures based on the recommended human dose (RHD).

Mortality	Animals were examined twice daily for mortality, abnormalities, and signs of pain or distress. One control male was found dead on day 21 soon after shaving. One female dosed with 10 mg/kg was found dead on day 15 (TK assigned animal). The death of the male was procedure related. Since there were no changes in weight or abnormal clinical findings in the female animal, the death of this animal is unknown, but it is not likely related to GS-6207 since there were no deaths at higher doses.
Clinical signs	Clinical signs were monitored at least once daily. No treatment-related findings.
Body weights	Body weights were recorded weekly. The week following the first dose there was a statistically significant decrease in body weight gain by 14 and 17% in males at 10 and \ge 30 mg/kg/dose, respectively. Additional in males, the week following the third dose, there was a statistically significant decrease in body weight gain by 16% at 100 mg/kg. In females, the week following the first dose there was a statistically significant decrease in body weight gain by 21 and 17% at 30 and 100 mg/kg/dose, respectively.
Feed consumption	Food intake was measured weekly. No treatment-related findings.
Ophthalmoscopy	Ophthalmic exams were conducted on the control and dosed groups prior to treatment and at week 12. No treatment-related findings.

On Day 57, there was a 29.7 and 32.8% increase in cholesterol in males and females, respectively, at 100 mg/kg/dose. On Day 85 (end of recovery period; 6 weeks after the last dose) the cholesterol remained increased in males only (by 18%) at 100 mg/kg/dose.
Urinalysis	Urine was collected during the overnight period prior to terminal sacrifice 1 (Day 57) and terminal sacrifice 2 (Day 85). No treatment-related findings.
Gross pathology	Thickening of the skin was observed at the SC injection sites at all doses in males; at doses \ge 30 mg/kg/dose in females at the end of dosing period and in all dosed groups at the end of the recovery period.
Organ weights	At the end of the dosing period there was an 8 and 11% increase in relative (to body and brain weights, respectively) liver weight at 100 mg/kg/dose in males. In females, there was a 7.6 and 11% increase in relative (to body and brain weights, respectively) liver weight at 100 mg/kg/dose. Although this increase appears to be test-article related there were no increases in hepatic enzymes or effects on liver histopathology to correlate with these effects. There were no effects on liver weights at the end of the recovery period.

Special evaluation:

L3002: ## A Single- and Two-Dose Subcutaneous Injection Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study With Three Formulations of GS-6207 in Wister Han Rats With a 13-Week Observation Period After Each Dose (TX-200-2014)

- Cmax and AUC0-672 values were 780 ng/mL and 284,000 ng·h/mL, respectively, in animals dosed with 200 mg/mL GS-6207 with (b) (4).
- Cmax and AUC0-672 values were 451 ng/mL and 211,000 ng·h/mL, respectively, in animals dosed with 400 mg/mL GS-6207 without (b) (4).

GS-6207 related effects on remaining animals dosed with 411 mg/kg were similar to those from the animals that were necropsied early and included increased white blood cells and/or neutrophile counts and fibrinogen concentrations noted at necropsy 1 (Day 73) but not present at terminal necropsy (Day 143) suggesting reversibility of these effects. GS-6207 related effects on animals dosed with 130 mg/kg included increased fibrinogen concentrations on Days 87 and 115 which correlated with inflammation at the injection sites noted during terminal necropsy (Day 268).

L3079: Parameter	Major Findings
GS-6207-related effects on remaining animals dosed with 411 mg/kg were similar to those from the animals that were necropsied early and included increases in bilirubin and bile acid (starting on Day 60) and increases in GGT, ALP, and ALT suggesting cholestasis and were noted at interim necropsy 1 (Day 73) and in individual animals on Days 87 and 115. In males on terminal necropsy Day 143, the increases in the aforementioned endpoints were not observed indicating reversibility. There were increases in cholesterol levels in males only on Days 60, 73, 87, and 115. However, there were the increase was not detected on terminal necropsy Day 143. In the animals that were necropsied early and dosed with 411 mg/kg, there were GS-6207 related decreases in albumin and total protein with a decrease in the A:G ratio. These effects were not observed at terminal necropsy (Day 143).
GS-6207-related effects in animals dosed with 130 mg/kg were similar to those at the 411 mg/kg, but at a lesser degree, and included an increase in ALT, GGT, and/or ALP and bile acid starting on Day 87 and at various time points up to terminal necropsy (Day 268). These effects correlated to histopathology findings in the liver and bile duct.

Urinalysis	
Urine was collected during the overnight period prior to Days 87, 115, 143, 171, 199, 227, 225, and 268. Two males dosed with 411 mg/kg had GS-6207 related orange discoloration and/or positive bilirubin reaction on Day 60, indicative of bilirubin in the urine.

Gross pathology	
Animals were sacrificed on Days 73, 143, and 268.
Unscheduled Necropsy Animals (411 mg/kg; n=3)
In one animal necropsied early there was a finding of bilateral yellow eye sclera and in another was discoloration noted in the aorta, kidney, liver, and oral mucosa and a thickened gall bladder. In animals dosed at \ge 130 mg/kg, there was thickening and/or discoloration at the injection sites.

Organ weights	
No treatment-related effects detected at terminal necropsy Day 1 (Day 143 in animals dosed with 411 mg/kg) or terminal necropsy Day 2 (Day 268 in animals dosed with control and 130 mg/kg).

L3091: ## 13.2.3.3. General Toxicology; Additional Studies (Nonpivotal)
L3092: ## A 7-Day Once-Daily Oral Gavage Tolerability and Toxicokinetic Study of GS-6207 in Female Nonpregnant New Zealand White Rabbits (TX-200-2035)
L3093: In a 7-day, non-GLP-compliant study, GS-6207 formulated in (b) (4) was administered to nonpregnant female new Zealand white rabbits (3/group) at doses of 0 (control), 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg with dose volumes of 1.3, 0.2, 0.6, and 2 mL/kg, respectively. On Day 4, one female was found dead and on Day 5 another had to be euthanized in extremis in the 1000 mg/kg dose group. The mortality and extremis condition were due to intubation errors at dosing. There were no test article related findings in this study. The NOAEL was 1000 mg/kg.
L3094: ## Assessment of Subcutaneous Depot Following a Single Subcutaneous Infusion of GS-6207 in Wister Han Rat (TX-200-2027)
L3095: In a single-dose, nonGLP-compliant abbreviated study, GS-6207 formulated in vehicle 1 (PEG300 (b) (4):water; (b) (4)) or vehicle 2 (PEG300:water (b) (4)) was administered to male Wister Han rats (3/group) at a dose concentration of 300 mg/mL in a volume of 0.25 mL. A 21-gauge needle was used in all groups, except that in the GS-6207 in vehicle 1 group a 25-gauge needle was used. Both control groups and all GS-6207 groups had similar depot volume following dosing 24 hours and 7 days postdose. There was a decrease in volume in all groups. The controls groups had a higher rate of decrease in volume. The infusion rate and needle gauge
L3096: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3097: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3098: did not significantly affect depot size or heterogeneity. All groups presented similar heterogeneity of the depot over the time course of the study.
L3099: ## A 7-Day Subcutaneous and Intramuscular Dose Range-Finding Toxicity Study of GS-714207 in Male Wister Han Rats (TX-200-2002)
L3100: In a 7-day, non-GLP-compliant exploratory study, GS-6207 formulated in [REDACTED] % sterile water for injection was administered to male Wister Han rats (5 males/group) at doses of 0 (control), 5, 30, and 100 mg/kg at a dose volume of 1 mL/kg via subcutaneous or intramuscular injection. Changes in hematology (increases in neutrophil, lymphocytes, and monocytes), coagulation (increase in fibrinogen), and serum chemistry (increase globulin and decrease in albumin) were observed in animals dosed \ge 30 mg/kg via SC administration, indicating an inflammatory response. Thickening of the injection site was noted in animals dosed \ge 30 mg/kg via SC administration, and discoloration was noted at the injection site in two animals dosed with 5 mg/kg via intramuscular administration. There was minimal to marked necrosis at the injection site at all doses via SC administration. The NOAEL for SC administration, based on injection site reactions, could not be determined due to necrotic tissue at injection sites. The NOAEL for SC administration based on systemic effects was 100 mg/kg. The NOAEL for intramuscular administration based on no injection site reactions or systemic effects observed was 5 mg/kg.
L3101: ## A 7-Day Subcutaneous Injection Dose Range-Finding Toxicity Study of GS-714207 in Male Beagle Dog (TX-200-2004)
L3102: In a 7-day, non-GLP-compliant exploratory study, GS-6207 formulated in [REDACTED] % sterile water for injection was administered to male beagle dogs (3 males/group) at doses of 0 (control), 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg at a dose volume of 0.75 mL/kg via subcutaneous injection. Changes in hematology (increases in neutrophil, monocytes, and white blood cells; decrease in reticulocytes), coagulation (increase in fibrinogen), and serum chemistry (increase in ALP; increase globulin and cholesterol; and decrease in the albumin globulin ratio) were observed at 10 and/or 30 mg/kg. A decrease in thymus weight that correlated with a decrease in thymus cellularity was observed during histopathology analysis. Injection site reactions included thickening at the site and a mass noted during gross pathology. Cellular inflammation, hemorrhage, and fibrin were detected at each dose. An abscess formation was observed at doses \ge 10 mg/kg and vascular inflammation in some animals was observed at 3 and 10 mg/kg. The NOAEL for SC administration, based on injection site reactions and abscess formation at doses \ge 10 mg/kg, was 3 mg/kg. The NOAEL for SC administration based on systemic effects was 30 mg/kg.

L3154: ## An Oral (Gavage) Dose Range-Finding Study of the Effects of GS-6207 on Embryo-Fetal Development in Sprague-Dawley Rats (TX-200-2031)
L3155: GS-6207 was administered to Sprague-Dawley rats (3 rats/control and 6 rats/dose group) from gestation day (GD) 6 to 17 at doses of 0 (b) (4), 3, 30, and 300 mg/kg with a dose volume of 2 mL/kg via oral gavage once daily. L3171: ## A 30-Minute IV Infusion Dose Range-Finding Study of the Effect of GS-6207 on Embryo-Fetal Development in New Zealand White Rabbits (TX-200-2032)
L3172: GS-6207 was administered to New Zealand White rabbits (6 presumed pregnant/group) once daily from GD 7 to 19 at doses of 0 (b) (4), 5, 10, or 20 mg/kg at a dose volume of 0.667 mL/kg via intravenous infusion over a 30-minute period. One female in the 10 mg/kg group was euthanized in extremis on GD 13. This animal had a reduction in body weight when compared to the controls and a decrease in food intake. Other clinical observations noted in this animal included a decrease in fecal output, soft or mucoid feces, and brown staining on the tail and hindlimbs. There were no test article-related deaths or effects on the endpoints evaluated (clinical signs, body weights, body weight gains, gravid uterine weights, food consumption, toxicokinetic parameters, gross necropsy findings, intrauterine growth and survival, and fetal morphology). The NOAEL for maternal and embryo-fetal development was 20 mg/kg. The day 19 AUC0-24h at the NOAEL was 178,000 ng·h/mL.
