L3223: ## Impurity Studies
L3224: ## **A Single-Dose Subcutaneous Injection Impurity Qualification Study With GS-6207 in Wister Han Rats With a 4-Week Observation (Recovery) Period (TX-200-2042; GLP)**
L3225: In single dose impurity study, GS-6207 (pure), GS-6207-A (with impurities), or GS-6207-B (with impurities) formulated in PEG-300/sterile water for injection/ (b) (4) was administered to male and female Wister Han rats (3/sex/control and 3/sex/dose group) at a dose of 0 (control) or 100 mg/kg (GS-6207-treated groups) with a dose volume of 1.34 mL/kg via subcutaneous injection. GS-6207-related changes in serum chemistry detected 5 days postdose (increases in globulin; decrease in albumin:globulin ratio; and a decrease in albumin [males only]) suggested inflammation. At the end of the recovery period, these findings were not detected. Injection site reactions were detected in all GS-6207-treated animals and included minimal to marked granulomatous inflammation. The inclusion of the impurities did not affect the injection site reactions detected.
L3226: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3227: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3228: ## **A Single Dose Subcutaneous Injection Impurity Qualification Toxicity And Toxicokinetic Study of GS-6207 in Wister Han Rats With a 13-Week Observation (Recovery) Period (TX-200-2050; GLP)**
L3229: In single dose impurity study, GS-6207 (pure, sodium salt form), GS-6207-A (with impurities, free acid form), or GS-6207-B (with impurities, sodium salt form) formulated in PEG-300/sterile water for injection(b) (4) was administered to male and female Wister Han rats (3/sex/control and 3/sex/dose group) at a dose of 0 (control) or 100 mg/kg (GS-6207 treated groups) with a dose volume of 1.34 mL/kg via subcutaneous injection. Injection site reactions were detected in all GS-6207, GS-6207-A, and GS-6207-B-dosed animals. Minimal to slight, focal or multifocal, infiltrates of macrophages were detected in at all doses in males and in GS-6207 or GS-6207-B females. The increase in incidence and severity of the macrophage finding was highest in males dosed with GS-6207-A and females dosed with GS-6207-B. Minimal granulomatous inflammation at the injection site was detected in a single female dosed with GS-6207. Dosing animals with GS-6207, GS-6207-A, and GS-6207-B did not induce micronuclei in the peripheral blood reticulocytes.
L3230: ## 14. Clinical Pharmacology: Additional Information and Assessment
L3231: ## 14.1. In Vitro Studies
L3232: ## 14.1.1. Absorption
L3233: Bidirectional permeability of LEN through Caco-2 cell monolayers was evaluated in Study AD-200-2009. Low forward permeability through monolayers of Caco-2 cells and evidence for efflux transport were observed for LEN.
L3234: ## 14.1.2. Distribution
L3235: Protein binding of LEN was evaluated in Studies AD-200-2020, AD-200-2021, AD-200-2032, and AD-200-2048. The binding of LEN to human plasma proteins, human hepatic microsomes, human serum albumin, or purified \alpha 1-acid glycoprotein was high, with mean fraction bound of 98.5%, 89.2%, &gt;99.9%, and 93%, respectively. The binding of LEN to human plasma proteins, human hepatic microsomes, human serum albumin, or purified \alpha 1-acid glycoprotein was high, with a mean fraction bound of 98.5%, 89.2%, &gt;99.9%, and 93%, respectively. The human blood-plasma ratio was 0.64, showing minimal binding to blood cells.
L3236: ## 14.1.3. Metabolism
L3237: LEN stability was evaluated in phosphate buffered saline, plasma, hepatic microsomes, hepatocytes, and Hurel® hepatic co-cultures in Studies AD-200-2047, AD-200-2022, AD-200-2008, and AD-200-2037. The studies showed that LEN exists in two(b) (4) forms,(b) (4) The LEN(b) (4) pattern was stable over time and is not influenced by binding proteins or enzymes in plasma. LEN showed high metabolic stability across all species in both hepatic microsomes, hepatocytes, and Hurel® hepatocyte co-cultures. LEN was predicted to have a low hepatic metabolic clearance in human.
L3238: ## 14.1.4. Drug-Drug Interaction Potential—LEN as a Victim
L3239: LEN was evaluated as a substrate of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes, UDP glucuronosyl transferase (UGT) enzymes, P-gp, BCRP, organic anion transporter peptide (OATP)1B1, and OATP1B3 in Studies AD-200-2030, AD-200-2054, AD-200-2033, AD-200-2005, AD-200-2025, and AD-200-2027. Very slow metabolism of LEN by CYP3A5 or UGT1A1 was observed in in vitro phenotyping studies, indicating LEN is a substrate for CYP3A5 and UGT1A1. LEN is also a substrate for P-gp. LEN is not a substrate for other CYP or UGT isozymes, nor a substrate for breast-cancer resistance protein (BCRP) or hepatic uptake transporters.
L3240: ## 14.1.5. Drug-Drug Interaction Potential—LEN as a Perpetrator
L3241: The potential of LEN as an inhibitor for CYP enzymes, UGT1A1, P-gp (MDR1), BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OAT1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT)1, OCT2, multidrug and toxin extrusion protein (MATE)1, MATE2K, and bile salt export pump was evaluated in Studies AD-200-2028, AD-200-2050, AD-200-2031, AD-200-2026, AD-200-2035. The results showed that LEN is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor, mainly through mechanism-based inhibition. The potential of LEN as an inhibitor was evaluated using static mechanistic models (Report AD-200-2055), described in the FDA Guidance for Industry: *In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies — Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions* (January 2020). Based on the criteria defined in the guidance, LEN is not expected to inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 or UGT1A1. LEN is an inhibitor of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3, but is not likely to inhibit P-gp, BCRP, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, MATE1, or MATE2K. LEN is expected to increase the concentrations of CYP3A substrates by about five- and two-fold with LEN oral and SC injection, respectively.
L3242: The induction potential of LEN on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, constitutive androstane receptor, and pregnane X receptor was evaluated in Study AD-200-2029. In vitro characterization of LEN for CYP induction potential was conducted using Sandwich Cultured Transporter-Certified™ hepatocytes in Study AD-200-2049. The data suggested no potential for activation of genes regulated by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor or constitutive androstane receptor. LEN activated pregnane X receptor, exceeding two-fold activation at concentrations of LEN \ge 2.5\mu\text{M}. In Study AD-200-2049, CYP3A4 mRNA was unchanged in two of the three donors; the mRNA fold over control increased more than two-fold in the third donor and reached a maximum of 23% of the positive control at 3\mu\text{M} LEN (a cytopathic dose). Thus, while this effect was only seen in one donor it suggests that induction of CYP3A4 and pregnane X receptor-regulated gene products by LEN cannot be ruled out completely. The potential of LEN as an inducer was evaluated using static mechanistic models. Based on the FDA in vitro drug-drug interaction (DDI) guidance, LEN would not be classified as an inducer following either SC or oral administration (Report AD-200-2055).

L3256: ## **Study 4333: Statistical Comparisons of PIT PK Parameters Following Administration Alone, PIT Administered Simultaneous With LEN, and PIT Administered Staggered From LEN Under Fed Conditions in Cohort 11 (PIT PK Analysis Set)**

Title	A Phase 1b Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo Controlled, Multi-Cohort Study of the Safety, Pharmacokinetics, and Antiviral Activity of GS-6207 Administered Subcutaneously in HIV-1 Infected Subjects
Trial design	
This was a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, multicenter, multicohort study of LEN (Part A) and TAF (Part B) monotherapy in people with HIV. Results from Part B of the study are not discussed here.
In Part A (Cohorts 1-5), participants in each cohort (n=8) were randomized in a 3:1 ratio to receive active LEN (n=6) or placebo (n=2). A single SC dose of LEN or placebo was administered in the abdomen on Day 1. The LEN doses evaluated in Cohorts 2 to 5 were determined based on cumulative safety data (to at least Day 14) and available PK and antiviral activity data from previous cohorts, as well as available safety data (to at least Day 14) and PK data from Study GS-US-200-4070. Doses of LEN 150, 50, 450, 20, and 750 mg were administered in Cohorts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively. The formulation of LEN used was LEN 100 mg/mL suspension, free acid.
All participants initiated once-daily bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (B/F/TAF, Biktarvy® [BVY]) on Day 10 after completion of all assessments and continued dosing through Day 225, as a standard-of-care oral combination ART to mitigate the potential risks of developing resistance to LEN.

PK Sample collection time points	
Plasma PK Sampling

Day 1: 0 (predose), and up to 225 days postdose.

L3351: ## Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics
L3352: Plasma concentrations of LEN were fit to an Emax model to evaluate the concentration-response relationship between LEN concentration at Day 10 and the reduction from baseline in HIV-1 RNA at Day 10. Due to the limited amount of data at low concentration values and reduction in HIV-1 RNA in the placebo group, the Emax model was not forced through the origin (0,0).
L3353: Following single-dose SC administration of LEN, the Emax was predicted to be a 2.13 log10 copies/mL decline in HIV-1 RNA at Day 10. The in vivo 90% effective concentration (EC90) of LEN on Day 10 demonstrated by the Emax model was 12.6 ng/mL. Based on this analysis, mean LEN concentrations \ge12.6 ng/mL are predicted to provide near maximal (94%) antiviral activity.

L3360: ## **Table 105. Study GS-US-200-4330**
L3361: Study number	GS-US-200-4330
Report location	GS-US-200-4330 Final CSR
Study title	A Phase 1 Open-Label, Parallel-Design, Single-Dose Study to Evaluate the Pharmacokinetics of GS-6207 in Participants With Normal Renal Function and Severe Renal Impairment
Description of trial design	Inclusion Criteria
Male and nonpregnant/nonlactating female subjects, ages 18 to 79 years with severe renal impairment or normal renal function (creatinine clearance [CL_{Cr}] \ge 90 mL/min), were eligible. Subjects must have had 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) without clinically significant abnormalities, with either severe renal impairment or normal renal function (CL_{Cr} \ge 90 mL/min using the Cockcroft Gault equation). Subjects with renal impairment must have had a severe renal impairment classification (15 \le CL_{Cr} \le 29 mL/min using the Cockcroft Gault equation) at screening that was unchanged during the 3 months prior to study drug dosing. Subjects with severe renal impairment requiring or anticipated to require dialysis within 90 days of study entry were not eligible.
Treatment
Subjects with renal impairment received a single dose of lenacapavir (LEN) (1\times300 mg tablet) administered orally on Day 1. Dosing in matched healthy controls with normal renal function began after a matched subject with renal impairment had completed pharmacokinetic (PK) assessments through Day 4. Matched healthy controls received a single dose of LEN (1\times300 mg tablet). Duration of dosing was 1 day. The study duration (not including screening) was approximately 60 days (\pm 1 day) including follow-up.
PK Sampling scheme	Plasma PK Collection
Intensive PK sampling occurred relative to the morning dose of LEN at the following time points for each cohort:
Day 1: 0 (predose, \le 5 minutes before dose), 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and 48 hours postdose.
L3362: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3363: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3364: Days 4, 6, 8, 15, 22, 29, 36, 43, and 50: A single anytime PK sample was collected.
L3365: Additional plasma samples were collected for plasma protein binding evaluation on Day 1 at 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, and 48 hours postdose. In addition, a plasma sample was collected on Days 15 and 50 and were utilized for plasma protein binding evaluation.
L3366: ## Urine PK Sampling
L3367: All urine samples were collected predose (void; within a 12-hour period prior to Day 1 dose), and over the following collection intervals after Day 1: 0 to 12, 12 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 72, 72 to 96, 96 to 120, 120 to 144, and 144 to 168 hours postdose.
L3368: **Results**

The plasma PK parameters of LEN (by renal group) are presented below. C_{max} and AUC were 2.6- and 1.9-fold higher, respectively, in subjects with severe renal impairment compared to subjects with normal renal function. However, larger increases in exposures were observed in other clinical studies. In Study 4332, the C_{max} and AUC_{tau} to Day 12 were 1070 ng/mL and 10,641 h\cdotng/mL, respectively, more than 7- and 12-fold higher, respectively, than the therapeutic exposure in the CAPELLA study. Similar results were observed in Study 5709. There are no safety concerns for both studies. Therefore, the observed exposure elevation in subjects with severe renal impairment is not clinically significant.

Description of trial design	Inclusion Criteria (Clinical Pharmacology Related)

Treatment

L3392: ## **Analysis of Plasma Samples for [^{14}C]LEN and [^{14}C]Metabolites**
L3393: Of the circulating radioactivity, 68.8% was associated with unchanged LEN. No single metabolite contributed &gt;10% of total radioactivity exposure through 1176 hours postdose. The total radioactivity exposure from the sum of all identified components in the plasma was approximately 88%.
L3394: ## **Analysis of Fecal Samples for [^{14}C]LEN and [^{14}C]Metabolites**
L3395: Unchanged LEN was the most abundant component recovered in feces and accounted for a mean abundance of 43.4% of the total fecal radioactivity. Adjusting for the 75.9% mean cumulative fecal recovery of the administered radioactive dose, LEN and the LEN-hexose conjugate metabolite (M42, M35) were the two most abundant components recovered in the feces and accounted for a mean abundance of 43.4% (32.9% of dose) and 8.7% (6.6% of dose) of the administered ^{14}C dose, respectively. Each of the other metabolites identified in feces accounted for &lt;2% of the dose.
L3396: ## **Summary of Mass Balance**
L3397: A mean 75.9% of the dose was recovered in feces and 0.237% was recovered in urine through the last collection interval, indicating that fecal elimination is the primary elimination route of LEN and its metabolites. Most of the administered radioactive dose was recovered in the first 1608 hours postdose (74.7% in feces and urine combined).

L3456: ## **PK/PD Results**
L3457: The results of the Applicant's and reviewer's separate analyses suggest an absence of significant QTc prolongation at the proposed therapeutic dose. The peak concentration observed with highest dose studied (i.e., 600 mg twice daily; Day 12 of study) is expected to offer approximately 8.8-fold margin over the therapeutic exposures associated with the maximum proposed dose at the steady-state (Phase 2/3 Study 4625 in HTE PLWH). At LEN concentrations approximately 9-fold the therapeutic concentrations from the recommended dosing regimen, lenacapavir does not prolong the QT interval to any clinically relevant extent.

L3469: ## 14.3.1. Applicant's Population PK Analysis
L3470: The population PK (popPK) analysis was based on PK data from seven studies (Table 114): five phase 1 studies in healthy subjects (4071, 4329, 4333, 4538, and 5709), one phase 2 study in treatment-naïve patients with HIV (Study 4334), and one phase 2/3 study in HTE patients (Study 4625). In phase 1 studies, LEN was administered as either an oral dose, a 1-hour IV infusion, an SC injection, or a combination of oral loading and SC injection. In phase 2 and phase 2/3 studies, LEN was administered as an oral lead-in followed by SC administration.
L3471: The analysis dataset comprised 7053 PK observations from 384 subjects, including 198 below limit of quantification concentrations. The limit of quantification was 0.5 ng/mL for Studies 4071, 4334, 4538, 4625 and 5709, and 0.1 ng/mL for Studies 4329 and 4333. below limit of quantification samples represented about 2.8% of the PK data, and therefore were excluded from the analysis.
L3472: The summary statistics for the continuous and categorical covariates are presented by study in Table 115. The analysis population was primarily male (77.6%) white (56.8%) subjects, with a median (range) age of 34 years (18 to 78 years), weight of 75.9 kg (41.4 to 164 kg), body mass index (BMI) of 26.1 kg/m2 (14.9 to 51.1 kg/m2), and 54.9% of subjects were patients with HIV.

L3492: ## Base PK Model
L3493: The PK of LEN was best described by a two-compartment distribution model with linear elimination from the central compartment. The oral LEN absorption was best characterized by a first-order absorption process, and the SC absorption was best characterized by a parallel direct first-order absorption and a delayed absorption process with four transit compartments. The PK model was parameterized in terms of clearance (CL), central and peripheral volumes of distribution (V_c and V_p, respectively), intercompartmental clearance (Q/F), oral (PO) absorption rate constant (K_a), PO bioavailability relative to IV (F_{po}), SC direct/rapid first-order absorption rate constant (K_{dir}), SC transit first-order absorption rate constant (K_{tr}), fraction of the SC dose absorbed through the rapid/direct process, and the SC bioavailability relative to IV (F_{sc}). Between-subject variability or inter-individual variability (IIV) was estimated on CL, V_p, dissociation rate constant (K_a), K_{tr}, and F_{sc}. The residual error model consisted of a combined additive and proportional error model. The final structural model for lenacapavir is presented in Figure 34.
L3494: Figure 34. Schematic of the Structural PK Model for LEN
L3495: DIRECT = fraction of SC dose absorbed through direct first-order absorption; GI = gastrointestinal; IV = intravenous;
L3496: PK = pharmacokinetic; SC = subcutaneous

L3498: Abbreviations: F_{po}, PO bioavailability relative to IV; F_{sc}, SC bioavailability relative to IV; K_{dir}, direct/rapid first-order absorption rate constant; K_a, dissociation constant; K_{dir}, direct/rapid first-order absorption rate constant; K_{tr}, transit first-order absorption rate constant; Q, intercompartmental clearance; V_c, central volume of distribution; V_p, peripheral volume of distribution

L3502: The following continuous covariates were evaluated during covariate model selection: Age, weight, PO dose, food, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease formula). The evaluated categorical covariates were: sex (male as reference), race (white as reference), ethnicity (non-Hispanic as reference), formulation (tablet, sodium salt solution [300 mg/mL], sodium salt solution [150 mg/mL], and IV solution), antiretroviral background therapies (none as reference see Table 115), and health status (patient with HIV as reference).
L3503: The following covariates were included in the final model:
L3504: - weight on (b) (4) Q, Vc and Vp (using allometric scaling standardized to 70 kg).
- (b) (4)
- Dose on (b) (4) Fpo (using a power model standardized to a 600 mg dose).
- Health status (healthy) on CL and Vp (using a proportional linear model).
- (b) (4) (using a proportional linear model).
- Formulation (sodium salt solution [155 mg/mL] versus [309 mg/mL]) on Ktr and Vp (using a proportional linear model).
- Antiretroviral background therapy (contains cobicistat [COBI] or ritonavir [RTV] as a booster versus all others) as a time-varying covariate on Fpo (using a proportional linear model).
L3505: ## Final Model
L3506: The parameter estimates from the final popPK model for LEN are listed in Table 116. According to the Applicant's popPK model, for an average 70 kg, 34-year-old male patient with HIV, receiving 600 mg (PO or SC) LEN with no interacting antiretroviral therapy, the population estimates for LEN CL, Vc, Q, Vp, PO Ka, Fpo, SC Kdir, SC Ktr, Fsc, and SC fraction for direct absorption are 4.05 L/h, 68 L, 41.2 L/h, 908 L, 0.0287 h-1, 6.24%, 0.000376 h-1, 0.00201 h-1, 103%, and 42%, respectively.
L3507: The estimated IIV expressed as the coefficient of variation (%CV) was 44%, 85%, 78%, 32%, and 39% for CL, Vp, Ka, Ktr, and Fsc respectively. The interindividual random effect (ETA) shrinkage from the final PopPK model was 9.9%, 5.4%, 10.1%, 41.9%, and 41.5% for CL, Vp, (b) (4) Ka, Ktr, and Fsc, respectively. Inclusion of IIV on additional parameters (b) (4) resulted in model instability, as indicated by large relative standard errors (RSEs) or high condition numbers.

L3519: The estimated effect of was small (at clinically relevant doses of 300 to 927 mg) and not precise (RSE of (b) (4)%). Besides, the physiological and mechanistic rationale of including this covariate was questioned by the review team.
L3520: Finally, the lower SC formulation strength (155 mg/mL versus 309 mg/mL) was found to have an effect on V_p and K_{tr}, with an estimated 79% lower V_p, and a more rapid SC absorption with a 34.5% higher K_{tr} for the 155 mg/mL SC salt solution. Accounting for the differences between the 2 SC formulation strength improved the PK model fit and the visual predictive checks. Only the 309 mg/mL SC formulation strength will be used for the commercial product.
L3521: The goodness-of-fit plots from the final popPK model, are shown in Figure 35. The plots of the observed concentrations versus population as well as the individual predicted concentrations show random normal scatter around the identity lines, indicating absence of systematic bias and show good agreement between the individual predicted and observed concentrations. The conditional weighted residuals versus time after last dose or versus population predicted concentrations also show random normal scatter around zero with no specific trend, indicating no major model misspecifications.

L3535: ## 14.3.2. Reviewer's Comments on the Applicant's Population PK Analysis
L3536: ## Assessment of the Covariate Analysis
L3537: - The Applicant's PK model reasonably describes the observed concentrations from LEN clinical studies.
L3538: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3539: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3540: - The PK parameters from the final model were estimated with acceptable precision, with a %RSE ranging between 4% and 32%, except for the covariate effect of [REDACTED] (b) (4).
- Among the PK parameters that are affected by the identified covariates, the ETA shrinkage was acceptable with a relatively higher shrinkage for K_{tr} (41.9%) and F_{sc} (41.5%), which makes the graphical assessment of covariates on these parameters less reliable. [REDACTED] (b) (4).
- The Applicant's popPK model included dose effect as a continuous variable on both F_{po} [REDACTED] (b) (4). As the less than dose proportional increase in AUC_{inf} and C_{max} from the PO formulation is likely due to saturable PO absorption, only the inclusion of dose effect on F_{po} is needed. In addition, the effect of dose [REDACTED] (b) (4) was not precisely estimated (%RSE of [REDACTED] (b) (4)) and most importantly, the range of doses included in the relationship was not limited to the PO doses but also included the SC dose.
L3541: The review team evaluation, in addition to the Applicant reassessment, found that [REDACTED] (b) (4) was not a statistically significant covariate [REDACTED] (b) (4) with an increase in OFV by less than 9 points (for 1 degree of freedom) after removal of the covariate. Therefore, as physiologically and mechanistically expected, only the effect of dose on F_{po} is clinically relevant and kept in the updated PK model. The removal of [REDACTED] (b) (4) from the PK model did not alter the initial PK parameters and their variability estimates.
L3542: - The Applicant classified background antiretroviral (ARV) therapies, potentially known to interact with the PO exposure of LEN, as ARV containing COBI (n=18), ARV containing ritonavir (RTV, n=19), ARV containing darunavir (DRV, n=19) with unreported booster (pharmcoenhancer) used, and other ARVs in 2 patients on multiple background regimens including DRV (fostemsavir, dolutegravir, ibalizumab, F/TAF and darunavir). All patients on comedication with known interactions were HTE patients belonging to Study 4625. In their initial assessment of the DDI effect on F_{po}, the Applicant grouped together patients receiving ARV containing COBI or RTV (n=37), and estimated a combined effect of 58.7% increase in F_{po}. The Applicant did not evaluate the effect of COBI- and RTV-containing ARVs separately. In addition, in the PK model, the Applicant evaluated the effect on F_{po} in patients either receiving DRV with unknown/unreported booster (n=19) or receiving multiple background regimens including DRV (n=2). After an information request to the Applicant, recommending separate evaluation of boosted ARV drugs, the Applicant estimated a separate effect on F_{po} for COBI- and RTV-containing ARVs, with an
L3543: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3544: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3545: estimated 28.6% increase for COBI-containing ARVs and 110% increase for RTV-containing ARVs. The Applicant did not address the investigation of DRV effect used either alone (with unknown/unreported booster) or as part of a multiple background regimen. The remaining PK parameters from the updated PK model were comparable to the initial final model PK parameters and their variability estimates.
L3546: The review team evaluation of ARVs DDI on F_{po}, estimated a 28% increase for COBI-containing ARVs, a 95% increase for RTV-containing ARVs, a 52% increase in HTE patients receiving DRV (with unspecified booster), with a high variability in the estimated mean effect (%RSE from 41.4% to 47.5%). In two HTE patients who received DRV at some point as part of a varying multiple background regimen, the estimated increase in F_{po} was about 37.4% compared to patients without a known DDI, and the estimated effect was not statistically significant and did not worsen the OFV. The PK model estimated effect of COBI-containing ARVs and DRV (with unspecified booster) on F_{po} was lower than the observed effect of COBI alone or DRV/COBI combination on LEN AUC_{inf} in the dedicated DDI Study 4333 (not included in the popPK dataset/analysis). In the dedicated study in healthy participants, COBI alone and the DRV/COBI combination increased AUC_{inf} by 128% and 94%, respectively. However, the head-to-head comparison of results from Study 4333 and the PK model estimated effect from Study 4625 is challenging. In fact, the PK data from Study 4333 were not included in the PK modeling and the estimated effects from the PK model were in HTE patients from Study 4625 with varying baseline ARVs backgrounds. In addition, the COBI-containing ARVs likely contained drugs/protease inhibitors other than DRV.
L3547: - The review team evaluation of the covariate plots for F_{sc} found that formulation strength had an effect on the SC bioavailability of LEN, with an estimated 71% higher F_{sc} for the lower SC formulation strength of 155 mg/mL compared to the 309 mg/mL SC formulation. However, the estimated effect was not found to be statistically significant (at a significance level of 0.001), with a decrease in OFV by 10.1 points (for 1 degree of freedom). The estimated effect of SC formulation strength on V_3 and K_{tr}, as determined by the Applicant, remained unchanged. Although not statistically significant, the effect of SC formulation strength on F_{sc} was kept in the revised PK model, given the 71% effect and the 10 point drop in OFV.
- Finally, the review team evaluation of the covariate plots for F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} (SC slow absorption), as well as the PK profiles, identified that BMI affected the LEN exposure, with trends of higher exposures in underweight subjects and lower exposures in obese patients. After an information request to the Applicant, recommending the evaluation of BMI (either continuous or categorical) as a covariate on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} and F_{sc}, the Applicant reported that the inclusion of BMI (as a continuous variable) on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} and F_{sc} resulted in a decrease in OFV of 10.2 points, respectively. Of the two, only the BMI effect on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} was retained by the Applicant, and the trends observed for the final model between weight and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} or F_{sc} were both addressed after inclusion of the BMI-F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} relationship. The Applicant's updated PK model included BMI as a continuous variable using a power model standardized to a median BMI of 26.1 kg/m^2, with an estimated power exponent of -0.55. The remaining PK parameters from the updated PK model were comparable to the initial final model PK parameters and their variability estimates.
L3548: The review team evaluation on BMI either as a continuous or categorical variable (using the same PK dataset) found that the BMI effect on F_{sc} was more pronounced than the effect on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} when the covariate was included on both F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)}. The ETA covariate plots, across different studies and SC formulation strength, showed higher F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} for underweight subjects (n=5, receiving SC), lower F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} for obese subjects (n=35), and comparable F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} for normal (n=90) and overweight subjects (n=75). The review team PK modeling using BMI as a categorical variable on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} and F_{sc} resulted in a drop in OFV by F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} and 16 points (for 2 degrees of freedom), respectively. The concomitant inclusion of BMI on both F_{sc} and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} in the PK model estimated a F_{sc}^{(b)(4)}% higher and F_{sc}^{(b)(4)}% lower F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} in underweight and obese subjects, and a 66% higher and 23% lower F_{sc} in underweight and obese subjects, respectively, compared to normal and overweight subjects. The mean effect of underweight BMI on F_{sc} (of 66%) was not precisely estimated (with a %RSE of 73.4%), likely due to the small number of underweight subjects (n=5) in the PK dataset and studies, as well as the high variability in PK profile observed in few of these subjects. The backward elimination of BMI on F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} did not significantly change the OFV (F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} increase in OFV). In agreement with the observed effect of BMI groups on the PK profiles (flatter PK profiles for obese and higher PK profiles in underweight subjects) and the absence of obvious faster or delayed absorption amongst the BMI groups, the inclusion and retention of the BMI effect on F_{sc} only instead of F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} was considered more relevant.
L3549: In conclusion, the Applicant's reassessment of the covariate analysis and the review team's separate evaluation of the Applicant's updated PK model found that according to the PK modeling:
L3550: - F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} were not significant or relevant covariates. Both covariates effect F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} was removed from the PK model.
- The inclusion of F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} in addition to F_{po}, was not mechanistically justified and was not relevant. The effect of F_{sc}^{(b)(4)} was removed from the model.
- Cobicistat-containing ARVs had a 28% increase in F_{po}. RTV-containing ARVs had a 95% increase in F_{po}. HTE patients receiving DRV (with unspecified booster) had a 52% increase in F_{po}.
- Underweight subjects were estimated to have a 66% higher LEN SC bioavailability and obese subjects to have 23% lower F_{sc}, compared to normal and overweight subjects. The BMI effect on F_{sc}, particularly in obese subjects, is not expected to impact the target of having the mean C_{trough} (and 90% CI of the mean) above the inhibitory quotient 4 (IQ4) of 15.5 ng/mL for a 26-week dosing window (Figure 14 and Figure 16, Section II.6.3.4).

L3614: ## 18. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance
L3615: ## Mechanism of Action
L3616: ## Co-Crystal Structure of Lenacapavir Bound to Cross-Linked Capsid Hexamer (Report No. PC-200-2022)
L3617: A 2.0-Angstrom protein X-ray crystal structure was determined for the cross-linked capsid hexamer in complex with LEN to characterize the interaction of LEN with the HIV-1 capsid. LEN binds directly at the interface formed by two adjacent capsid monomers, such that up to six molecules of LEN can bind to each capsid hexamer. LEN forms extensive interactions with the binding pocket (Figure 39). The central amide and pyridine ring of LEN form hydrogen bonds with Asn57 within the N-terminal domain of one monomer, whereas the indazole and sulfonamide groups of LEN make hydrogen bonds with Gln179 and Asn183 within the C-terminal domain of the neighboring monomer. Thus, LEN binds at the intermolecular interface between the N-terminal domain of one subunit and the C-terminal domain of the neighboring subunit within the same capsid hexamer. Additionally, the LEN binding site is shared by capsid-binding host nuclear import factors (Price et al. 2012; Matreyek et al. 2013; Bhattacharya et al. 2014). This observation supports that LEN may compete with nuclear import machinery for binding to capsid and thereby interfere with nuclear transport.

L3623: ## **LEN Binding to Recombinant Capsid Proteins (Report No. PC-200-2022)**
L3624: The binding affinities of LEN to wild-type capsid hexamers and hexamers containing the M66I substitution (identified in resistance selection studies) (Report PC-200-2025) were evaluated by surface plasmon resonance. Surface plasmon resonance sensorgrams showed dose-dependent and saturable binding of LEN to cross-linked wild-type capsid hexamer with an equilibrium binding constant of 1.4nM. LEN binding to cross-linked M66I mutant hexamers was 80-fold weaker, with an equilibrium binding constant of 110nM.
L3625: ## **Effect on Capsid Assembly in a Biochemical Assay (Report No. PC-200-2022)**
L3626: Capsid protein can spontaneously oligomerize under high ionic strength conditions to form open-ended, tube-like structures comprised of repeating capsid hexamers. The assembly kinetics of full-length capsid were measured under high ionic strength condition (2M NaCl) in the presence and absence of LEN using an assembly assay based on monitoring the change in sample absorbance at 350 nm. LEN showed a dose-dependent increase in the rate and extent of capsid assembly with a mean concentration yielding 50\% activation of 0.32\mu M (mean of six independent determinations).
L3627: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3628: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3629: Additionally, assembly products formed under both low ionic strength (0.5\text{M} NaCl) and high ionic strength (2\text{M} NaCl) conditions were visualized by negative staining and transmission electron microscopy. Under low ionic strength (0.5\text{M} NaCl) conditions, full-length capsid did not undergo self-assembly, but in the presence of 40\mu\text{M} LEN, formed large numbers of capsid polymers that were shorter and generally more disordered (Figure 40A) relative to the long capsid tube-like structures universally observed in the absence of the compound in the high ionic strength buffer, a condition that is permissive for capsid protein assembly in the absence of LEN (Figure 40A). At a higher NaCl concentration (2\text{M}) with LEN, capsid polymers were also shorter and malformed (disordered and closed) relative to the uniform tubular polymers formed by full-length capsid in the absence of this compound (Figure 40B). LEN induced the production of poorly organized multimeric capsid polymers.

L3634: ## Effects on Capsid Morphology (Report PC-200-2023)
L3635: The morphology of capsid structures was examined in ultrathin-sectioned virions produced in the presence and absence of LEN by transmission electron microscopy (Figure 41). The vehicle
L3636: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3637: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3638: (dimethyl sulfoxide)-treated controls showed the expected conical capsids with an encased dark signal at the wide end of the cone consistent with negative staining of viral nucleic acids. In contrast, virions produced in the presence of LEN contained predominantly malformed capsid cores in which the nucleic acids were either regionally or diffusely confined within the irregularly shaped capsid core. This altered capsid morphology is consistent with the finding that LEN accelerates the assembly of recombinant capsid protein into poorly organized capsid polymers. The morphology of HIV-1 particles produced in the presence of LEN was distinct from virions produced in the presence of the protease inhibitor atazanavir, which uniformly contained an immature, discontinuous Gag/Gag-Pol polyprotein lattice. Virions produced in the presence of LEN or atazanavir were noninfectious when serially diluted well below the EC50 concentration of each compound and used to infect CEM-NKR CCR5+Luc+ indicator cells.

L3643: ## **Inhibition of Production of Mature HIV-1 Virions by Capsid Binding**
L3644: The effects of LEN on virus production and cell viability was assessed in HEK293T cells following transient transfection with plasmids encoding the vesicular stomatitis virus envelope and a single-cycle HIV-1 reporter virus. LEN showed a dose-dependent reduction in the amount of mature wild-type HIV-1 released into cell culture supernatants, with a mean 50% effective concentration (EC50) value of 0.305nM as determined by p24 (capsid) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Figure 42). The effect on the production of mature extracellular virions occurred at concentrations of LEN within the range of its late-stage antiviral EC50 value of 0.44nM, which suggests that this effect may represent the major mechanism by which LEN mediates its late-stage antiviral activity. The effect of LEN on virus production required the wild-type capsid domain since this effect was not observed with the M66I capsid mutant (mean

L3647: EC_{50} &gt; 2 \mu M). In addition, the compound effect is virus-specific since LEN showed no cytotoxicity in HEK293T cells up to the highest concentration tested (10 \mu M) (Figure 42).

L3651: ## **Dose-Dependent Reduction in Intracellular HIV-1 Gag/p24 Levels by a Mechanism That Requires Capsid Domain Binding**
L3652: The effect of LEN on HIV-1 Gag polyprotein expression and maturation was assessed by anti-p24 western blot analyses using cell lysates from HEK293T cells producing infectious virus (Figure 43). Cells producing wild-type HIV-1 in the presence of 10 to 100nM LEN (23- to 227-fold its late-stage EC_{50} value) showed reduced intracellular levels of capsid (p24) and Gag (p55) proteins relative to the vehicle-treated (mock) control sample. At lower concentrations of LEN (0.1 to 1nM), Gag levels remained unaffected by the presence of the compound whereas capsid levels were reduced relative to the mock control. The Applicant states LEN is unlikely to act by inhibiting Gag/Gag-Pol polyprotein cleavage since reduced capsid levels were not associated with a concomitant increase in Gag levels, as would be expected, and because malformed capsid cores were readily observed in virus particles produced in the presence of LEN. The intracellular downregulation of these viral proteins is dependent on a specific interaction between LEN and the capsid domain of mature (p24) and immature (Gag/Gag-Pol) capsid proteins, because these proteins were not reduced by LEN when using the M66I capsid HIV-1 mutant (Figure 43). These data suggest that the reduced production of virus particles observed with LEN is likely due to an increased rate of Gag/p24 intracellular turnover following specific binding of LEN to the capsid domain of intracellular Gag/Gag-Pol precursor polyproteins by a mechanism that is not yet determined.

L3659: ## **Effect of LEN on the Early Stages of HIV-1 Replication (Report PC-200-2024)**
L3660: LEN retains full antiviral efficacy when the presence of the compound is selectively restricted to the target cell infection phase (i.e., the early stage of the replication cycle), with a mean early stage EC50 value of 0.023nM. The antiviral activity of LEN was assessed in CEM-NKr CCR5+Luc+ T cells infected with pseudotyped HIV-1 expressing one of four different viral envelope proteins. These viral envelope glycoproteins were selected because their surface expression confers either broad host cell tropism (VSVG) or restricted HIV-1 entry into CD4+ cells expressing the C-X-C chemokine receptor (CXCR)4 coreceptor (NL4-3), the C-C chemokine receptor (CCR)5 coreceptor (JRFL), or other chemokine coreceptor (HT593.1). LEN displayed similar antiviral activity against all pseudotyped HIV-1 viruses tested with a range of EC50 values between 0.046 and 0.106nM (Table 122). These data indicate that LEN functions independently of the viral envelope protein.

L3668: The BlaM-Vpr reporter assay was used to quantify HIV entry into peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) treated with LEN. This assay uses HIV-1 variant containing copackaged \beta-lactamase enzyme which, when transferred to the target cell's cytosol following virus-host cell membrane fusion, can be detected and quantified through enzymatic cleavage of the fluorescent substrate CCF2. The PBMCs from three donors were independently infected with BlaM/HIV-1 (NL4-3 strain) in the presence of LEN or control compounds, loaded with CCF2 substrate dye, and CD3+ CD4+ CD8- cells containing virus entry were enumerated by flow cytometry to detect the cleaved CCF2 dye after 16 hours of incubation. Whereas only a low proportion of blue CD3+ CD4+ CD8- cells were detected in PBMC cultures following a mock-infection (mean 0.6%), mean infection rates with BlaM/HIV were 17% in the presence of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; vehicle control). As expected, treatment with the CXCR4 small-molecule control inhibitor AMD3100 (1\muM) greatly reduced virus entry to near background levels (mean 0.8%). In contrast, treatment with 1\muM of either LEN or the INSTI dolutegravir did not reduce HIV entry into PBMCs (mean 18 to 21%). These data indicate that LEN induces a post-entry block in HIV replication.
L3669: A time-of-drug-addition assay was used to determine how long after initiating a synchronized HIV-1 infection LEN could be added to the culture before a 50% decline in its maximal antiviral efficacy was observed. MT-2 cells were infected with VSVG-HIV-LUC reporter virus, washed to remove unabsorbed virus, and then compounds were added to the culture either immediately postinfection (time 0) or at 4-hour intervals (+4, +8, +12, +16, +20, +24, +28, and +32 hours) postinfection. Compounds were added at a fixed drug concentration conferring maximal viral suppression, equivalent to 10- or 100-fold their respective EC50 value. The mean time postinfection to maintain at least half maximal inhibition (T1/2) for LEN was ~ 15.3 hours. The T1/2 observed with the non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) efavirenz and nevirapine were 10.2 and 11.3 hours, respectively, whereas the T1/2 for each of two integrase strand-transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) (raltegravir, DTG) was 16.6 hours. These data indicate that LEN inhibits HIV infection sometime after reverse transcription but before HIV integration.
L3670: The effect of LEN on the accumulation of early HIV-1 replication products in acutely infected MT-2 cells was assessed by quantitative PCR. Cells were infected with single-cycle VSVG-HIV-LUC virus and then treated with DMSO (vehicle control), LEN, efavirenz, dolutegravir, or atazanavir. Total DNA was harvested 12, 24, and 48 hours postinfection. The amounts of reverse transcribed strong-stop and second-strand transfer DNA products (early and late reverse transcription, respectively) and abortive 2-long terminal repeat (2-LTR) circles produced only in
L3671: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3672: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3673: the nucleus were quantified by quantitative PCR at 12 and 24 hours postinfection, respectively, whereas the amounts of integration products (Alu-LTR) were quantified by digital-droplet PCR at 48 hours postinfection. All measured quantities were normalized against the corresponding CCR5 gene copies in the same sample and expressed as a fold-change value relative to the DMSO-treated infected control (set to 100%) for each target amplicon measured (Table 123). As expected, treatment with the late-acting PI atazanavir had no effect on the accumulation of any of the four replication products analyzed in this single-cycle infection study. In contrast, the NNRTI efavirenz significantly reduced the accumulation of all four replication products as expected. Treatment with the INSTI dolutegravir specifically reduced integration products, and thus, increased integration failures, leading to a three-fold increase in the accumulation of abortive 2-LTR circles in the nucleus. Although high concentrations of LEN (244-fold its EC50 value) produced an HIV replication product profile similar to efavirenz, indicating LEN can inhibit reverse transcription under conditions of extremely high drug exposure, this was not the case at lower and still fully suppressive LEN concentrations. For instance, MT-2 cells treated with 0.25 to 2.5nM LEN (6.1- to 61-fold its EC50 value) showed a unique impact on HIV infection product profile relative to the control inhibitors, with no effect on the accumulation of reverse transcription products, but profoundly reduced levels of integration products and abortive 2-LTR circles. Thus, LEN primarily inhibits HIV replication at a step after reverse transcription, but before integration. Two-LTR circles did not accumulate in the presence of LEN as observed with dolutegravir, but instead were reduced, suggesting that the compound likely prevents integration by inhibiting the translocation of viral preintegration complexes into the nucleus.

L3681: In summary, there is evidence that LEN acts through mechanisms both at early and late stages of HIV-1 replication and is a multistage inhibitor (Figure 44). LEN binds directly to the interface between capsid protein subunits. Lenacapavir inhibits HIV-1 replication by interfering with multiple essential steps of the viral lifecycle, including capsid-mediated nuclear uptake of HIV-1 proviral DNA (by blocking nuclear import proteins binding to capsid), virus assembly and release (by interfering with Gag/Gag-Pol functioning, reducing production of capsid protein subunits), and capsid core formation (by disrupting the rate of capsid subunit association, leading to malformed capsids).

L3687: ## Antiviral Activity
L3688: The antiviral activity of a novel HIV-1 capsid inhibitor LEN was evaluated using a 5-day cytopathic assay in the MT-4 T-lymphoblastoid cell line acutely infected with HIV-1IIIb (Report PC-200-2018). In parallel, the cytotoxicity of LEN was assessed in corresponding uninfected MT-4 cells. LEN had an EC50 value of 0.19nM in MT-4 cells and a selectivity index (50% cytotoxic concentration [CC50]/EC50) of 140,000. In addition, the EC95 value of LEN in MT-4 cells was calculated as 0.23nM from the EC50 value and Hill slope values that were accurately determined from a 40-point dose response curve. Taking into account the human serum shift determined by equilibrium dialysis (AD-200-2020), LEN exhibited a plasma protein binding-adjusted EC95 (paEC95) value of 4nM.
L3689: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3690: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3691: The antiviral activity of LEN was evaluated in acutely infected human CD4+ T-lymphocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages from three independent donors using 7- and 12-day virus production assays, respectively (Report PC-200-2019). In parallel, the cytotoxicity of LEN was determined in these cells. In CD4+ T lymphocytes, LEN had a mean EC50 and CC50 values of 0.06 nM and &gt;50\muM, respectively, with a selectivity index of &gt;833,330. LEN had mean EC50 and CC50 values of 0.03nM and &gt;50\muM, respectively, in monocyte-derived macrophages with a selectivity index of &gt;1,670,000. In comparison, the EC50 values of LEN in primary CD4+ T cells and macrophages were lower compared to control INSTI dolutegravir and PI atazanavir.
L3692: When LEN was tested against HIV-1NL4-3 in CEM-NKR CCR5+Luc+ T-lymphoblastoid cells infected with a wide range of multiplicities of infection (MOIs; 0.01 to 1.25), there was antiviral activity at all tested MOIs (Report PC-200-2031). EC50 values increased as MOI increased, with EC50 values ranging from 0.028 to 0.455nM (16-fold increase) across the 125-fold range.
L3693: ## **Antiviral Activity Against Clinical Isolates**
L3694: The antiretroviral activity of LEN was tested against 23 clinical isolates of HIV-1 and two isolates of HIV-2 in freshly isolated human PBMCs (Report PC-200-2020). LEN showed antiviral activity against all tested HIV-1 clinical isolates representing all major subtypes with mean and median EC50 values of 0.05 and 0.04nM, respectively, and a range of EC50 values between 0.02 and 0.16nM (Table 124). The range of means for subtype B isolates was 0.03 to 0.08nM and median was 0.04nM. LEN had lower activity against the two tested isolates of HIV-2 with EC50 values of 0.57 and 1.02nM, which is 4- to 50-fold.

L3702: In a separate study testing the activity of LEN against 40 clinical HIV-1 isolates of diverse subtypes using the PhenoSense Gag-Pro Antiviral Assay, there were no notable differences observed in the mean LEN EC50 values for any of the HIV-1 subtypes evaluated (Report PC-200-2041). L3710: ## **Activity of LEN Against HIV Capsid Protein Polymorphisms (Report PC-200-2032)**
L3711: A publicly available source of 10,512 capsid population sequences representing eight major HIV-1 subtypes was used to evaluate the conservation of the capsid protein and the LEN binding site (Table 126). Capsid consensus sequences across the eight subtypes were found to have &gt;91% sequence identity across the whole protein sequence. Of the 24 amino acid residues within the LEN binding site defined by x-ray crystallography, 20 residues (83%) had a sequence conservation between 94% and 100% across all 8 subtypes, including all 7 capsid amino acid positions associated with cell culture resistance to LEN (L56 [100%], M66 [100%], Q67 [99% for CRF01_AE, 100% for other subtypes], K70 [100%], N74 [100%], A105 [100%], and T107 [94-99%]). The CRF01_AE subtype contained a 1% prevalence of the Q67H substitution that confers ~6-fold resistance to LEN. None of the T107 substitutions identified was the T107N variant that is associated with reduced susceptibility to LEN. The T107N substitution conferring 4-fold resistance to LEN was identified in a single patient and was the only established LEN resistance-associated substitution detected in capsid by deep sequencing among the analyzed patient isolates.
L3712: The remaining four binding site residues (S41, T54, Y169, and Q179) were mutated in &gt;5% of patient isolates (n=104) and three of them (S41, T54, and Y169) were variable in &gt;25% of patient isolates in at least one major HIV-1 subtype. The impact of these identified substitutions on the susceptibility of isolates to LEN is assessed below.
L3713: Collectively, these data indicate a high degree of sequence conservation within the LEN binding site in HIV-1 capsid, which suggests a low-risk of capsid binding site polymorphisms having an impact on LEN antiviral efficacy.

L3722: The antiviral activity of LEN was measured against a panel of 36 site-directed HIV-1NL4.3 capsid mutants in MT-4 T-cells (Table 127). These capsid variants were comprised predominantly of LEN binding site polymorphisms (n=30) previously identified by population-level and higher
L3723: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3724: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3725: resolution next generation sequence analyses above. The 30 capsid polymorphisms spanned eight codons (S41, Q50, T54, N57, T107, Y169, L172, and N183) located within the LEN binding site as defined by x-ray cocrystallography, with asparagine 57 and, to a lesser extent, asparagine 183 providing important hydrogen bond interactions with LEN.
L3726: Ninety-three percent of the capsid polymorphisms (28/30) remained fully susceptible to LEN antiviral activity (0.7- to 2.4-fold change in susceptibility) (Report PC-200-2038). The remaining two capsid polymorphisms, Q50E and N57H, conferred low-level (3-fold) and high-level (&gt;5,000-fold) resistance, respectively, to LEN relative to wild-type virus while remaining fully susceptible to efavirenz and bictgravir. The Q50E and N57H variants, neither of which is selected for in cell culture with LEN, showed reduced infectivity in MT-4 cells (20% and 30% of wild-type, respectively) and were detected in HIV-1 at only 1% prevalence exclusively in either subtype C (Q50E) or subtype D (N57H) isolates.
L3727: Additionally, LEN was tested against six resistance-associated substitutions (S41A, K70R, H87P, L111I, V165I, and L172I) previously identified by cell culture selection with the Pfizer capsid inhibitor PF74 or its close analogue PF-3759857. These capsid inhibitors bind a site on capsid that partially overlaps with that of LEN. LEN retained full activity against five of the PF74-related resistance substitutions with susceptibility ranging from 1.1- to 1.6-fold. One substitution (V165I) could not be evaluated for potential LEN resistance due to a significant loss of HIV-1 infectivity (0.2% of wild-type).

L3743: ## **Inhibition of Early and Late HIV-1 Replication (Report PC-200-2021)**
L3744: The antiviral activity of LEN was evaluated in the MT-2 T-lymphoblastoid cell line using a single-cycle reporter assay. These assays were set up such that the compound was present selectively at the early stage, late stage, or during the full course of a single round of HIV infection. LEN had a mean EC50 value of 0.025nM against a single round infection of MT-2 cells with wild-type HIV-1 reporter virus (Table 128). In contrast, LEN had decreased antiviral activity against the capsid M66I resistant HIV-1 variant during a single round infection with an EC50 value &gt;50nM. LEN retained full antiviral efficacy when the presence of the compound was selectively restricted to the target cell infection phase with a mean early stage EC50 value of 0.023nM, indicating LEN predominately targets at least one essential capsid-mediated step involved in the early stages of HIV replication. However, even when restricted to the late stage in virus producer cells, LEN had a mean late stage EC50 value of 0.439nM with no cytotoxicity in the HEK293T producer cells up to the highest concentration tested (CC50 value &gt;50nM). Thus, LEN also targets with ~18-fold reduced activity late-stage capsid-mediated HIV replication functions. As controls, the INSTI raltegravir and the PI atazanavir showed a much more restricted antiviral effect specific only to the early and late stages of HIV replication, respectively. Finally, LEN was capable of irreversibly inactivating fully infectious cell-free HIV-1 with a mean EC50 value of 25nM. Collectively, these data show that LEN has antiviral activity against both early- and late-stage essential processes in the HIV-1 replication cycle.

L3746: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use

L3754: ## **Antiviral Activity of LEN Against Non-HIV Viruses**
L3755: LEN was tested against hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus, human rhinovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus in cell-based assays. LEN did not display selectivity in cell culture antiviral activity against HCV or HRV up to the highest concentration tested (44 to 50µM) (Table 129). LEN did demonstrate antiviral activity against HBV and respiratory syncytial virus at low micromolar concentrations, with EC50 values and corresponding CC50/EC50 ratios of 1.5µM and &gt;34, and 8.2µM and &gt;6.1, respectively. These data indicate that LEN is approximately 25,000-fold more active against HIV as compared to HBV. However, a proper clinically active therapy against HBV should be used in HIV/HBV coinfected patients to maintain the HBV suppression.

L3763: ## Cytotoxicity
L3764: The cytotoxicity of LEN was assessed in parallel uninfected MT-4 cultures. LEN showed low cytotoxicity in MT-4 cells with CC_{50} values of 26,600nM, yielding a selectivity index of 140,000 (Report PC-200-2018).
L3765: LEN showed mean CC_{50} values of &gt;50\mu M in both human CD4^+ T-lymphocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages giving selectivity indices of &gt;833,330 (Report PC-200-2019). LEN cytotoxicity was measured in normal resting and activated human PBMCs, demonstrating a lack of cytotoxicity, with CC_{50} values of &gt;44 and &gt;50\mu M, respectively.
L3766: LEN was tested for cytotoxicity in a panel of four human cell lines nonpermissive to HIV-1 infection, including two hepatoma cell lines (Huh7 and HepG2), a prostate carcinoma cell line (PC-3) and a normal embryonic lung fibroblast line (MRC-5) (Report PC-200-2028). The HepG2 and PC-3 cells used in this study were galactose-adapted for enhanced sensitivity to mitochondria toxicity (Marroquin et al. 2007). LEN did not display any significant cytotoxicity against the four tested cell lines. CC_{50} values for LEN in the tested cell types were &gt;44\mu M. Relative to its EC_{50} value for anti-HIV-1 activity in primary human CD4^+ T-lymphocytes (EC_{50} 0.06nM), a selectivity index of &gt;730,000 was achieved for LEN in all cell types tested. Puromycin was used as a positive control and showed CC_{50} values of 0.3 to 1.0\mu M.
L3767: In addition to these cell lines, the cytotoxicity of LEN was tested in primary human hepatocytes from three independent donors. LEN yielded CC_{50} values &gt;50\mu M in primary hepatocytes following a 5-day incubation with the tested compounds, while CC_{50} values for the positive control puromycin ranged from 0.93 to 2.10\mu M in these cells.
L3768: ## Antiviral Combination Activity in Cell Culture
L3769: The anti-HIV-1 activity of LEN was examined in combination with representative inhibitors from four major classes of antiretrovirals comprising the INSTI dolutegravir, the NNRTI efavirenz, the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) tenofovir alafenamide, and the HIV protease inhibitor (PI) darunavir. Pair-wise combinations of LEN with dolutegravir, efavirenz, tenofovir alafenamide, or darunavir showed synergistic anti-HIV activity when tested using HIV-1_{III B}-infected MT-2 cells (Table 130). No antagonistic antiviral interaction was observed between LEN and any of the clinically approved anti-HIV drugs tested.

L3778: ## Resistance Selection
L3779: Selection for HIV-1 variants resistant to LEN was performed in cell culture using two approaches (Report PC-200-2025). In the first approach, resistance selection using an increasing concentration method was performed with LEN in MT-2 cells infected with clonal HIV-1HXB2D. Parallel resistance selections were performed in the presence of efavirenz and elvitegravir as comparative controls and in the absence of drug. The kinetics of resistance emergence was similar among all three compounds early in the selection, but then LEN progressed more slowly relative to efavirenz and elvitegravir as drug concentrations were increased (Figure 45).

L3781: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3782: **Figure 45. Dose Escalation Resistance Selections With LEN, Efavirenz (EFV), and Elvitegravir (EVG) in MT-2 Cells**
L3783: Resistance selections were initiated at a drug concentration equal to 1x the EC50 determined for each drug (i.e., EC50 = 0.070 nM, 0.9 nM and 1.0 nM for GS-6207, EFV and EVG, respectively). Whenever extensive CPE was observed in the cell culture, the viral supernatant was harvested and a 100 \muL aliquot was used to infect fresh MT-2 cells in the presence of 1x and 2x the previously tested drug concentration.

L3786: At lower LEN drug pressure (8- to 16-fold the EC50), LEN selected for virus encoding the capsid substitution N74D (Table 131). At higher drug concentrations, LEN selected for virus encoding the dual capsid mutant N74D+T107N (passage 6), which was immediately replaced in the next passage by another dual capsid variant Q67H+N74D, which persisted to the end of selection after 103 days in culture at LEN concentrations 512-fold the EC50. These substitutions are located in the LEN binding site defined by X-ray crystallography. Clonal sequencing results confirmed that the Q67H and T107N substitutions were each individually linked to the N74D substitution on the same viral genome. Additional sequencing of the matrix and SP1 regions adjacent to the capsid gene, as well as the viral protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase coding regions, showed no additional genotypic changes relative to the HXB2D parental sequence.

L3795: The passage 4 (P4) virus selected with 0.56nM LEN (8× EC50) and encoding the capsid N74D substitution showed 5.5-fold reduction in susceptibility to LEN with no change in susceptibility to EFV, dolutegravir, EVG, or atazanavir. L3796: In the second approach, resistance selection was conducted in MT-2 cells infected with HIV-1HXB2D using a 10-fold higher MOI and several fixed concentrations of LEN (0.92, 1.9, 3.7, 5.5, and 9.2nM) over a 32-day selection. These test concentrations correspond to tissue culture equivalent (IQs of 4, 8, 16, 24, and 40, respectively, with an IQ of 1 defined as a concentration corresponding to the EC95 for LEN (0.23nM)). The rate and frequency of viral breakthrough for fixed LEN concentrations was compared to that of emtricitabine, efavirenz, rilpivirine, and atazanavir, with each used at a fixed drug concentration equal to their respective tissue culture equivalent (i.e. adjusted for protein binding) of the clinical plasma trough concentration (Cmin). At a fixed concentration of 0.92nM LEN (IQ of 4), a replicating virus emerged in three of eight independent infected samples tested and each isolate encoded the capsid N74D substitution identified at low LEN concentrations. No breakthrough virus emerged at any of the higher concentrations of LEN tested here. In comparison, parallel selections with emtricitabine and rilpivirine resulted in rapid emergence of the M184I/V variants in seven of eight samples and a breakthrough of the Y181I RT variant in one of eight infected samples tested, respectively, while selections with efavirenz, atazanavir and dolutegravir each did not lead to any breakthrough of drug-resistant HIV-1 variants.
L3797: Viral breakthrough selections were also conducted over a period of 35 days using a similar set of LEN and control test concentrations in human PBMCs infected separately with six different patient-derived isolates of HIV-1. Four weeks into these selections, an aliquot (1/10th) of the cell-free culture supernatants was transferred onto fresh target cells and cultured for another
L3798: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3799: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3800: 7 days to enrich for HIV-1 breakthrough variants that retained significant infectivity and replication capacity in the presence of each tested drug. Day 35 cell-free culture supernatants were harvested and analyzed for the presence of breakthrough virus by measuring the presence of virus by p24 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and virus infectivity on CEM-NKr CCR5+Luc+ indicator cells.
L3801: Among the six analyzed HIV-1 isolates, dolutegravir was the only compound to completely suppress viral breakthrough. Emtricitabine, rilpivirine and efavirenz each showed some frequency of viral breakthrough in PBMCs against the six tested isolates, with clinically relevant mutant HIV-1 variants emerging. At an IQ of 4, LEN showed a breakthrough better than emtricitabine and comparable to rilpivirine. Within its projected human plasma exposure range (IQ 4 to 8), LEN breakthrough viruses encoded the capsid substitutions L56I, or Q67H±N74S, N74D, or T107N. At IQ 16 and IQ 24 equivalent LEN concentrations, N74D and Q67H single capsid substitutions were less frequently observed and instead, the emergent viruses encoded capsid substitutions L56I, M66I, K70N or M66I+Q67H.
L3802: ## **Assessment of Site-Directed Resistance Mutants**
L3803: The antiviral activity of LEN was tested against 11 site-directed HIV-1 mutants encoding the major p24 domain substitutions identified in the drug selection studies including both single and double capsid mutants (L56I, M66I, Q67H, K70N, N74D, T107N, M66I/Q67H, Q67H/N74D, Q67H/N74S, Q67H/T107N, and N74D/T107N) (Report PC-200-2026). Antiviral activity was tested using both single-cycle and multi-round infection assays performed in the MT-2 and CEM-NKR CCR5+Luc+ T cell lines, respectively. In the single-cycle infection assay, mutant viruses, Q67H and T107N, conferred 4- to 6.3-fold decreased susceptibility to LEN relative to the wild-type virus; K70N, N74D and Q67H/N74S conferred 22- to 32-fold decreased LEN susceptibility; and L56I and M66I, as well as each of the remaining four double mutant viruses, all conferred 58- to &gt;3,226-fold decreased LEN susceptibility (Table 132). LEN showed 8.8-fold and 21-fold reduced activity, respectively, against the Q67Y and A105E substitutions previously identified upon drug selection with structurally similar analogs of LEN but not with LEN itself.
L3804: In addition to these drug resistant variants, HIV-1 containing the capsid P90A site-directed substitution conferring loss of host cyclophilin A binding to capsid was also studied. This P90A variant remained fully susceptible to inhibition by LEN in MT-2 cells indicating LEN inhibits HIV replication independent of cyclophilin A binding to capsid. The replication kinetics of the major drug resistant capsid variants was investigated in parallel with wild-type virus over a period of 19 days in primary human CD4+ T cells and in monocyte-derived macrophages. With the exception of the Q67H substitution, each capsid mutant that was tested displayed severely diminished replication capacity relative to the wild-type virus in both cell types. Moreover, the replicative fitness of these mutants was not significantly improved in the presence of LEN in either cell type.

L3813: Phenotypic resistance to the mutant variants was similar between the single-cycle and multi-round replication assays except the magnitude of fold-resistance to LEN appeared to be ~3-fold lower in the multi-round assays relative to the single-cycle assays.
L3814: The effect of the major LEN-resistant substitutions on HIV-1 replication capacity was investigated in parallel with WT HIV-1 over a period of 19 days in primary human CD4+ T cells and in monocyte-derived macrophages. The Q67H variant displayed 87 to 100% replicative capacity in CD4+ T lymphocytes and ~60% in monocyte-derived macrophages through 19 days. The L56I mutant had low replication fitness (3 to 14%) in T lymphocytes but 44 to 57% in macrophages. The other capsid mutants tested displayed diminished replication capacity in one or both of the primary target cells tested, with the N74D and Q67H/N74D showing the most diminished replication fitness (&lt;5%). In general, these mutants were less fit in primary CD4+ T cells (0.03 to 28%) than in monocyte-derived macrophages (1.9 to 72%) over the 19 days in culture. The degree of replicative rescue observed in the presence of the LEN compound in both cell types was marginal for all tested mutants.

L3842: ## **Antiviral Activity Against Treatment-Experienced and -Naïve Patient Isolates**
L3843: The antiviral activity of LEN was tested against a panel of treatment-experienced and treatment-naïve HIV-1 patient isolates that contained naturally occurring gag polymorphisms. Fifty-one patient-derived isolates comprising 36 treatment-experienced (TE) and 15 treatment-naïve (TN) were cloned into pXXLAI, and their drug susceptibilities to capsid inhibitor (LEN), protease inhibitors (atazanavir, darunavir), and investigational protease cleavage site inhibitors (bevirimat, GSK-3532795) were measured in the multicycle HIV-1 assay in MT-2 cells.
L3844: The cloned Gag and protease fragment sequence of the isolates were assessed for the presence of resistance-associated substitutions of PIs, capsid inhibitors (CAI), and protease cleavage site inhibitors (Report PC-200-2036). None of the TE or TN isolates contained CAI resistance substitutions. A majority of the TE isolates (94%) harbored primary PI resistance substitutions while none were found in the TN isolates. Most TE (81%) and TN (93%) isolates contained naturally occurring gag polymorphisms associated with protease cleavage site inhibitor resistance (V362I, Q369H, V370A/M/I, T371Q/Del/S). In both TN and TE isolates, LEN exhibited average EC50 values of 88 and 89pM, respectively, with minimal variability across all isolates. In contrast, the investigational protease cleavage site inhibitors bevirimat and GSK-3532795, showed 40- to 94-fold reduced activity in both TN and TE isolates, reflecting the occurrence of naturally existing gag polymorphisms associated with resistance to the cleavage site inhibitor class (Table 134). Resistance to the PIs atazanavir and darunavir was higher in TE isolates as expected in the presence of PI resistance substitutions, with mean fold-change EC50 above wild-type of 21 and 34, respectively, compared to fold-change of 1.0 for both drugs in TN isolates (Table 134). The NRTI control compound showed wild-type susceptibility across all isolates, reflective of the wild-type reverse transcriptase sequence.
L3845: LEN displayed wild-type-WT-like activity against the panel of patient isolates, regardless of the level of previous exposure to antiretroviral therapy in these patients. The antiviral activity of LEN was not affected by the presence of naturally occurring Gag polymorphisms and prior treatment experience with PI resistance did not alter the antiviral activity of LEN.

L3854: ## **Antiviral Activity of LEN Against HIV Gag Cleavage Site Polymorphisms**
L3855: The antiviral activity of LEN was tested against a panel of site-directed mutant viruses (n=19) and HIV-1 isolates from TE people living with HIV (PLWH) (TE; n=24) containing Gag cleavage site polymorphism substitutions with or without protease inhibitor resistance (Report PC-200-2037). Substitutions at the capsid/SP1 cleavage site (L363F/M, A364V) have been associated with resistance to investigational protease cleavage site inhibitors, such as bevirimat. Substitutions at the NC/SP2 (Q430R, A431V, K436E/S, I437T/V) and SP2/p6 (L449H/V/F, P453L) cleavage sites are associated with resistance to PIs.
L3856: Drug susceptibilities of the capsid inhibitor (LEN), protease cleavage site inhibitors (bevirimat, GSK-3532795), and PIs (atazanavir, darunavir) were assessed in the multicycle HIV-1 assay in MT-2 cells. LEN showed wild-type activity with an average EC50 value of 102pM across all 19 mutants, with fold-changes from wild-type ranging from 0.7 to 1.9. Reduced susceptibility (&gt;5-fold) to bevirimat and GSK-3532795, was seen with substitutions at positions 363 and 364, as expected.
L3857: ## **Susceptibility of LEN Site-Directed Mutants to PIs and Protease Cleavage Site Inhibitors**
L3858: The antiviral activity of LEN, PIs, and protease cleavage site inhibitors was tested in a multicycle HIV-1 antiviral assay in MT-2 cells against a panel of twelve site-directed mutants (SDM) viruses containing LEN resistance substitutions selected in cell culture resistance experiments (Table 135). The antiviral activity of LEN, PIs, and protease cleavage site inhibitors was tested in a multicycle HIV-1 antiviral assay in MT-2 cells against a panel of twelve site-directed mutants viruses containing LEN resistance substitutions selected in cell culture resistance experiments (Table 135). Data were obtained for only seven of twelve site-directed mutants, and showed that relative susceptibility to LEN ranged from 4.1- to 306-fold change (mean 52.3-fold) in these mutants compared to the wild type virus in the multicycle assay, which correlated well with LEN phenotypic data obtained for these mutants in a single-cycle assay.
L3859: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3860: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3861: Drug susceptibility for the remaining five site-directed mutants could not be evaluated, as the mutants did not show adequate infectivity in this multicycle HIV-1 antiviral assay, consistent with the reduced replication capacity previously observed for these mutants in single cycle HIV-1 antiviral experiments. Susceptibility of site-directed mutants to the PIs atazanavir, darunavir, nelfinavir, and saquinavir was similar to the wild-type control (mean FC of 1.2, 1.2, 1.0, and 1.2, respectively), indicating a lack of cross-resistance to PIs in these LEN-resistant mutants. Susceptibility of site-directed mutants to the protease cleavage site inhibitors was similar to that of the wild-type virus, indicating the absence of cross-resistance.

L3938: ## Next-Generation Sequencing Analysis
L3939: An independent assessment was performed by Dr. Eric Donaldson, clinical virology reviewer, using the next-generation sequencing data derived from subjects in clinical Study 4625 who were determined to be treatment failures (note: this analysis included eight subjects from Cohort 2).
L3940: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3941: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3942: The independent analysis compared the capsid gene changes from baseline and postbaseline samples for each virologic failure subject to determine if treatment-emergent substitutions could be detected. Different capsid sequences were used as references for the mapping of capsid genes from different HIV-1 genotypes and subgroups, including 1) AE (n=2), HIV-1 isolate M114 subtype CRF01_AE from Thailand (DQ354117.1); 2) B (n=16), HIV-1 isolate JRFL from USA (U63632.1); and 3) BF (n=1), HIV-1 isolate CH80 subtype BF from Chile (FJ358521.1).
L3943: Fastq files for all samples from virologic failures in clinical Study 4625 were mapped to reference sequences using the CLC Genomics Workbench. Variants were detected using the Low Frequency Variant Caller. Substitutions associated with treatment were detected by comparing baseline samples to post-baseline samples and identifying substitutions that were not detected at baseline (frequency &lt;3%) but were detected at later timepoints in multiple subjects and at frequencies \ge5%.

L3951: Among subjects treated with LEN who were infected with subtype B HIV-1, treatment-emergent substitutions in the capsid occurred in two or more subjects at five positions, including substitutions N21S (n=2, low frequency), M66I (n=5, treatment-emergent at &gt;20% in all subjects), Q67H (n=3, treatment-emergent at &gt;20% in all subjects), K70R (n=3, treatment-emergent at &gt;25% in two subjects), and A105T (n=3, treatment-emergent at &gt;35% in two subjects).
L3952: ## Exploratory Analysis of Other Capsid Substitutions
L3953: The subjects in Cohort 1 of Study 4625 were analyzed for presence at screening and postbaseline of LEN capsid binding site variants including polymorphisms (S41, Q50, T54, N57, T107, Y169, L172, and N183) and six resistance-associated substitutions (S41A, K70R, H87P, L111I, V165I, and L172I) previously identified by cell culture selection with the Pfizer capsid inhibitor PF74 or its close analogue PF-3759857 (Table 141). No subjects in Cohort 1 had substitutions at N57, K70, L111, V165, Y169, or Q179 at screening.
L3954: - Of the 10 subjects with substitution S41T or A at screening in the phase 1A and 1B cohorts of the trial, 6 (60%) were virologic failures. Phenotypic data for a site-directed mutant with S41T showed a 1.5-fold change (Table 141).
- Only one subject had the Q50A/S substitution at screening and this subject in the placebo cohort was a virologic failure at Week 26. Site-directed mutant variant Q50E conferred low-level (3-fold) decreased susceptibility to LEN.
- Two subjects had T54M at screening, one in the placebo cohort was a success and the other in the LEN cohort was a virologic failure at Week 4. Phenotypic data for site-directed mutant with T54M showed a 1.3-fold change (Table 141).
- Six subjects had H87Q, 1 of 3 in placebo arm was a virologic failure and 1 of 3 in the LEN cohort was a virologic failure. Phenotypic data for a site-directed mutant with H87P showed a 1.1-fold change (Table 141).
- Four subjects had T107S at screening, (2 placebo and 2 LEN) and only one in the placebo cohort was a virologic failure. Phenotypic data for site-directed mutant with T107S showed a 1.3-fold change (Table 141).
L3955: NDA 215973 lenacapavir injection, for subcutaneous use
L3956: NDA 215974 lenacapavir tablets, for oral use
L3957: - Only one subject had L172L/I (LEN cohort) and this subject was a virologic failure. Phenotypic data for site-directed mutant with T107S showed a 1.6-fold change (Table 141).
L3958: These results are summarized in Table 141. The data are too limited to make definitive conclusions and no action is indicated regarding these substitutions in the package insert at this point. However, we note that S41T in combination with other polymorphisms (S41T+Q50A/S+T107S, S41T+T54M, S41T +H87Q) was associated with virologic failure and emergence of capsid resistance substitutions (Subjects (b) (6)).

L3970: ## 21. Data Integrity-Related Consults (Office of Scientific Investigations, Other Inspections)
L3971: Routine PDUFA inspections were completed by the Office of Scientific Investigations. The data from Studies 4625 and 4334 submitted to the Agency in support of NDAs 215973 and 215974, appear reliable based on available information. Please also refer to Section II.10 for a list of clinical sites.
L3972: Clinical site inspections were conducted for two clinical investigators, Drs. DeJesus and Ruane. The inspections covered one clinical trial, Protocol GS-US-200-4625. Overall, the study appears to have been conducted adequately, and the data generated by these two sites appear acceptable in support of the respective indication.
L3973: During the inspections, the primary efficacy endpoint source data (i.e., the HIV-1 RNA test results at baseline [Day 1] and at the end of the functional monotherapy period [Day 15]) were verified against the Applicant's data line listings for all subjects randomized at the two sites selected for inspection. No discrepancies were noted.
L3974: Important enrollment and other protocol deviations were noted for three of the five subjects enrolled at Dr. DeJesus' site (Site 00698). These protocol deviations are not likely to have an impact on the overall study results.
