L3980: ## 23. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L3981: The following postmarketing requirements (PMRs) were considered:
L3982: - Pediatric Research Equity Act PMR-1: Conduct a study to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, safety, and antiviral activity (efficacy) of lenacapavir in treatment-experienced children living with HIV-1 infection who are less than 18 years of age and weighing at least 35 kg. The safety and antiviral activity of lenacapavir in pediatric subjects must be evaluated for a minimum of 24 weeks.
- Injection site reactions PMR-2: Submit final study reports from Studies 4625 and 4334. Assessments of adverse events related to injection site reactions must be followed until resolution or until study completion.
- Carcinogenicity PMR-3: Submit final study report from a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study.
- Carcinogenicity PMR-4: Submit final study report from the 13-week mouse carcinogenicity study.
L3983: PMRs are not applicable for these applications, however, because the recommended approval action is a complete response.

L4064: Re: DDD Consult #2116: Lenacapavir (NDA 215973, NDA 215974)
L4065: Lenacapavir (LEN) is currently under review as an NME under two NDAs, 215973 [injectable (SC) (b) (4)] and 215974 (tablets). The proposed indication by the Applicant is (b) (4)
L4066: Injection site reactions (ISRs) were the most common adverse reaction with lenacapavir subcutaneous injection. Based on preclinical histology in rats, rabbits and dogs these reactions were observed to be inflammatory granulomas. DAV is requesting DDD advice regarding the need for additional safety data regarding these reactions and any recommendations for communication of ISRs in labeling.

L4076: - DDD recommends that in ongoing trials, where possible, injection site nodules be followed to resolution or stabilization. In addition, DDD recommends that human histopathology be obtained (e.g., punch biopsy in a few subjects). L4077: the pathophysiology of nodule formation. This in turn can increase understanding of which treatments are most likely to be useful.
L4078: ## **Background:**
L4079: ## **From Consult Request:**
L4080: Background: "Lenacapavir (LEN) is currently under review as an NME under two NDAs. NDA-215973 [REDACTED](b) (4), and documentation for LEN tablets is included in NDA-215974 with cross-reference to NDA 215973). The proposed indication is for treatment of heavily treatment experienced patients with HIV-1 infection. The proposed regimen is 927 mg by subcutaneous injection (2 x 1.5 mL injections) with an oral lead-in, followed by maintenance with 927 mg by subcutaneous injection (2 x 1.5 mL injections) every 6 months (26 weeks).
L4081: Injection site reactions were the most common adverse reaction with lenacapavir subcutaneous injection. Based on preclinical histology in rats, rabbits and dogs these reactions were observed to be inflammatory granulomas. Our concern is that injection site nodules and indurations were not all completely resolved by the primary data safety cut with at least 26 weeks interim follow-up in Study GS-US-200-4625, and among the resolved reports, were approximately 1-4 cm at maximum size and lasting several weeks/months.
L4082: The sponsor has provided additional safety data in response to our information requests based on data from Study GS-US-200-4625 and a supportive study, Study GS-US-200-4334. Anecdotally, in lower body fat individuals, investigators had more difficulty finding adequate injection sites and nodules were more pronounced (see photographs provided in response to our Question 4 in their response: SDN 9, m1.11.3).
L4083: Several formulations were evaluated (e.g., in Study GS-US-200-4538, with free acid, sodium salt, [REDACTED](b) (4)), and the sponsor chose a sodium salt solution (solvent: PEG 300) with a high pH ([REDACTED](b) (4)) as the final proposed drug product. The kits include 22G ½ inch needles provided for the injections."

L4085: ## **Histopathology:**
L4086: ## **Clinical Histopathology:**
L4087: There is no human histopathology included in the pivotal Phase 2/3 trial (GS-US-200-4625) to support NDA 215973.
L4088: ## **Nonclinical Histopathology:**
L4089: The Applicant notes that nonclinical studies of rats (TX-200-2014), rabbits (TX-200-2033) and dogs (TX-200-2047) showed microscopic findings of granulomatous inflammation at subcutaneous (SC) injection sites. The Applicant notes further that granulomatous inflammation has been observed after SC and intramuscular implantation of bioactive material, including those for HIV treatment and concludes that inflammation and foreign body response to the lenacapavir (LEN) SC depot is an expected host response. (IR response received 9/23/2021, p. 12)
L4090: ## **Discussion of Injection Site Reactions/Nodules:**
L4091: Injection site reactions are a local phenomenon defined as a constellation of symptoms, that can include swelling, erythema, pruritus, and pain around the site of injection. Injection site reactions
L4092: can be divided into two groups according to their mechanism of action: irritative reactions (immediate) and allergic reactions (immediate or delayed) to the excipient or to the drug itself.1 Allergic or hypersensitivity reactions are induced by IgE, IgG/IgM, complement or T cells and can be categorized into Types I-IV.
L4093: There was no standardized definition of nodule or induration provided to Investigators for the pivotal clinical trial, GS-US-200-4625 or for the supportive trial, GS-US-200-4334.
L4094: The Applicant, however, has included the following definitions of induration and nodule in Injection site manuals for the Phase 1 trials: GS-US-4070, GS-US-200-4538. (IR response received 10/26/2021, pp. 41/65 and 49/65)
L4095: **Induration:** (Palpable thickening, firmness, or hardening of soft tissue). Usually well demarcated with palpable borders, can be visible (raised or sunken compared to surrounding skin), is often 'woody' to touch and has a flat shape (versus the rounder shape of a nodule); it can best be described by palpation.2
L4096: **Nodule:** Discrete or well-demarcated soft tissue mass or lump that is firm.3
L4097: ## **Specifically, regarding injection site nodules:**
L4098: In the literature injection site nodules have been reported with a number of drug products.
L4099: One class of drug products includes glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists used for treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes. General injection-site reactions (e.g., erythema, pain, or rash) have been reported with all of the commercially available GLP-1 receptor agonists (i.e., exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide).4
L4100: Though not common, a number of cases of injection site nodules have been reported with use of exenatide extended-release. Jones et al (2015) reviewed FAERS reports of injection site nodules associated with use of exenatide-extended release and reviewed published cases. They found that exenatide extended-release-associated injection-site reactions may induce large nodule formation and, in isolated cases, may require hospitalization, surgical excision, or some other medical

L4105: intervention to mitigate.1 Riswald and Flynn (2018)2 reported the case of a 60-year-old man who presented with 6 large, persistent nodules of the abdomen and left thigh, occurring after each of his exenatide extended-release weekly injections. A nodule that was treated with serial intralesional triamcinolone injections showed significant improvement obviating the need for multiple surgical procedures.
L4106: The specific mechanism by which exenatide extended-release can cause serious injection-site nodules is not entirely clear. The clinical description of some cases is consistent with a hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., local induration, warmth, and pruritus). Available histopathology data reveal the presence of eosinophils and granuloma in these sites, and therefore hypersensitivity to the formulation may be one plausible mechanism.3
L4107: Hearn and Sherman (2021)4 report a case of injection-site nodules associated with semaglutide injected subcutaneously once-weekly. The patient did not experience nodules until reaching the appropriately titrated maximum dose 6 weeks after therapy initiation. The authors state that this delay in adverse reaction supports the hypotheses of antibody or eosinophilic response. Such responses occur most commonly after multiple exposures over time. The nodules were reported to be quarter-sized, hard, erythematous, pruritic, and raised, appearing within minutes of injection and typically disappearing within 2 to 4 days. The case report did not include histopathology.
L4108: Ko et al (2020)5 report a case of eosinophilic panniculitis by histopathology in a patient developing a nodule on the thigh over the period of a week after exenatide extended-release injection. The nodule was described as “tender.”
L4109: Subcutaneous nodules at the injection site may occur following use of a wide range of vaccines.
L4110: Miliauskas and Mukherjee (1993)6 reported on four patients having a single subcutaneous nodule at the site of a previous vaccine injection. Three nodules occurred after injection of diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccination and one after tetanus toxoid vaccination. Presentation was with a mass 4-22 months after vaccination at the site of injection. Histologically, three patients had a necrotizing granulomatous reaction with a surrounding infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes, and associated fibrosis. The fourth patient demonstrated a lymphohistiocytic reaction with a predominance of histiocytic cells as well as associated plasma cells, fibroblasts, and fibrosis. The lymphoid infiltration in these reactions showed a predominance of T-lymphocytes versus B-lymphocytes. Aluminum was demonstrated in necrotic foci, inflammatory stroma, and the granular

L4117: cytoplasm of histiocytes. The reactions are thought to be immunologic or hypersensitivity reactions associated with the aluminum contents of the preparation.
L4118: Silcock et al (2020)1 studied subcutaneous nodules following immunization in children in Victoria Australia. They found that nodules were associated with immunizations containing aluminum (74%, 36/49 nodules), no aluminum (8%, 4 nodules) and unknown (18%, 9 nodules). Most cases developed symptoms within 3 days postimmunization (59%, 24 cases). Pruritus was associated in 41% (17 cases). Around 1/3 (34%) of nodules resolved 6 months post immunization, 2/3 (68%) by 12 months, however 1/4 (24%) remained persistent for &gt;24 months. Five cases had prior nodules and 1 case had recurrence with subsequent immunization. Eighty-three % (34 cases) were fully immunized for age at follow-up.
L4119: In a discussion of literature, the authors note that the injection method likely contributes to nodule development in immunization, with inadvertent subcutaneous injection associated with high rates of nodules. The subcutaneous injection is associated with greater local inflammatory reaction compared to intramuscular (IM) delivery. This is supported by evidence that longer needle length reduces immunization reactogenicity, to ensure vaccine delivery to an intramuscular location despite variations in individual delivery technique.
L4120: Other drug classes reported to be associated with injection site nodules include low-molecular weight heparin and gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists used to treat prostate cancer.
L4121: Val and Val-Bernal (2014)2 reported on a subcutaneous infiltrative nodule occurring at the injection site of low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH). They describe a 23-year-old woman having a 3.8-cm solitary, fibrofatty, poorly demarcated nodule involving the subcutaneous tissue of the infraumbilical abdominal wall. The nodule appeared 4 years after repeated local administration of LMWH. Microscopically, the nodule showed atypical cells, with bizarre nuclei in the septa of cellular fibrous tissue dissecting the adipose lobules, in the absence of any other malignant changes. The authors speculate that the lesion may result from the combination of an idiosyncratic reaction to the LMWH with local trauma being a probable promoting factor. Alternatively, they state that the reactive proliferation may be entirely due to the trauma represented by repeated injections.
L4122: Shiota et al. (2007)3 described injection-site granulomas resulting from the administration of both leuprolerin acetate (Leuprolide acetate Eligard) and goserelin acetate (Zoladex) for the treatment of prostatic cancer. The authors noted that injection-site granulomas caused by leuprolerin acetate had been previously reported. They present the case of an 81-year-old man having subcutaneous nodules of the abdominal wall and upper arm, where 11.25 mg of leuprolerin acetate had been injected for the treatment of prostate cancer. Because of these nodules, treatment was changed to goserelin acetate. Nevertheless, the patient developed another subcutaneous nodule at the injection
L4123: 1Silcock R, Crawford NW, Selvaraj G, McMinn A, Danchin M, Lazzaro T, Perrett KP. Subcutaneous nodules following immunization in children; in Victoria, Australia from 2007 to 2016. *Vaccine*. 2020 Mar 30;38(15):3169-3177. doi: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2019.12.066. Epub 2020 Mar 5. PMID: 32147295.

L4126: site. Histological examination showed that these nodules consisted of CD3- positive T lymphocytes and CD68-positive histiocytes associated with granulomatous changes. The authors state that the granulomas had likely been caused by delayed-type hypersensitivity to leuporelin acetate injection. They state further that the granuloma that formed after goserelin acetate injection might have developed owing to the immunogenicity of the previous leuporelin acetate injections.
L4127: ## **FDA Approved Drug Product Labeling:**
L4128: Approved FDA labeling for a number of drug products includes the adverse reaction of injection site nodules. For some products information regarding injection site nodules is present in Warnings and Precautions. Among the most extensive descriptions of injection site nodules occurs in approved FDA labeling for exenatide injection, suspension, extended-release product **BYDUREON BCISE**® (see Appendix B).
L4129: ## **Regarding the current NDAs under review: 215973, 215974**
L4130: The primary study that supports the safety and efficacy of LEN is the Phase 2/3 study in HTE (heavily treatment experienced) PWH (Study GS-US-200-4625), which is further supported by a Phase 2 study of LEN in treatment-naive PWH (Study GS-US-200-4334).
L4131: Supportive safety data are also provided from 2 Phase 1 studies in healthy participants (Studies GS-US-200-4538 and GS-US-200-5709); these Phase 1 studies also contributed to the characterization of the pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of LEN and its metabolites, supporting the clinical pharmacology of LEN and the dosing interval.
L4132: The primary data (for establishing safety and efficacy) is based on 26-week data from **GS-US-200-4625** (CAPELLA), described by the Applicant as a “partially randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind multicenter trial.” The proposed indication, as of the time of this consult (11/30/21 – labeling sent to applicant 11/23/2021), is “the treatment of (HIV-1) infection in heavily treatment experienced adults with multidrug resistant HIV-1 infection failing their current antiretroviral regimen due to resistance, intolerance, or safety considerations.”
L4133: Trial **GS-US-200-4625** was conducted 31 sites in 9 countries (US, Thailand, Italy, Dominican Republic, Spain, France, Canada, Taiwan, and South Africa).
L4134: The trial was composed of two cohorts. Subjects were enrolled into the randomized cohort (Cohort 1) if they had a &lt; 0.5 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA decline compared to the screening visit. Subjects were enrolled into the non-randomized cohort (Cohort 2) if they had a \ge 0.5 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA decline compared to the screening visit or after Cohort 1 reached its planned sample size.
L4135: **Cohort 1 (N=36, randomized):** In the 14-day functional monotherapy period, subjects in Cohort 1 were randomized in a 2:1 ratio in a blinded fashion to receive either drug product or placebo, while continuing their failing regimen. This period was to establish the virologic activity of the drug product. After the functional monotherapy period, subjects who had received drug product continued on drug product along with an optimized background regimen (OBR); subjects who had received placebo during this period were to initiate drug product along with an OBR (A regimen, at the discretion of the investigator, that has at least one fully active drug in addition to LEN).
L4136: **Cohort 2 (N=36, non-randomized):** Subjects in cohort 2 initiated drug product and an OBR on Day 1.
L4137: ## **Study Endpoints:**
L4138: The primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of subjects in Cohort 1 achieving \ge 0.5 \log_{10} copies/mL reduction from baseline in HIV-1 RNA at the end of the functional monotherapy period.
L4139: The secondary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of participants in Cohort 1 with plasma HIV-1 RNA &lt; 50 copies/mL and &lt; 200 copies/mL at Weeks 26 and 52 of treatment based on the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-defined snapshot algorithm
L4140: ## **Trial Outline:**
L4141: ## **Study Design Schema**
L4142: This trial design shows that there is no arm where active injected drug is compared with placebo injected drug. There are two enrolled cohorts: Cohort 1, if subjects had a &lt; 0.5 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA decline compared to the screening visit and Cohort 2, if subjects had a \ge 0.5 \log_{10} HIV-1 RNA decline compared to the screening visit or after Cohort 1 reached its planned sample size. Regarding Cohort 1, in the 14-day functional monotherapy period, subjects in Cohort 1 were randomized in a 2:1 ratio in a blinded fashion to receive either drug product or placebo, while continuing their failing regimen.
L4143: - **Cohort 1A** subjects received subcutaneous (SC) LEN on day 1 SC (14 days after 1st dose of oral LEN) and once every 6 months (26 weeks). Also initiate their OBR
- **Cohort 1B** subjects received placebo for 14 days, then oral LEN for and initiate their OBR on Day 15, then SC LEN at Day 1 SC (14 days after 1st dose of oral LEN and 28 days into trial) and once every 6 months (26 weeks).
- **Cohort 2**: received oral LEN for 14 days, then SC LEN at Day 1 SC (14 days after 1st dose of oral LEN) and once every 6 months (26 weeks).

L4157: ## 1.5 mL Injection Preparation and Administration Instructions:
L4158: 13. With one hand, pinch a fold of skin where the injection is to be given. The initial injection should be given in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. If a subject has a tattoo or scar in the right lower quadrant, another quadrant may be used. For the second injection, rotate injection site clockwise, ensuring the subsequent injection is at least 4 inches away from the previous injection site. For additional injections, rotate injection sites clockwise, ensuring subsequent injections are at least 4 inches away from the other injection site(s). The injection site location(s) should be noted in the source documents.

L4200: **Applicant's assessment of injection site reactions:** Response to IR of 10/12/2021 received 10/23/202, pp. 11, 12
L4201: "To summarize, we have conducted a comprehensive assessment of injection site reactions (ISRs) across the LEN program, including detailed review of individual cases with the investigators. Our overall assessment is as follows. In Studies GS-US-200-4625 and GS-US-200-4334, approximately half or fewer of the participants (55.6% and 38.8%, respectively) experienced at least 1 AEs of LEN-related ISRs, which were mostly non-serious, Grade 1 or 2, and rarely led to study drug discontinuation. Most AEs of ISRs resolved within days, but those of induration and nodules lasted longer (as described in Gilead's previous response, Seq 0008). These AEs of induration or nodules were generally small (less than a few centimeters), not visible to the participant or the investigator, not causing persistent discomfort to participants, and only detectable upon deep palpation. There were rarely any gross inflammatory components, such as tenderness or erythema, to these AEs of induration or nodules, and when there was coincident pain or erythema, they resolved quickly. There were no reports of tissue destruction (e.g. necrosis), or, upon careful review, suggestion of other more serious reactions such as sterile abscess or persistent tissue damage. No participants appeared to have any safety signal suggesting that LEN was being administered into a deeper tissue than the intended subcutaneous space (e.g. muscle). In written, verbal, and video communication with investigators who took care of participants with AEs of persistent induration or nodule, none were concerned with any potential long term permanent adverse effect, none felt the AEs required additional consultation (e.g. with a dermatologist), and all agreed that those AEs were resolving slowly over time. In general investigators commented on the benign nature of nodules, with some noting that nodules might be more visible in a person who is lean and self-conscious of body image."
L4202: ## **Nodules:**
L4203: "Based on the totality of Gilead's nonclinical assessment, the induration or nodules after SC LEN injection appears to be a normal and expected tissue body response, manifesting as chronic granulomatous inflammation histologically, to a foreign body (i.e. a drug depot) without permanent adverse effect. We have not found evidence of injection site nodules or induration being reflective of more serious complications, or resulting from aberrant injections, nor have we found evidence that nodules are related to body habitus or immunologic status .... The presence of injection site nodule or induration appears not to in any way diminish the efficacy of LEN. That assessment is also supported by the findings from the popPK modeling where LEN exposures were similar between participants with and without
L4204: injection site induration/nodules, indicating the lack of impact of induration/nodules on LEN release profile.... In summary, our assessment is that nodules that rise to the level of AE reporting occur in a subset of individuals receiving LEN, represent subcutaneous deposition of the drug itself and expected tissue reaction, and are not associated with adverse clinical or pharmacologic consequences."

L4225: ## **Location in labeling:**
L4226: It is noted that adverse reactions of injection site nodules were included in section 6.1 Clinical trials Experience and not in Warnings and Precautions. DDD agrees with the review division based on the following:
L4227: Nodules were all considered grade 1, and information on associated symptoms, where available, indicated that they were not serious. It is noted that one subject ( [REDACTED](b) (6) ) in Study GS-US-200-4625 prematurely discontinued study drug (day 379) due to treatment-emergent AEs of injection site nodules. The subject was a 56-year-old black female in the USA. The subject experienced an injection site nodule on Day 18 and on Day 380. Both nodules were Grade 1 (2.5 to &lt; 5 cm in diameter OR 6.25 to &lt; 25 cm2 surface area AND symptoms causing no or minimal interference with usual social and functional activities) and were ongoing (GS-US-200-4625, 90-Day Safety Update, Listing 4). The investigator reported that “the nodules were uncomfortable, and the subject did not want the nodules to return.” Although the subject withdrew due to injection site nodules available information does not indicate that the event was serious.
L4228: (Relevant criteria for Warnings and Precautions (per October 2011 Guidance for Industry: *Warnings and Precautions, Contraindications, and Boxed Warning Sections of Labeling for Human Prescription Drug and Biological Products – Content and Format*) include the following: Serious AEs: Death, Life-threatening AE, hospitalization, significant disruption of ability to conduct normal life functions, congenital anomaly; medical judgement may jeopardize patient. Indication; relative seriousness of condition, Incidence high absolute risk of AE; AE that could lead to serious outcome unless dosage changed, Preventable by patient selection to avoid potentially serious outcome, AE significantly affecting compliance.)
L4229: ## **Medication Guide:**
L4230: The DAV reviewer does not recommend inclusion of a Medication Guide since nodules, as a safety issue, did not satisfy criteria that would necessitate a Medication Guide. DDD agrees with the review division.
L4231: Per the Guidance of November 2011, Medication Guides – Distribution Requirements and Inclusion in Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS):
L4232: Section 208.1(c) authorizes FDA to require a Medication Guide if FDA determines one or more of the following circumstances exist: (1) The drug product is one for which patient labeling could help prevent serious adverse effects. (2) The drug product is one that has serious risk(s) (relative to benefits) of which patients should be made aware because information concerning the risks could affect patients' decision to use, or continue to use, the product. (3) The drug product is important to health and patient adherence to directions for use is crucial to the drug's effectiveness.
L4233: ## • **Additional DDD Recommendations for Ongoing or Future Trials:**
L4234: DDD recommends that for ongoing trials where possible that nodules be followed to resolution or stabilization. In addition, DDD recommends that human histopathology be obtained (e.g., punch biopsy in a few subjects). The presence of findings such as necrosis, hypersensitivity, granulomas, foreign bodies, fibrous tissue, etc. can aid in understanding the pathophysiology of nodule formation. This in turn can increase understanding of which treatments are most likely to be useful.

L4242: **5.9 Injection-Site Reactions** There have been postmarketing reports of serious injection-site reactions (e.g., abscess, cellulitis, and necrosis), with or without subcutaneous nodules, with the use of BYDUREON [see Adverse Reactions (6.3)]. Isolated cases required surgical intervention.

L4248: ## **Adverse Reactions Leading to Discontinuation of Therapy**
L4249: The incidence of discontinuation of therapy due to adverse reactions was 3.9% for BYDUREON BCISE-treated patients in the two comparator-controlled 28-week trials in adults. The most common classes of adverse reactions leading to discontinuation of therapy for BYDUREON BCISE-treated patients were Gastrointestinal Disorders 2.0% and General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions 1.2%. For BYDUREON BCISE-treated patients, the most frequent adverse reactions leading to discontinuation of therapy within each of these respective classes were diarrhea (0.7%), nausea (0.7%), vomiting (0.5%) and injection-site nodule (0.5%).
L4250: **Injection-Site Adverse Reactions** In the two comparator-controlled 28-week trials in adults, injection site reactions (including injection site nodule, injection site pruritus, injection site bruising) were observed in 23.9% of patients treated with BYDUREON BCISE. The formation of subcutaneous nodules is consistent with the properties of the microspheres used in BYDUREON BCISE.

L4255: ## **CABENUVA (cabotegravir extended-release injectable; rilpivirine extended-release injectable suspension), co-packaged for intramuscular use**
L4256: **Initial U.S. Approval: 2021**
L4257: ## **Section 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience**
L4258: ## **Injection-Associated Adverse Reactions**
L4259: *Local Injection Site Reactions (ISRs):* The most frequent adverse reactions associated with the intramuscular administration of CABENUVA were ISRs. After 14,682 injections, 3,663 ISRs were reported. One percent (1%) of subjects discontinued treatment with CABENUVA because of ISRs. Most ISRs were mild (Grade 1, 75%) or moderate (Grade 2, 36%). Four percent (4%) of subjects experienced severe (Grade 3) ISRs, and no subjects experienced Grade 4 ISRs. The most commonly reported ISR was localized pain/discomfort (79%) regardless of severity or relatedness. Other manifestations of ISRs reported in more than 1% of subjects over the duration of the analysis period included **nodules (14%)***, induration (12%), swelling (8%), erythema (4%), pruritus (4%), bruising (3%), warmth (2%), and hematoma (2%). Abscess and cellulitis at the injection site were each reported in less than 1% of subjects. The median duration of ISR events was 3 days.

L4281: BEST AVAILABLE COPY
Flowchart illustrating the Study Design Schema:
Screening leads to Cohort Selection visit (between 14 and 30 days after screening).
From the Cohort Selection visit, subjects are split based on HIV-1 RNA decline:
Cohort 1 (Blinded): Subjects with < 0.5 \log_{10} decline in HIV-1 RNA from Screening and HIV-1 RNA \ge 400 copies/mL. These subjects are randomized (standard to participant, investigator site and Sponsor) into two groups:Group 1 (n=24): 14-day Functional Monotherapy Period: Oral GS-6207 + Failing Regimen. Followed by Unblinding on Day 15, leading to 14-day oral dosing: Oral GS-6207 + OBR. This group then proceeds to Cohort 1A Maintenance (SC GS-6207 + Optimized Background Regimen (OBR)) from Day 1 SC to Week 52.
Group 2 (n=12): 14-day Functional Monotherapy Period: Placebo-to-match + Failing Regimen. Followed by Unblinding on Day 15, leading to 14-day oral dosing: Oral GS-6207 + OBR. This group then proceeds to Cohort 1B Maintenance (SC GS-6207 + OBR) from Day 1 SC to Week 52.

Cohort 2 (Non-randomized, Unblinded): Subjects with \ge 0.5 \log_{10} decline in HIV-1 RNA from Screening and/or HIV-1 RNA < 400 copies/mL. This group (n=54) proceeds to 14-day Oral Lead-in: Oral GS-6207 + OBR. This group then proceeds to Cohort 2 Maintenance (SC GS-6207 + OBR) from Day 1 SC to Week 52.

The X-axis ranges from 1 to 150 ng/mL, and the Y-axis ranges from 1.0 to 3.0 \log_{10} copies/mL. Data points are shown for five dose groups: GS 6207 20 mg (O), GS 6207 50 mg (+), GS 6207 150 mg (X), GS 6207 450 mg (\Delta), and GS 6207 750 mg (\square). L4325: Diagram illustrating the HIV-1 replication cycle and the essential capsid-mediated processes inhibited by LEN (Lenacapavir).
The cycle involves four main stages:
Assembly: In the PRODUCER CELL, Gag and Gag-Pol proteins are synthesized in the NUCLEUS and assemble into a viral core.
Capsid Core Formation: The core undergoes Maturation, forming the Capsid Core.
Disassembly: The Capsid Core enters the TARGET CELL, leading to Reverse Transcription and the formation of a Pre-integration complex.
Nuclear Translocation: The Pre-integration complex moves to the NUCLEUS, where Integration occurs.
LEN inhibits these processes by targeting the Capsid Core.

L4329: BEST AVAILABLE COPY
Flowchart illustrating the Study Design Schema:
Screening leads to Cohort Selection visit (between 14 and 30 days after screening).
Cohort 1 (Randomized, blinded to participant, investigator site and Sponsor):
Condition: < 0.5 \log_{10} decline in HIV-1 RNA from Screening and HIV-1 RNA \ge 400 copies/mL.
Subjects (n=24) enter the 14-day Functional Monotherapy Period.
Subjects are randomized (2:1 ratio) to receive either Oral GS-6207 + Failing Regimen or Placebo-to-match + Failing Regimen.
At Day 15, subjects undergo Unblinding and 14-day oral dosing.
Subjects then enter Maintenance Cohort 1A or Cohort 1B Maintenance.
Cohort 1A Maintenance: SC GS-6207 + Optimized Background Regimen (OBR).
Cohort 1B Maintenance: Oral GS-6207 + OBR.
Cohort 2 (Non-randomized, unblinded):
Condition: \ge 0.5 \log_{10} decline in HIV-1 RNA from Screening and/or HIV-1 RNA < 400 copies/mL.
Subjects (n=54) enter the 14-day Oral Lead-in period, receiving Oral GS-6207 + OBR.
Subjects then enter Maintenance Cohort 2, receiving SC GS-6207 + OBR.
The timeline spans from Day 1 to Week 52, including Day 1 SC and Maintenance phases.
